docs.title: cbom-workbench
docs.text:
The live demo

This site is the reading beside a demonstration. The stage plays eight beats recorded from one run of the workbench against the test agency; inside the CBOM opens the document that run produced, entry by entry; the record is that run's ledger, CBOM and score, with their hashes; and page by page shows the running workbench's other screens as they were captured. The tabs at the top, and the title, always lead back.

A cryptography bill of materials, built from evidence and kept on a signed ledger, that carries an organization from not knowing what it runs to changing an algorithm and proving the change landed — with the role of AI in that work measured, not assumed.

By Ken Rollins, Federal Field CTO — Emerging Technologies at Dell. Repository: cbom-workbench; the command is pqch.

A workbench that builds a CBOM from wire, host and code evidence, keeps it current, and uses it to take a mixed estate from Opaque to Agile — verified by re-scan, recorded on a ledger signed with ML-DSA-65. Language models are used where interpretation is needed and nowhere else, and which model does which role was decided by measurement against a floor written before the run.

The inventory is not a report. It is the thing the change was made from and verified against.

docs.title: The clock
docs.text:
Federal policy fixes the dates. The one that shapes this project is the one nobody can plan against yet.

Date What Source 2026-10-22 Each agency's PQC migration plan was due (passed) OMB M-26-15 2026–2027 Discovery phase: inventory, assessment, governance OMB M-26-15 2027-03-19 CISA and NIST publish the minimum elements of a CBOM EO 14412 2030-01-02 TLS 1.3 everywhere OMB M-26-15 2030-12-31 Key establishment post-quantum on prioritized systems EO 14412 2031-12-31 Digital signatures post-quantum on prioritized systems EO 14412

The inventory is required now; what it must contain is published five months later. So the workbench keeps every finding with its evidence on a ledger and treats the CBOM as a projection of that record: when the minimum elements arrive, meeting them is a new projection, not a new scan (note 03).

docs.title: What the demonstration does
docs.text: An eight-service test estate — a benefits portal, a partner API, an inter-agency gateway already post-quantum, a records database and its SFTP drop, a message queue, a case-management application and an administrators' jump host — is scanned, scored against an answer key with decoys in it, and planned from: the CBOM says what depends on what and what comes first. Then it is changed: the central crypto policy moves a listener to hybrid key establishment, the change is rehearsed on a copy, approved by a person, applied, and verified on the wire by a pair of probes that no model takes part in. The machine's time and the wait for a person are reported apart.

Items correct of 30, measured through the lab gateway in three rounds (2026-10-07 to 2026-10-16) across fifteen arms: every model the lab holds, on a desk-side GB10, four L4 GPUs and a second host. One role of six needs a 120B model; the rest run on a 31B model on the L4s at a few seconds a call. The GB10's reasoning slot changed model on 2026-10-19 (Nemotron 3 Super to Nemotron 3.5 Super VL at medium-effort thinking); the one role bound to it was re-measured on the live lane the next day, and the same model's reasoning setting moved its result more than the change of model did (lesson 26). Each step up is a measured row (models and hardware).

docs.title: What it is actually about
docs.text:
• Evidence over inference. Every entry carries the raw tool output it came from, by hash. A model is consulted only where interpretation is needed; rules, scanners and parsers do the rest, and a model never decides whether a change worked.
  • Enabled is not enforced. A listener that offers the hybrid group still serves every client that does not. The verifier is a pair of probes: a hybrid-only client must succeed, and a client offering any classical group must be refused.
  • A record that can be checked by someone else. An append-only ledger, hash-chained, with checkpoints signed by a service that holds the key where nothing else can read it, and timestamps bracketed by the signer's clock.
  • The honest baseline. The workbench is scored beside the open-source scanners run alone, by layer. At the first rung it finds what they find; what it adds is structure, posture and the change.
  • It runs where the inventory belongs. A map of where an organization is weakest, down to the line of code, is not something to send to someone else's cloud. Everything here runs on infrastructure the owner holds, and what each step up in models or hardware changes is measured, or marked not measured.

docs.title: What this deliberately does not claim
docs.text:
• Not that AI solves PQC. It does not. The models here read call sites, classify, and trace a finding to a line; the scanners, rules and probes do the work, and two of six roles went back to rules because no model reached the floor.
  • Not a replacement for commercial discovery platforms. Those are fielded products with sensors across live estates. This is an open exploration of what the CBOM enables once it exists.
  • Not faster than anyone. The numbers shown are coverage, verification and time-to-change, on the hardware and the model they ran on.
  • Not a product. Nothing here is for sale or supported.

Every number on this site is measured, computed or cited, and says which.

docs.title: What this project is
docs.text: cbom-workbench is a personal exploration by Ken Rollins into one question: what does a fully developed cryptography bill of materials let an organization do? Federal policy now requires the inventory. This project builds one from evidence and then puts it to work — prioritizing, detecting change, and carrying out and verifying an algorithm change.

docs.title: What this project is not
docs.text:
• Not an official Dell product. There is nothing to buy.
  • Not a Dell reference architecture. This work has not been produced, endorsed or reviewed through any official Dell channel. Views and findings are the author's own.
  • Not a replacement for commercial discovery platforms. Those are fielded products that observe live estates. This is an open exploration of what the inventory enables.
  • Not a compliance determination. Nothing here certifies that a system meets a federal requirement.
  • Not a vulnerability report. Where public source code is analyzed, the results describe what an inventory reveals.

docs.title: Disclaimer
docs.text: This site and the repository it is built from are a personal exploration, published under the Apache-2.0 licence. They are not an official Dell product, reference architecture or Dell position, and have not been produced, endorsed or reviewed through any official Dell channel. Nothing here is a compliance determination, a security assessment of any named system, or a vulnerability disclosure. Numbers are measurements on the hardware named beside them.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Five layers of the approach and the ledger beside every one; whatever a layer does is an event first. Hardware is named once, as where a run was recorded.

The same work as a pipeline of roles, and who does each:

   SCOUT ─────► INVESTIGATOR ─────► ASSESSOR ─────► MIGRATOR ─────► VERIFIER
 (scanners,      (a model reads      (rules first;    (renders policy;  (paired probes;
  normalizers)    call sites)         a model on       applies only      no model)
                                      conflicts)       what it built)
                                            │
                                   CBOM LEDGER — CycloneDX CBOM + append-only,
                                   hash-chained, signed JSONL event log
Component What it does Holds the Docker socket Scout Runs the scanners through the runner and normalizes their output into one finding schema no Runner The one container on the target network with the Docker socket. Accepts named scan profiles only, refuses any target outside the scope file, applies an approved change id, and keeps its own log of every job and every apply where nothing else can write yes Investigator A model that reads a call site or traces a wire finding to the configuration line behind it, with step and token budgets no Assessor Rules first — quantum-vulnerable or not, key establishment or signature, deadline, queue; a model only where findings conflict no Migrator Renders the central crypto policy into each service's configuration, proposes the change with its diff, rollback and the check that will count, and hands it to the runner once approved no Verifier The paired probes and the witness; a verdict bound to the container and certificate it probed no Signer Signs ledger checkpoints with ML-DSA-65; holds the key on storage nothing else mounts; no network no UI service The one page: the scan button, the CBOM with its evidence, the score, the change. Behind the lab's front door no

docs.title: Who may write what
docs.text:
One process appends to the ledger: the UI service. Every other component returns a result to it, or refuses. What makes an event trustworthy is stated per kind, and so is where that trust stops:

  • Runner events are written from the runner's own job results, and a reader checks each apply, recreate and cited probe against the runner's own log — the job it was asked for, when it ran, against which container, with what raw output.
  • Human events carry who approved and how they were authenticated: the front door's sign-on, believed only on a connection from the front door.
  • Timestamps are the harness's, held within two seconds of the signer's clock on each side of the events a person causes.
  • What remains: whoever controls the UI process could write an approval no person gave. Approvals signed by the approver's own key would close that; they are stated and not built.

docs.title: One deployment, one bundle
docs.text: The workbench runs in one lab: an x86_64 server, inference through a gateway with a scoped key, the test estate beside it on an internal-only bridge. Every model the lab serves — from the server's own GPUs, from a desk-side GB10 and from a second GPU host — is reachable through one inference seam, and a role is given to a model only by measurement. The offline bundle is a feature, not a second target: every image multi-arch and pinned by digest in a local registry, so the whole thing loads on another host with the network cut. What each step up in models or hardware changes is a measured row on the models and hardware page.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text: Three decisions everything else rests on, each with its architecture decision record (ADR) under Decisions: the ledger is the system of record and the CBOM a projection of it (ADR-0001); one deployment in the lab, with the bundle as a feature and every model the lab holds in scope by measurement (ADR-0004, superseding ADR-0002); and the harness changes only an estate it built, handing off a change package anywhere else (ADR-0003). Two more followed: a server is an estate of its own (ADR-0005), and the public copy of this project is a recording, a record and notes, never a facsimile (ADR-0006).

docs.title: Data handling
docs.text: What the workbench keeps, how sensitive it is, where it lives, what mode it is written with, how long it is kept and how it is destroyed. A CBOM is a map of an estate's weakest cryptography: every quantum-vulnerable algorithm, with the host and port it was found on. Treat everything below that carries findings as the agency treats vulnerability information about its own systems; whether that is controlled unclassified information (the CUI Registry's Information Systems Vulnerability Information category) is the agency's decision, not the workbench's.

docs.title: Modes
docs.text:
Everything under var/ is written with the process's umask unless the deployment sets PQCH_VAR_PRIVATE=1 on every service that writes there. Then every file is created 0600 and every directory 0700, and pqch var harden brings what was written before into line:

# compose.yaml or an overlay, on the app, runner and signer services
PQCH_VAR_PRIVATE: "1"
# once, for what is already there
docker compose run --rm app pqch var harden

It is not the default because one shape reads across users: the kit's system runner writes raw output as root and the app reads it as the operator's uid. Turn it on where every writer and reader runs as one uid. The estate's rendered configuration (agency/generated/) is not under var/ and keeps its mode: the estate's own services read it.

docs.title: Marking, retention, roles
docs.text:
Three settings turn the deployment's handling rules into facts the workbench enforces or shows:

  • Marking. PQCH_MARKING (for example CUI) puts a banner on every page the app serves, writes pqch:marking into every document a run writes (the CBOMs, the consumer copy) and adds a marking column to the register. A marking is applied at creation, as 32 CFR 2002.20 asks; the projection itself stays a function of the ledger, and the marking is added where the file is written.
  • Retention. pqch retention apply --days N (or PQCH_RETENTION_DAYS) deletes the raw scanner output and the written documents of every run older than the period and records each deletion as an artefact.destroyed event in a run of kind retention, with the person and the basis. The ledgers stay: they are the record. --dry-run lists what would go.
  • Roles and separation of duties (ADR-0008). PQCH_APPROVER_GROUP names the identity provider's group an approver must be in, read from the front door's groups header (PQCH_GROUPS_HEADER, default X-Forwarded-Groups) on a trusted connection; every approval records the role and groups it rested on. PQCH_SEPARATION_OF_DUTIES=1 makes the runner refuse an apply approved by the person who asked for the change, or approved without the role, and splits the page's approve and apply into two requests; the command line then approves only in a labelled single-operator mode.
  • Rules of engagement. PQCH_REQUIRE_ROE=1 on the runner refuses a scope whose authorization does not name the signed rules-of-engagement document by hash (rules_of_engagement_sha256).
  • Logs for a collector. The ledger of every run is JSON lines already. PQCH_ACCESS_LOG names a file the app appends one line to per request (pqch.access/1): the time, the signed-on name, the path, the status, how long it took, whether it was a download of a ledger, a CBOM, a register or a plan, and the marking. Shipping that file to a collector is the deployment's job.
  • The clock. Every run.started records what the kernel says of the host's clock (clock): synchronized or not, and the error it estimates, read with a call that changes nothing. An unsynchronized clock is recorded, not refused.

docs.title: What leaves the box
docs.text:
• Prompts to a model carry findings with hosts and ports, source lines, service files and CBOM facts. They go only to the inference endpoints in the tier map; on the kit those are engines on the same box, reached over its own bridge.
  • Exports (a server's recording, the public demo) pass through the sanitizer and a leak check that deletes the output on any match.
  • The scans themselves touch only what the scope lists (ADR-0003).
  • Nothing else is sent by the workbench: it loads no asset from a CDN and makes no update check.

docs.title: What the host must provide
docs.text:
• Encryption at rest for the disk that holds var/, the signer's volume and the capture directory (LUKS or the platform's equivalent). The workbench does not encrypt its own files.
  • A time source (NTP or the platform's), since every event and every signature carries the host's clock; the signer refuses a ledger more than two seconds ahead of its own time.

docs.title: Where this stops
docs.text: Retention runs when an operator runs it: nothing is removed on a schedule. Removing a file by hand, outside pqch retention apply, records no event. The access log is a file; sending it to a collector, and an alert on what it holds, are the deployment's. Accessibility was tested by rule and by an automated keyboard pass, not by a person with a screen reader (docs/ACCESSIBILITY.md in the repository).

docs.title: The demonstration
docs.text:
The spine is the crypto-agility maturity model. Each rung is a question the agency can now answer, and each is a screen.

Rung What the agency has What the CBOM answers Passes when Opaque A stale spreadsheet Nothing reliable — (the starting point) Enumerated Scanner output Where is quantum-vulnerable cryptography? Coverage by layer is scored against the key, with decoys not flagged Structured A CBOM with dependencies What depends on it, and how long must the data stay secret? Every discovered link resolves to a ledger event with evidence; supplied links are labelled as supplied Managed Owners, priorities, approvals What first? What is blocked on a supplier? What changed since yesterday? Every key item has an owner, a queue, a blocker state and the rule id that put it there Agile Change as routine If policy changes, how fast can we respond, and did it land? Time-to-change is under the limit and every affected endpoint has a verdict

docs.title: The opening 90 seconds
docs.text:
Inside the opening there is no model call and no engine swap: anything a model produced was produced earlier, is read back from the ledger, and carries its ledger timestamp on screen. Each step is marked.

  1. The spreadsheet. "This is most inventories today." (static)
  2. One button. Targeted scans run against the test estate; the list fills. (live — targeted checks with a per-endpoint time budget; image scans replayed from the ledger)
  3. The list folds into a CBOM. One entry opens: the chain from the wire finding to the file holding the key, the evidence for each link. (replayed)
  4. The priority view. Two queues, and the reason each item sits where it does. (live — rules over OMB M-26-15, quoted)
  5. A policy change is approved. The configuration regenerates, the wire is re-scanned by a hybrid-only and a classical-only probe, and the elapsed time is on screen. (live)
  6. The receipts. Coverage against the answer key, the two baselines beside the workbench, and the ledger entry for the change just made.

docs.title: What is built today
docs.text:
Every step of the opening runs on the eight-service mini-agency, live in the lab; the published copy shows it as a recording on the stage and as screenshots page by page. Measured on the lab's x86_64 server:

A scan of the estate 25 runner jobs; 206 s with every image scanned, about 100 s with image scans replayed; wire 38 of 40 keyed items found, images 20 of 20, no decoy flagged, the posture of all 9 listeners correct The scanners run alone the same 38 on the wire, 14 of 20 in images with both image decoys flagged, no posture The queues 7 of 8 services prioritized by the memo's criteria; 14 migration items open, 7 of them blocked on their supplier A trace to the cause one per listener on the 120B reasoning engine, a median of 27.6 s, eight of nine agreeing with the answer key and the ninth correcting it A policy change, rendered by rule and verified twice on the wire 55.6 s from the policy event to the last verdict on the four-service slice A change drafted by a model and rehearsed on a copy before approval the records database: drafted from its CBOM entries in about 5 s a reply, rehearsed enforced in 33 to 37 s

The source of each number is the facts table in the repository's BRIEF.md, which names the run.

docs.title: The walkthrough
docs.text: After the opening, the same path at full depth and live: a full scan, an investigator trace run from cold on the larger model with its ledger event and measured time, a policy change that moves from enabled-not-enforced to enforced through a compatibility matrix, a change event arriving in Watch mode, and the table of which roles need which model and what each step up in models or hardware was measured to change. The waits are part of the demonstration, labelled with the engine and the machine that produced them. Built so far: the full scan, the investigator's trace, watch mode, and changes drafted by a model and rehearsed on a copy; the compatibility matrix and the three applies of the build plan's M3 are not.

docs.title: The offline bundle
docs.text: A local registry carrying every image by digest for both architectures, the registry's own image as a tarball, and a checksum file whose own hash is carried separately. docker save and docker load do not preserve digest references, which is why the registry is there (lesson 03); the loader hashes every blob against its name before serving anything (lesson 15). Still to be shown: a load on a second host with the cable out and an empty image store.

docs.title: Evidence first, a model only where interpretation is needed
docs.text:
Three layers of evidence feed one inventory:

Layer Tools What they see Wire testssl.sh, ssh-audit, OpenSSL probes; Zeek beside a client What a listener accepts: protocol versions, key-exchange groups, RSA key transport, the served certificate; what a client offers Host cbomkit-theia on container images Certificates, keys and configuration files in the image Code CBOMkit's source scanners (Java, Python, Go); an Opengrep rule pack for Ruby Call sites

Each tool's output is normalized into one finding schema and appended to the ledger with the raw output's hash. Rules link findings across layers — the certificate served on the wire to the file in the image that holds it — and state a posture per listener. A model is called for the things that need reading: a call site, an unfamiliar spelling, a conflict between findings. Which of those roles needs the larger of the two models is decided by measurement (spike S3), not assumption.

docs.title: Enabled is not enforced
docs.text:
Adding the hybrid group to a server changes nothing for a client that does not offer it. A scanner that offers the hybrid group sees it negotiated and reports success; the server's posture toward every other client is unchanged. So the verifier runs a pair:

Hybrid-only client Classical-only client Status accepted refused enforced accepted accepted enabled-not-enforced — a real state, not a pass refused — not-landed

The classical-only probe offers every classical group a client could offer, not the two the server used to be configured with: a listener set to the hybrid group and P-384 passed a probe that refused only X25519 and P-256 (lesson 01). A second tool of a different kind enumerates what the listener accepts and can only lower the verdict. Each probe records the container it reached, and the check is repeated after the service is recreated. No model takes part. Note 08 has the full mechanism.

docs.title: The ledger is the system of record
docs.text: Every finding, link, approval, applied change and verdict is an event: hash-chained to the one before, naming its actor, its inputs and its evidence. The CBOM is a projection of the ledger and can be deleted and rebuilt. A separate signer service checkpoints the chain with ML-DSA-65, keeps its own record of what it signed, and puts its own time in each signature, so that events cannot be cut from the end, rewritten behind a checkpoint, or stamped with a time the signer did not see. The runner — the only component that can touch the estate — applies a change only after reading the ledger itself and finding the approval under a signature. Note 12 describes the record and what was tried against it.

docs.title: Scored against an answer key, beside the scanners run alone
docs.text: The test estate is built with every weakness planted, so the answer key is exact: items that are present, decoys that look like findings and are not, items that are real and out of reach, and items that were typed in rather than discovered. The workbench is scored by layer beside two baselines: CBOMkit alone, and all the scanners run alone with no harness. At the first rung the workbench finds exactly what the scanners find; what it adds is the link from a wire finding to the file holding the key, the judgement that a certificate sitting in an image is not served, and a stated posture per listener (note 15).

docs.title: The workbench, page by page
docs.text: The published copy of this project is a recording, a record and these notes (ADR-0006): the stage plays eight beats recorded from one run, inside the CBOM opens that run's document, and the record holds its ledger, CBOM and score. The running workbench has more screens than those. They are shown here as they were captured from the same recorded runs, rather than copied as pages whose buttons do nothing. Each is one screen as a reader in the lab sees it; what lies below the fold is described under the picture.

docs.title: The overview
docs.text: NIST CSWP 39's picture of crypto agility, with the workbench's own counts in each box, read from the ledgers when the page is shown. Each box opens to the page behind it. Above the drawing: a switch between the test agency and the servers read whole, a link to the plan, and the story of one weakness followed from the scan that found it to the scan that shows it gone, step by step around the loop.

docs.title: The test agency
docs.text: The eight services the demonstration scans, read from the estate's own compose files and configuration: a benefits portal, a partner API, an inter-agency gateway already post-quantum, a records database and its SFTP drop, a message queue, a case-management application and an administrators' jump host. For each, what was planted in it and where the answer key expects it to be found. This is the estate the record's score is measured against.

docs.title: The walkthrough
docs.text: Top to bottom, the path from a stale spreadsheet to a plan: the clock, the sheet, the scan button and its progress, the list that folds into a CBOM, one entry opened to its evidence, the queues from OMB M-26-15 with the memo quoted beside each, and the receipts against the answer key with the two baselines beside the workbench. In the lab the scan runs when the button is pressed; the stage plays the same path as a recording.

docs.title: The plan
docs.text: What the CBOM says depends on what, what comes first and in what order, computed by rules from the scan every time the page is shown. Left, the spreadsheet planned from: independent rows, nothing behind two of them. Right, the plan from the CBOM: steps tied to the entries they move, the dependencies that tie services together, what must wait. Below, the lanes: one per service, the certificate authority and the estate-wide work in lanes of their own, a line for each dependency. A step opens to why it is there and the fields it was computed from; a what-if frees what waited on an assumed step.

docs.title: Change packages
docs.text: For each item that no configuration change can move, because the software lists no post-quantum algorithm for that function, a package: the evidence from the capability snapshot, the item's queue and deadline, and what would unblock it. These are the items that start now, since replacement takes procurement time.

docs.title: Imports
docs.text: Bring your own scanner: any tool's CycloneDX CBOM, imported as evidence on a run of its own, its assets named by the workbench's normalizers, and scored against the same answer key by layer, so a vendor's inventory and the workbench's can be compared on the same estate.

docs.title: Resolve
docs.text: A change from proposal to verdict: the policy event, the configuration rendered from it, the rehearsal on a copy of the service, the approval by a person signed on to the workbench, the apply, and the verifier's two probes, a hybrid-only client that must succeed and a classical-only client that must be refused. Every step is a ledger event; no model takes part in the verdict.

docs.title: Not shown
docs.text: Hosts, the servers read whole below their operating system, and the lab's own network: both carry the owner's hardware identifiers and addresses and stay with the deployment (note 20 describes the first in general form).

docs.title: The record
docs.text:
What the stage shows is a recording of one run; this page is what that run produced, so the one can be checked against the other. Run 01M6Z41DJB5911EF1Y65K2FBTY, started 2026-11-09 03:01:14 UTC on xr7620 (x86_64); every event on the ledger is chained to the one before it and the chain is signed (how the record is kept).

Against the answer key, by layer: on the wire 35 of 35 keyed items present were found (2 out of reach, 0 false positives); in the images 20 of 20 (0 false positives); the posture of 9 of 9 listeners correct. The baselines beside it are in score.json.

Document What it is Bytes SHA-256 ledger.jsonl the ledger: every event of the run, hash-chained, with its signed checkpoint 1,013,387 76570db472c6eb89e1854935c2cf8b0cc21f56c1832ecd4cd8ae7fffe1203fca workbench.cdx.json the CBOM the workbench projects from the ledger (CycloneDX 1.6) 635,290 454e9dbe05c8bf50d05265bdd10f0aec3f74850c6a2f6dade763dd6579182e9f baseline-cbomkit.cdx.json the baseline: CBOMkit alone, on the same estate 140,283 2eea733c4353d1f36d5d57e45eacd7abbf245165816a38ca54cf90b73dedb00a baseline-scanners.cdx.json the baseline: the open-source scanners alone, merged with no harness 231,450 2f80ce8c14941b204fe4c55a963b03b55d891376f4ba9d1affda2da15d7f5cbf score.json the score against the answer key, by layer, with the decoys 10,832 0f98e814b8005524a107911a0ff1f7650b76f00d521d498c466e94767a31f3a4 projection/agency-inventory.csv an agency inventory projected from the same ledger 19,122 c063e565120d905e807193f15bf70c4d57d55ec048449f2192ad3bee9ffef4b5

To check a document: download it, take its SHA-256, and compare. To check the ledger's chain and its checkpoint, the verifier is in the repository (pqch ledger verify --signed --pub ledger.pub ledger.jsonl, with the public key the stage's run carries beside its ledger). The CBOM is a projection: rebuilding it from the ledger gives the same document, byte for byte.

docs.title: Model role cards
docs.text: Every place a language model takes part in the workbench, one card each: what the role decides, what data it sees, the floor written before it was measured, what was measured on which model and hardware, what checks its output, and what happens when no model answers. Bindings are those of kit/inference.yaml; a deployment's own config may bind differently, and only by measurement.

docs.title: How models are used here, in one paragraph
docs.text: Models inform; rules and people decide. No model decides whether a change worked: that is a re-scan, a certificate parse or a pair of probes. No model output enters the inventory unlabelled: the one model-set fact in the CBOM (a code line's in-use) carries the model, engine and hardware that set it. Every call is on the ledger with its model, tier, hardware and, where the endpoint says, the engine that served it. Inference runs on the deployment's own hardware through one seam, which can refuse a model whose declared origin is not on an allowlist. A role moves to a model only when a model reaches a floor written before the run.

docs.title: call-site-read (spike S3 R1)
docs.text: Decides Whether a line a rule flagged in source code is a live cryptographic use, and its family and function. Sees The flagged line and its surrounding lines from a repository read at a pinned commit; nothing is run. Output The code finding's in-use, carried in the CBOM with pqch:in-use-by (model, engine, hardware) and pqch:in-use-agreement. What gates it Three calls per line, the majority kept, every call on the ledger; no rule acts on it, and the CBOM marks it as a model's. Floor 27 of 30, 1 harmful allowed Bound in this config tier fast, reasoning on When no model answers The line's in-use stays unknown and is shown so; nothing else waits on it. docs.text: Decides The standard name of an algorithm spelling the name table does not hold. Sees The tool, the field and the spelling. Output A fallback name, shown as unconfirmed. What gates it The name table decides every spelling it holds; a model's name is a labelled fallback. Floor 28 of 30, 0 harmful allowed Bound in this config tier deliberate, reasoning on When no model answers No pipeline step calls the role today: the name table decides every name the CBOM carries. Output An assessment recorded with used_by_rules false and whether it agrees with the policy data. What gates it The policy pack's table decides vulnerability; the model's answer is a cross-check only. docs.text: Decides Which layer's evidence is in force when the wire, the host and the configuration disagree, in plain words. Sees The conflicting findings for one asset. Output An explanation beside the rule's resolution, recorded with whether it agrees. What gates it A rule resolves every conflict (conflict/resolve/1); the model only explains, and is not used by any rule. Floor 24 of 30, 2 harmful allowed Bound in this config not bound: no model is called When no model answers The rule's resolution is shown alone. docs.text: Decides The configuration line that causes a listener's finding, or that a default applies. Sees The finding, the service's configuration files, and what it greps and reads in them within a step and token budget. Output A trace on the ledger, marked as the model's claim, scored against the answer key where there is one. What gates it Settles nothing by itself: a change built on it is rehearsed and verified by paired probes before it counts. docs.text: Decides A draft configuration change for a service: the edits, or that it is blocked on a supplier or a protocol. Sees The service's findings, the intent, and its configuration files (up to 400 lines each). Output A proposal on the ledger marked as drafted by a model. What gates it Rehearsed on a twin, approved by a person, applied by the runner and verified by paired probes; a model never judges whether it worked. docs.title: Pointing it at your own network
docs.text:
The demo runs against the mini-agency, a test estate built for it with every weakness planted. The same workbench can look at a real network — it was built and measured that way on the author's own lab — but it is not packaged for that. This page says what is involved, step by step, and what you will have to wire up yourself. Expect an afternoon for the targeted scan and a day for passive capture, for someone comfortable with Docker networking and a switch's mirror port.

Only a network you are authorized to scan

Scan only a network you own or have written permission to test. The workbench records that authorization as the first event of every run and refuses an external scan without it, but the permission is yours to obtain. It never changes anything on a network it did not build: an external estate gets findings and a plan, never an applied change.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
• Every listed listener asked directly (testssl.sh for TLS, ssh-audit for SSH): every key-exchange group, suite and protocol version it accepts, its certificate, its posture — classical, mixed or post-quantum.
  • Optionally, everything on the wire seen passively (Zeek on a mirror port): what every client offers and what every server chooses in real handshakes, by VLAN, with the capture's loss beside every count. Nothing is sent.
  • One CBOM of the network merging both, an entry per asset with both layers' evidence; the overview on NIST's crypto-agility plan; and a plan of who holds whom back — servers refusing what their clients offer, clients that can never offer a hybrid group, and the share of today's handshakes each change would refuse.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Linux host with Docker and Docker Compose, Python 3.12 and uv, on a network that can reach the listeners you will scan.
  • For passive capture: a switch that can mirror (SPAN) a port or VLAN, and a spare network interface on the host to receive it.
  • No language model: the external path is scanners and rules only. (Models help with the code layer and with drafting changes, neither of which applies here.)

docs.title: 1. Run the workbench as for the demo
docs.text:
The stack expects the mini-agency beside it, so bring that up first; it also proves the scanners, the signer and the ledger on your host before anything touches your network. From the repository root:

uv sync
uv run pqch scanners pull                                   # every scanner image, by its pinned digest
docker build -t pqch-agency/pki:m1 agency/pki               # the test estate's internal CA
uv run pqch policy render                                   # the portal's TLS settings, once
docker compose -f agency/compose.yaml up -d --build         # the mini-agency
uv run pqch scope generate agency/compose.yaml --out var/scope/scope.json
PQCH_AGENCY_DIR=$PWD/agency docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.local.yaml up -d --build

The base compose.yaml gives the web app no network at all, deliberately; a small overlay of your own publishes it on the host only:

# compose.local.yaml
services:
  app:
    network_mode: !reset null
    ports: ["127.0.0.1:8080:8080"]

Open http://127.0.0.1:8080/, run a scan from the walkthrough, and check the overview and the plan fill in. agency/README.md has the details of the test estate.

Not yet rehearsed on a clean machine

This sequence is the one the author's deployment uses, written out; it has not been run from an empty host by someone else. If a step fails, the error usually names the missing setting.

docs.title: 2. Write the scope
docs.text:
The scope is the list of what may be touched. It lives with your deployment, never in the repository. A minimal one, with two listeners:

{
  "schema": "pqch.scope/1",
  "id": "01JABCDEFGHJKMNPQRSTVWXYZ0",
  "estate": "external",
  "owned": false,
  "authorized_by": "Your Name, network owner, 2026-11-01: targeted TLS and SSH checks of the listeners listed here",
  "endpoints": [
    {"host": "192.0.2.10", "port": 443, "transport": "tcp", "protocol": "tls", "sni": "intranet.example.org"},
    {"host": "192.0.2.20", "port": 22, "transport": "tcp", "protocol": "ssh"}
  ],
  "images": [],
  "sources": [],
  "reach": {"kind": "local"}
}
  • id is a ULID: uv run python -c "from pqch.common import ulid; print(ulid())".
  • protocol is tls, ssh or postgres (TLS after PostgreSQL's upgrade). A listener with a server name gets sni.
  • authorized_by is a sentence, in your words: who authorized what, and when.
  • To find listeners you did not know about, run passive capture first (step 5): its page lists every server that spoke, and you add the ones you are permitted to probe.

The schema with every field is in the interfaces specification.

docs.title: 3. Give a second runner a leg on your network
docs.text:
The demo's runner sits on the mini-agency's internal network and is bound to its scope. A second runner, with your scope, needs an address on the network it will scan. A Compose overlay beside compose.yaml — kept with your deployment, not in the repository — adds it. With a macvlan on a VLAN interface, for example:

docker network create -d macvlan -o parent=eth0.100 \
  --subnet 192.0.2.0/24 --gateway 192.0.2.1 --ip-range 192.0.2.240/28 pqch_ext

# compose.ext.yaml — docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.local.yaml -f compose.ext.yaml up -d
services:
  app:
    volumes:
      - ext-runner-sock:/run/pqch-lab:ro        # where `pqch scan-external` looks by default
  runner-ext:
    image: pqch/harness:m0
    restart: unless-stopped
    user: "${PQCH_UID:-1000}:${PQCH_GID:-1000}"
    command: ["uvicorn", "pqch.runner.service:app", "--uds", "/run/pqch-lab/runner.sock", "--log-level", "warning"]
    group_add: ["${DOCKER_GID:-999}"]
    environment:
      PQCH_SCOPE: /etc/pqch/scope.json
      PQCH_RAW: /var/pqch/raw
      PQCH_TARGET_NETWORK: pqch_ext                # scanners are started on this network
      PQCH_RUNS: /var/pqch/runs
      PQCH_RUNNER_LOG: /var/pqch-runner
      PQCH_SIGNER_SOCKET: /run/pqch-signer/signer.sock
      PQCH_AGENCY_DIR: ${PQCH_AGENCY_DIR}
      HOME: /tmp
    volumes:
      - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock
      - /path/to/your/scope.json:/etc/pqch/scope.json:ro
      - ${PQCH_VAR}/raw:/var/pqch/raw
      - ${PQCH_VAR}/runs:/var/pqch/runs:ro
      - ext-runner-sock:/run/pqch-lab
      - signer-sock:/run/pqch-signer:ro
      - ext-runner-log:/var/pqch-runner
      - ${PQCH_AGENCY_DIR}:${PQCH_AGENCY_DIR}:ro
    networks: [pqch_ext]
volumes:
  ext-runner-sock:
  ext-runner-log:
networks:
  pqch_ext:
    external: true
  • Size the address range to the parallelism: each scanner takes an address for its run, and eight at once need more than a /29 (lesson 25).
  • The runner only ever starts the scanners its profiles name, against the endpoints the scope lists; anything else is refused before it starts.

docs.title: 4. Scan
docs.text:
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.local.yaml -f compose.ext.yaml exec -T app pqch scan-external

Each listener gets one job; the run is a ledger of its own, signed, and the page's The lab tab, the CBOM page's second estate and the plan's second estate read from it.

docs.title: 5. Optionally, capture passively
docs.text:
1. Mirror the traffic you want to see to a spare port on the host — the switch's own configuration is specific to the switch. A trunk carries every VLAN; mirror both directions.
  2. Give the receiving interface no address, set it promiscuous, and turn generic receive offload off (ethtool -K <iface> gro off): with it on, merged segments are counted as loss and the loss figure reads many times too high.
  3. Add the capture point to the scope: "captures": [{"interface": "<iface>", "host": "<this host>", "vlans": [10, 20], "mirror": "switch port 1/2/1, both ways"}].
  4. Run Zeek from the repository root, with the interface and a log directory set:
PQCH_CAPTURE_IFACE=<iface> PQCH_CAPTURE_DIR=/path/to/capture-logs \
  docker compose --project-directory . -f capture/compose.yaml up -d
  1. Ingest the rotated logs into a capture run, daily for instance, and prune what is ingested:
PQCH_VAR=/path/to/var uv run pqch capture ingest --scope /path/to/scope.json --capture-dir /path/to/capture-logs
PQCH_VAR=/path/to/var uv run pqch capture prune --capture-dir /path/to/capture-logs

What the capture can and cannot see is in note 05. Capture logs hold addresses, names and certificates of a real network: keep them, and the var/ directory, out of any repository.

docs.title: What does not carry over
docs.text:
• The wording. The pages call the second estate "a real network" and "the owner's lab"; there is one such estate, not several.
  • Ranking. The mini-agency's plan is ranked by the owner's facts (mission, how long the data must stay secret, impact). There is no such file for an external estate yet, so its plan orders by who holds whom back and by use, not by mission.
  • Images and code. The external path reads the wire. Host and code evidence for your systems would need their own scope entries and their own authorization.
  • Changes. None are applied to an estate the workbench did not build. A change package for an external estate is planned, not built.
  • Testing. The path has been run on one network, the author's. Yours will find something it did not.

Questions and improvements are welcome as issues on the repository.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
An ADR is an architecture decision record: one page per decision that everything else rests on, with the context it was made in, the decision itself, what it costs, and the alternatives rejected. Each is the file in the repository's docs/adr/, unchanged, numbered in the order the decisions were made. A superseded record stays, marked, so the reasoning that was replaced can still be read.

  1. 01 The ledger is the system of record; the CBOM is built from it (2026-10-01 — Accepted)
  2. 02 Two targets, one codebase (2026-10-01 — Superseded by ADR-0004 on 2026-10-08)
  3. 03 Deployment shapes — where the harness runs and where the estate lives (2026-10-03 — Accepted)
  4. 04 One deployment, in the lab; the bundle is a feature, not a target (2026-10-08 — Accepted)
  5. 05 A server is an estate — its listeners, its files, its firmware and its controller, recorded and replayable (2026-11-04 — Accepted)
  6. 06 The public site is a recording, a record and notes, never a facsimile of the running workbench (2026-11-08 — Accepted)
  7. 07 Where CycloneDX 1.6 has no field, write the fact twice: under the workbench's name and under the name the consumers read (2026-11-09 — Accepted)
  8. 08 Who may act, and how the ledger shows it (2026-11-09 — Accepted)

docs.title: ADR-0001: The ledger is the system of record; the CBOM is built from it
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-01
  • Amended: 2026-10-03 — decisions 3 and 5 made precise after design review (docs/fable-review/, F-03, F-04, F-19)
  • Deciders: Ken Rollins

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The workbench has several actors — scanners, a code investigator, a rules engine, a migrator, a human approver — all contributing to one inventory. A federal reader will ask of any entry: where did this come from, who or what decided it, and how do you know the change landed. A CBOM file alone records the state, not the reasons.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. An append-only JSONL event log is the system of record. Every finding, classification, decision, approval, model swap and verifier verdict is one event with an id, a timestamp, an actor, its inputs by reference, and its evidence.
  2. Each event carries the hash of the previous event. Altering any record breaks the chain.
  3. Checkpoints are signed with ML-DSA. A post-quantum migration tool whose own audit trail is quantum-vulnerable would be inconsistent. A checkpoint is written on every approval, on every verifier verdict, and at close. The public key and the latest checkpoint hash are shown in the UI, so a reader can record them outside the system. The signature detects alteration by anyone without the checkpoint key; it does not defend against the operator who holds it, and the UI says so.
  4. The CycloneDX CBOM is a projection. It is rebuilt from the ledger and never edited directly. Fields the standard does not define (owner, approval state, deadline, evidence references) live in the ledger and are mapped into CycloneDX properties.
  5. Verification is never a model's judgment. A change is recorded as verified only by a verifier event: a wire re-scan, a certificate parse, or a compatibility run.
  6. A wire verdict is a pair of probes. A client offering only the new algorithm must succeed, and a client offering only the old one must be refused. Both hold: enforced. Only the first: enabled-not-enforced — recorded as its own state, never as a pass.
  7. A verdict is bound to what was scanned. The event records the target address, container id, image digest, served certificate fingerprint, scanner image digest, scan start and end times, and the hash of the raw output. The scan must start after the apply event; a failed or timed-out scan produces no verdict.
  8. A verdict is repeated after the service is recreated, and confirmed by a second witness of a different kind.
  9. A finding class with no verifier is recorded as such, and counted in the receipts.
  10. Nothing is applied without an approval event.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• CBOM file as the source of truth. Simple, but it loses provenance and makes change detection a diff of two snapshots rather than a stream.
  • A database as the record. Queryable, but not portable to the standalone target as easily, and not tamper-evident without extra machinery. SQLite is used as an index over the ledger, never as the record.
  • Framework-native tracing only. Useful for debugging; not an evidentiary record and not in a format an agency already recognizes.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Watch mode falls out for free: new events are the deltas.
  • Any screen can show "why" by following references back through the ledger.
  • The event schema is a public interface and must be versioned from the first commit.
  • The official minimum elements for a CBOM are still being defined; the mapping layer between ledger and CBOM is where that change is absorbed.

docs.title: ADR-0002: Two targets, one codebase
docs.text:
• Status: Superseded by ADR-0004 on 2026-10-08. The one-GB10 target was withdrawn; decisions 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9 and 11 survive in ADR-0004, the rest are retired. Kept for the record of why the design looked as it did.
  • Date: 2026-10-01
  • Amended: 2026-10-03 — the GB10 is a stated subset of the lab, not its equal; the runner added; memory bounds made precise (docs/fable-review/, F-08, F-11, F-15, F-16, F-20)
  • Deciders: Ken Rollins

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The workbench is developed in a lab with an x86_64 host, a model gateway backed by more than one machine, and shared services. It must also run as a standalone demonstration on a single arm64 Dell Pro Max GB10 with no internet at runtime and whatever models that machine carries. The demonstration has two jobs: to show the full path working on one box, and to show honestly where one box stops and what more hardware changes.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. The lab is the superset; one GB10 runs a stated subset. The subset is the full path from Opaque to Agile, offline, on one box, and it must stand on its own. Anything outside it is listed in the BRIEF's "what one GB10 does" table with the reason, the measurement, and what more hardware changes. A feature that works only in the lab and is not in that table is a defect.
  2. One inference seam. Code asks for a tier — fast, deliberate, embed. A config file maps tiers to an OpenAI-compatible base URL, key and model id. Profiles: lab and standalone.
  3. Engines take turns on the standalone target. The fast engine is the default. Work for the deliberate engine is queued in the ledger and drained in batches; a residency controller starts and stops engines and records each swap with its duration. The controller is not built here: the harness speaks a three-call contract — load, unload, status — to an existing engine manager. The lab's own vLLM orchestrator already offers those calls and is the first choice; an NVIDIA-supplied manager is used instead if spike S6 finds one that fits better. The swap is shown, not hidden: one GB10 can do this work, with waits that more capable hardware removes. Which roles go to the deliberate engine is decided by the role bake-off (spike S3, spikes/s3/) against a threshold written before it runs.
  4. No shared services. State is the ledger plus SQLite on local disk.
  5. Multi-arch, digest-pinned images for everything in the subset. amd64 and arm64 for every container, including scanners and every mini-agency service the GB10 hosts. An image with no arm64 build is lab-only and is listed.
  6. Containers, not virtual machines, for all targets.
  7. Offline by construction. Policy packs and reference documents are local files. UI assets are vendored. A bundle script produces everything needed to load, and to rebuild, the demonstration from a disk: images, a local registry, Python dependencies, models, repositories. Internet may be used at build time; never at run time.
  8. Explicit memory bounds. Each engine is bounded by its serving flags (memory fraction, context length), because on unified memory a container limit does not reliably cap an engine's allocations. Each container is bounded by a cgroup limit. The budget — each engine, the workload, the twin, the scanners, a reserve for page cache — is in the BRIEF and sums to less than the machine.
  9. A runner holds the Docker socket. It sits on the target networks, has no public leg, and accepts a fixed set of jobs. The service that serves the UI never holds the socket, on either target.
  10. Compose profiles select the target; application code does not branch on it.
  11. Numbers carry their hardware. A timing is labelled with the machine it was measured on. The lab's fast tier does not run on a GB10, so no gateway timing is presented as a standalone number.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Develop in the lab, port later. Porting late is where architecture assumptions surface. Checking the subset at every milestone is cheaper.
  • Require everything to run on one GB10. It forces either cutting depth the lab can show, or claiming more for one box than it does. A stated subset keeps both the depth and the honesty.
  • Both engines resident. On a 128 GB unified-memory machine the two engines leave too little for the workload and fail quietly under pressure. This is shown as what a second GB10 buys.
  • Single small model throughout. Simplest; adopted for any role where the role bake-off (spike S3, spikes/s3/) shows it is sufficient. The seam makes this a config change.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Every milestone's done-criteria include an arm64 and offline check of the subset.
  • The "what one GB10 does" table is a deliverable, filled by measurement.
  • The escalation queue is part of the core design, not an optimization.
  • With a second GB10, queuing is switched off and both engines stay resident — the same code, a different profile.

docs.title: ADR-0003: Deployment shapes — where the harness runs and where the estate lives
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-03
  • Amended: 2026-10-08 by ADR-0004 — the harness-placement value gb10 becomes bundle: the same build loaded from the offline bundle on a host the operator chooses. The demo-box uses below read as bundle uses; the estate axis, the scope file, the change package and the line between showing a change and making one are unchanged.
  • Deciders: Ken Rollins
  • Builds on: ADR-0002, now ADR-0004

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The project has four uses, and they pull in different directions:

  • A lab build on the xr7620 that carries every feature and remains the place to demonstrate the work after the workshop. In the lab, the GB10 serves inference only.
  • A demo box: one GB10 that shows the full path on its own files, with nothing else attached. This is what the workshop builds.
  • The same demo box scanning an estate that lives on a second machine, such as a laptop on a direct cable.
  • A kit: a public repository from which someone else can stand up the same thing on their own GB10, as a personal open-source research project and not a Dell product.

Treated as four products, this is four things to build and keep working. Treated as two independent choices, it is one codebase with two seams.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Two axes, not four products.
Axis Values Harness placement — where the service, scanners and inference run lab (xr7620, inference through the gateway) · gb10 (everything on one box, engines taking turns) Estate placement — where the thing being inventoried lives colocated (the mini-agency in containers beside the harness) · remote (the mini-agency on a second host over a private link) · external (a network the operator names)
  1. The four uses are points on those axes.
Use Harness Estate Notes Lab lab colocated Every feature. The standing demonstration venue. Demo box gb10 colocated The workshop build, and the fallback for every other GB10 use. Must stand alone. Demo box with a second machine gb10 remote The estate is on the laptop; the twin stays on the GB10, so rehearsal happens off the estate. Hosts x86-only legacy images. Kit gb10 colocated out of the box; external when the operator supplies a scope Published. Ships pointed at the bundled mini-agency.

  1. The estate seam is a scope file. The harness never discovers what to scan. It reads a scope: the hosts or address ranges, the ports, how each host is reached for host and image evidence, and where its source and configuration are. For colocated and remote, the scope is generated from the mini-agency's compose file. For external, the operator writes it. The runner refuses any target not in the scope.

  2. Scope is authorization, and it is on the ledger. The first event of any run is the scope with its hash. For an external estate the operator also records who authorized the scan. The author's own use — lab and demo — still scans only networks built for the purpose.

  3. The runner reaches a remote estate through one mechanism: a Docker context over SSH on a private link with fixed addresses. No agent is installed on the estate.

  4. The demo box is the kit. There is one GB10 build. The kit is that build as published: the repository, the specification, the evaluation kit, and a bundle script. The bundle script fetches images and model weights from their publishers on the operator's own connection; the repository redistributes neither.

  5. The kit states when it was last verified on a GB10, with the date and the evaluation score from that run. After the workshop there may be no GB10 to test on; arm64 emulation in the lab is a smoke test, not a verification, and the kit says so.

  6. Every published surface carries the disclaimer: a personal research project, open source, not a Dell product, reference architecture or supported offering.

docs.title: The line between showing a change and making one
docs.text:
1. The harness changes only estates it built. On the mini-agency and its twin it runs the full loop: propose, rehearse, approve, apply, verify.
  2. On any other estate it hands off and then verifies. It produces a change package: the configuration diff, the rollback, the compatibility matrix, and the exact test that will count as verified. Where the operator has supplied images and configuration, the change is rehearsed in a twin first and the package carries the rehearsal's verifier verdicts. Where they have not, the package is still produced and is labelled not rehearsed. The operator makes the change through their own process; the harness sees it arrive as a change event, re-scans, and issues the verdict.
  3. Enforced by construction. The runner's apply job acts only on containers it created itself. There is no setting that extends it. The repository is public and open source; someone who wants more can change the code, and that is their decision to make and to own.
  4. Evidence for an external scope: wire always; images and source where the operator points at them; credentialed host inspection later.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• A separate kit repository. Two codebases drift. The kit is a published view of the one build.
  • Lab only, with the GB10 as a slide. Leaves the workshop with nothing running on the box, and the claim about one machine untested.
  • GB10 only. Leaves no way to demonstrate the work once the workshop machine is returned.
  • An agent on the estate for host evidence. More capable, and one more thing to install on a system that belongs to someone else.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The scope file and the runner's refusal of out-of-scope targets are built in the first slice, not added for the kit.
  • colocated on the GB10 is the configuration every milestone checks; remote and external are the same code with a different scope.
  • The lab build must not depend on anything the GB10 build lacks without that feature being listed in the BRIEF's "what one GB10 does" table.
  • The published repository needs an operator's guide: prerequisites, the bundle step, the scope file, and what the kit does not do.

docs.title: ADR-0004: One deployment, in the lab; the bundle is a feature, not a target
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-08
  • Deciders: Ken Rollins
  • Supersedes: ADR-0002 (two targets, one codebase)
  • Amends: ADR-0003 (deployment shapes) — the harness-placement axis

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
ADR-0002 made one arm64 Dell Pro Max GB10 a second target: a stated subset of the lab build had to run on that one box, offline, with two inference engines taking turns in its unified memory, and the design carried that cost everywhere — a memory budget, an escalation queue, an engine-swap controller, a hardware table whose first column was "on one GB10".

On 2026-10-08 the requirement that something run on one GB10 alone was withdrawn. The lab stays the venue. Nothing the lab holds is off limits: the models served from the xr7620's GPUs, the models the lab GB10 serves through its orchestrator, and what ollama on a desktop GPU host can run are all in scope for the model roles. What the project is about has also come into focus: the cryptography bill of materials (CBOM) and what language models, measured role by role, add to building and using one — not an agent harness sized to a desk-side box. The project is titled cbom-workbench; the import package and the command are pqch.

Two things from ADR-0002 remain true and are kept: the inventory belongs on infrastructure the organization holds, and every number carries the hardware and the model it was measured on.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. One deployment: the lab. The harness runs on the xr7620, inference through the lab gateway, the mini-agency beside it. There is no second target to keep in step at every milestone, and no "subset" table.
  2. The bundle is a feature. The offline bundle — images by digest in a local registry, dependencies, repositories, reference documents, the built site — stays, because it demonstrates that the whole thing moves on a disk and starts with no network. It is rehearsed by loading it on a second lab host with the network cut. It is not a separate build, and nothing in the application depends on which host it runs on.
  3. Every model the lab holds is in scope, through the one inference seam. Which model does which role is decided by measurement against a floor written before the run (spike S3, lesson 21), never by assumption and never by a model name in code. Adding an engine is a line in the tier map.
  4. What more brings is a measured table. Each step up — a larger model, a second engine resident, more GPUs — is recorded as a row in the BRIEF's "what more models and hardware bring" table with the measurement, the hardware and the model, or marked not measured. The journal records what each step changed for this workload. The table is a deliverable; the journal is where the reasoning lives.
  5. Multi-arch, digest-pinned images; no CDN assets; no shared services; state in files. Kept, because they are what makes the bundle honest and the deployment portable, not because of any one machine.
  6. The runner holds the Docker socket; the UI service never does. Kept from ADR-0002, decision 9.
  7. Numbers carry their hardware and their model. Kept from ADR-0002, decision 11, widened: a model timing names the engine, the serving settings and the machine.

Retired with ADR-0002: the memory budget on one GB10; engines taking turns and the escalation queue as a core design element; the residency controller; compose profiles that select a target; the "what one GB10 does" table; spike S6 and the standalone parts of milestone M4.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Keep the GB10 subset as an optional profile. Every milestone would still be checked against a box no longer required, and the honest table would keep reporting on hardware the project does not run on. Dropped; the bundle keeps the one property that mattered, portability.
  • Drop the bundle too. It is already built and measured, it is the proof that nothing depends on the lab's shared services, and a kit without it cannot be stood up offline. Kept.
  • Rename the repository now. A rename mid-build breaks the deployment's paths, the bundle's image names and every link in the journal. The page and the site carry the new name now; the repository is renamed once, at the public export.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The BRIEF's claim loses its "stated subset on one GB10" clause and gains the measured role of the models as a clause with a pass test.
  • Milestones M1–M3 absorb the effort the standalone target was taking: the Managed rung, the investigator, the full agency, the second bake-off arm on the models now in scope.
  • Spike S3's latency half is measured in the lab, per engine, where the roles actually run, instead of waiting for a GB10 window.
  • The site's "Hardware" page becomes "Models and hardware": what each step up was measured to change.
  • ADR-0003's harness-placement axis has two values, lab and bundle (the same build loaded from the bundle on a host of the operator's choosing); the estate-placement axis is unchanged.

docs.title: ADR-0005: A server is an estate — its listeners, its files, its firmware and its controller, recorded and replayable
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-04
  • Deciders: Ken Rollins
  • Builds on: ADR-0001 (the ledger is the system of record), ADR-0003 (external estates and the scope)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The workbench's estates so far are networks: the mini-agency, built with its weaknesses planted and an answer key, and the lab, a real network seen through a mirror port and targeted scans. Both see a server as the listeners it exposes. A server's cryptography is not all there. Its own key files sit on its disk; its firmware holds the keys that decide what it will boot; and a management controller beside it (a BMC: Dell's iDRAC, HPE's iLO) runs its own TLS and SSH, holds its own identity certificates, and is configured separately from the operating system. None of that is reached by a wire scan of the server, and none of it changes when the operating system is patched.

Two further needs come with a real server. Its evidence is the owner's and identifies the hardware (service tag, serials, MAC addresses), so it cannot be published as it is. And it has to be shown where the server is not: on a demonstration machine with no route to it.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. A server is an external estate, with the operator's authorization in its scope like any other, and two additions to pqch.scope/1: systems (the paths that may be read, the addresses that are the server's, whether its firmware is read) and controllers (its management controller, read through DMTF Redfish with GET requests only).
  2. The runner does every read. It packs exactly the scoped paths, read-only and as the user it runs as, into an archive handed to readers with no network, the way an image's archive is handed to the image readers. cbomkit-theia reads the archive as a directory; the workbench's own readers read key material, and the firmware's identity, TPM and Secure Boot databases. The controller is a runner job too. No scanner is installed on the server and nothing is written to it.
  3. A new layer, platform, for what sits below the operating system: the Secure Boot databases' certificates, the TPM's banks, the controller's configuration and certificates. Facts that are not cryptographic assets (the device, its firmware and their versions, its security settings) are a platform.observed event, and the CBOM projects them as CycloneDX device and firmware components with dependencies: the device on its firmware, listeners and files; the BIOS on the keys it enforces; the controller's firmware on its own configuration, certificates and listeners.
  4. A run is exported as a recording and replayed as a new run. The export applies the operator's map of identifiers (with their case and hexadecimal spellings) and, optionally, replaces every MAC address and UUID with a consistent stand-in; it stops if any of the operator's leak patterns survives. Replay checks every raw output against the recording's hash and records it again with replayed_from naming the recording and the original read's time. The new ledger is signed where it is replayed; the evidence and its times are the recording's, and every page that shows the run says it was replayed and when the server was read.
  5. A server's plan is its own planner, returning the same structure as the others: lanes per part of the server (its services, its operating system, its controller, its firmware), waves from what the owner can set today through what waits for the vendor, and the traps a plan from a device list falls into.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• An agent on the server. Reads everything, including private keys, but is software installed on the target, which the project does not do (CLAUDE.md, "Scanners"). The runner's archive covers the same ground for what the reading user can open, and says what it could not.
  • Read the controller through IPMI. Available in-band without credentials, but reports little beyond the controller's firmware version; Redfish is the standard interface and carries the configuration and certificates.
  • Publish the recording with the repository. It is the owner's real evidence; recordings live in the deployment, never in the repository, like captures and the lab's ledgers.
  • Merge the server's findings into the lab's run. A chain is bound to one scope (ADR-0001 and the ledger's design); a combined view is a projection over several chains.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A server's CBOM names its firmware, its controller and the keys its boot chain trusts, and its plan can say which steps are settings, which are updates and which wait for the vendor.
  • A read as an unprivileged user misses private keys the user cannot open; the inventory lists them as unreadable, and a privileged read-only pass is a step in the plan.
  • Recordings make a real server demonstrable anywhere, at the price of an identifier map the operator maintains and a leak check that must know the server's identifiers.
  • Reading a remote server's files needs a transport the runner does not have yet (an SSH session packing the same paths); the first server read is the host the runner runs on. The controller is already read remotely.

docs.title: ADR-0006: The public site is a recording, a record and notes, never a facsimile of the running workbench
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-08
  • Deciders: Ken Rollins
  • Builds on: ADR-0001 (the ledger is the system of record), ADR-0004 (one deployment in the lab)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The workbench runs in one place, the lab, behind a door. What the public sees is a static site on GitHub Pages, generated from the private repository by tools/publish.py and leak-checked. Until this decision that site rendered eleven of the running application's pages statically from one recorded run, with every control that needs the workbench disabled and annotated, beside the demo stage (eight beats, recorded) and the field notes.

That shape grew by accretion. Each page the application gained was given a public rendering, a recorded fixture, a public branch in its template and a note under each dead button: twelve such branches across the templates by 2026-11-08. Host scans, imported CBOMs and normalization were about to add more. Two things were wrong with it. The cost of publishing grew with the application's features rather than with the story it tells, which made the public site a second rendering target for the whole application, the thing ADR-0004 exists to avoid. And a page that looks interactive and is not teaches the engineer who checks to distrust the pages that are honest.

The site serves three audiences: a person shown the project on a machine that cannot run it, who wants a walk-through; a person who checks, who wants the record and the method; and a reader, who wants the notes. A facsimile of the application serves the first badly and the second worse.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The public site is three things, each with a contract and a cost per feature that is a page of writing, not a port of code:

  1. The demo: the stage's eight beats, recorded from one run, labelled as recorded, with the recorded Ask answers and the ledger's citations re-checked when the page is built. New capability enters the public demo only as a beat in that story. The Pages root is the stage.
  2. The record: the recorded run's own documents, the CBOM, the ledger, the score and the two baselines, downloadable with their hashes, and one viewer, Inside the CBOM, that opens an entry field by field with the evidence behind each field. Data a person can verify, not a user interface.
  3. The notes: the field notes, with the running workbench shown page by page as screenshots captured from the recorded run, under the book's conventions for a marked screenshot. A screenshot has no dead button and costs nothing in code.

Four application pages are rendered publicly: /demo, /cbom (and the entries it and the demo link to), /ask (recorded) and /about. The overview, the test agency, the walkthrough, the plan, the change packages, the imports and the resolve page are not rendered publicly; their templates carry no public branch. The shared header shows only the four in a public build.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A new feature costs the public site one screenshot and one note, or one beat if it belongs in the story; never a static rendering.
  • The guarantee that a public page offers no way into the lab moves from branches in every template to one list in tools/build_public.py, tested.
  • The person on the restricted machine loses the feeling of the whole application in the browser, and gains pages that are each a recording, a document or a picture: the standard the journal already holds itself to.
  • The public tooling shrinks rather than grows as the application does.

docs.title: ADR-0007: Where CycloneDX 1.6 has no field, write the fact twice: under the workbench's name and under the name the consumers read
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-09
  • Deciders: Ken Rollins
  • Builds on: ADR-0001 (the ledger is the system of record; the CBOM is a projection)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
CycloneDX 1.6 defines, for a cryptographic asset, an algorithm's primitive, parameter set, curve, functions and security levels; a certificate's names, dates, format and two references, to the algorithm it was signed with and to its public key; a key's type, size, identity, state and a reference to its algorithm; and a protocol's type, version, cipher suites and a reference array to the assets on it. It has no field for the key-exchange group a TLS server selected or accepts, and none for an SSH server's key-exchange, host-key, encryption or MAC algorithms. It has no field that says whether a certificate is in use.

Until this decision the workbench's writer filled few of the fields the standard does define and kept nearly every judged fact in its own pqch: properties (lesson 48). Uploaded to a commercial policy engine, the CBOM was inventoried and judged on nothing: the engine reads the standard's fields and its own named properties, and found neither. Reshaped with the standard's fields alone it drew twenty findings, fifteen of them false, because the engine judged each certificate's key by its algorithm's family name and nothing else; reshaped with the engine's property names it drew nine, all correct, four of them on two certificates the workbench had marked not in use.

Three things follow. The standard's fields must be filled wherever the finding has the fact, with references that resolve inside the document. For a fact the standard has no field for, a property name has to be chosen, and the consumers already read particular names. And "not in use" has to travel somehow, or a consumer will raise findings on retired material.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Every standard field the finding has the fact for is filled. A TLS listener's protocolProperties carry type, version (the highest accepted), cipherSuites (every suite accepted at any version, by IANA name with its hex identifier) and cryptoRefArray (every asset on the listener). An SSH listener carries type: ssh and the protocol version from its banner. A PostgreSQL listener that negotiates TLS is typed tls. A certificate carries signatureAlgorithmRef and subjectPublicKeyRef; a key carries algorithmRef and id (its SubjectPublicKeyInfo hash). An algorithm carries parameterSetIdentifier, curve, classicalSecurityLevel computed from its key size by SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5 Table 2, nistQuantumSecurityLevel for a post-quantum set from FIPS 203 and 204, and its oid. The identifiers and categories are data (policy/algorithm-ids.yaml), each with its source.
  2. A reference points at a component of the document. The algorithm a certificate was signed with, the algorithm of a key and a certificate's public key are not findings of their own, so the projection adds one component per distinct value (alg:signature:<x509 name>, alg:<role>:<name>[-<size>|-<curve>], key:spki-sha256:<hash>), marked pqch:kind: referenced and carrying no layer. The scorer, the inventory projection and the answer key ignore them; a consumer's reference resolves.
  3. For a fact with no field, the property is written twice: under the workbench's name (pqch:tls-groups, pqch:ssh-key-exchange, pqch:ssh-host-key, pqch:ssh-encryption, pqch:ssh-mac, pqch:signature-algorithm) and under the name the consumers surveyed read (Supported Groups; Key Exchange Algorithm, Host Key Algorithm, Encryption Algorithm; Signature Algorithm, Subject Public Key Algorithm). The pqch: name is the one this project's own readers use; the other is a courtesy to tools that read a fixed name, and is dropped the day the standard gains the field.
  4. A name a consumer can judge alone. A component's name stays the family (RSA, ECDSA), which is the answer key's convention and the rules'; the size or curve is in the standard's fields and in the referenced algorithm's name (RSA-2048, ECDSA-P-256), and the certificate's Subject Public Key Algorithm property carries it the way the surveyed engine reads it.
  5. "Not in use" travels two ways. A key the rules found no listener serving carries relatedCryptoMaterialProperties.state: deactivated, the one in-use signal the standard has a field for. And every run writes a second document, workbench-consumer.cdx.json, which is the same projection with every entry marked pqch:in-use: false left out, the dependencies that named them pruned, and the count and reason in its metadata. The full document remains the record; the consumer copy is a view of it for an engine that cannot read pqch:in-use.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Write only the standard's fields and wait for the standard. Rejected: the groups and the SSH algorithms are what the migration is about, and a document that cannot carry them is not an inventory of the estate's cryptography. The draft after 1.6 was not checked for new fields; when it is, a field that exists replaces the property.
  • Write only the consumers' names. Rejected: they are one vendor's spellings, and adopting them as the project's own would make the writer answer to a product rather than to the evidence. Both names cost nothing and keep the project's vocabulary its own.
  • Rename components to carry the size (RSA-2048). Rejected: the answer key, the family tables and the rules name by family, and the fingerprint includes the name; a rename would re-key every entry for the sake of one reader. The size travels in the fields and the referenced component.
  • Leave never-served material out of the only document. Rejected: the record would then omit what the scanner found. A second document that says what it left out keeps both.
