  • Emit cipher-suite algorithm references. Deferred: a suite's symmetric cipher and hash are not findings, and inventing components for them would put unobserved entries beside observed ones. The suite is carried by name and identifier, which is what the surveyed consumer reads.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A consumer that reads the standard's fields sees versions, suites, the signature algorithm and key behind each certificate, each key's algorithm with its size, and security levels; one that reads the surveyed names sees the groups and the SSH algorithms. Lesson 48's step 5, the proof by re-upload, is still to be done with the next access to a consumer.
  • The document gains referenced components (one per distinct algorithm, signature algorithm and public key) that carry no layer; counts on the pages that count by layer are unchanged, and the component total rises.
  • tests/test_interop.py holds the writer to this: every reference resolves, a PostgreSQL listener that negotiates TLS is typed tls, the consumer copy drops exactly the not-in-use entries, and the schema still validates.

docs.title: ADR-0008: Who may act, and how the ledger shows it
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-09
  • Deciders: Ken Rollins
  • Builds on: ADR-0001 (the ledger is the system of record), ADR-0003 (the runner enforces the scope)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The workbench was built for one owner. Anyone signed on through the front door could propose a change, approve it and have the runner apply it in the same request, and the command line took a typed name. The federal readiness review (FR-01) found that this is the first thing an authorizing official stops on: there is no role, no separation between the person who asks for a change and the person who approves it, and nothing on the ledger says which role an approval rested on. The review deferred the work; an engagement with more than one person triggers it.

What exists already is the right foundation. Identity is the front door's sign-on header, believed only on a connection from the front door, and an approval is a human event under a signed checkpoint that the runner reads for itself before it acts. The missing pieces are a role, its source, and a refusal.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Role comes from the identity provider, through the front door. The front door sends the signed-on person's groups in a second header (PQCH_GROUPS_HEADER, default X-Forwarded-Groups), read only on a connection from a trusted proxy like the sign-on itself. The deployment names the group an approver must be in (PQCH_APPROVER_GROUP). The page refuses an approval by a person not in it and says which groups the front door listed.
  2. The approval event records what it rested on. approval.granted and approval.denied carry role: approver, groups (the front door's list) and, as before, authenticated_by (the provider or the console). A reader of the ledger sees not only who approved but why they were allowed to.
  3. Separation of duties is a setting the runner enforces (PQCH_SEPARATION_OF_DUTIES=1). Under it the runner refuses an apply whose approval was given by the person who asked for the change (the one who recorded the policy, or proposed the change as a person), and one whose approval carries no approver role. The page then approves in one request and applies in another, by a second button, and the runner reads the ledger again before the apply.
  4. The command line approves only in a labelled single-operator mode. Under separation, pqch change approve refuses unless --single-operator is given, records the approval as made in that mode with the approver role, and does not apply; pqch change apply is the second step. One person at a console can still run the whole loop, and the ledger says so in words.
  5. Reads keep needing identity behind the front door, as they do: the lab's pages answer only a signed-on viewer from a trusted proxy.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Roles typed into the context file. Rejected: a role is the identity provider's fact, not the owner's; typed in, it would be a supplied fact anyone with the file could change.
  • The workbench as its own identity provider. Rejected: one more credential store, with its own controls to assess, for a system whose deployments sit behind an agency's front door that already has one (ADR-0004).
  • Separation always on. Rejected for now: the kit on one box has one operator by design, and the demo's loop is one person's. The setting is on in any deployment with more than one person, which is the review's trigger, and the single-operator mode is labelled so the ledger does not pretend otherwise.
  • The approver also recorded on change.proposed. Not needed: the requester is on the ledger as the person who recorded the policy or proposed by hand, and the refusal compares the two.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• An approval with no groups (the console, or a front door that sends none) is still an approval where no approver group is set; where one is set it is refused, and the message names the gap.
  • A deployment that turns separation on after the fact finds earlier approvals have no role and will not apply again; they are already applied, and the runner's log says so.
  • The assessment the review asked for (AC-5, AC-6, CM-5) now has a setting to point at and events to read; the identity provider's groups claim is the agency's to map onto PQCH_APPROVER_GROUP.

docs.title: Lessons
docs.text:
Standing guidance: the rule, why it holds, when it applies.

  1. 01 When verifying that a post-quantum key exchange is required, offer every classical group, not the ones the server was configured with — A refuse-probe built from the server's old configuration proves only that the old configuration is gone; build it from the whole class being retired, and let an enumerating scan overrule it.
  2. 02 Give an isolated Docker network no host address, and test for it — An internal Docker bridge has no route out, but the host still sits on it as the gateway; set the gateway mode to isolated, and probe for the host as well as for a route.
  3. 03 Carry a registry in an offline bundle; docker save and docker load do not preserve digest references — An image saved by digest loads back as an untagged id, and an image saved by tag loads back under a new digest; an air-gapped bundle that pins by digest needs a local registry, filled registry-to-registry with every platform.
  4. 04 Believe an identity header only on a connection from the proxy that sets it — A forward-auth proxy strips and sets the user header, but an upstream that listens where anything else can reach it will accept the same header typed by hand.
  5. 05 Score an inventory for what it invents, and put a decoy in every layer it is scored on — A coverage score with no penalty for unplanted claims is maximized by claiming everything; count claims the answer key does not hold as false positives, and never show an untested decoy as avoided.
  6. 06 Record which container a scan reached, and join evidence only when it is the one you think it is — An address is not an identity: before linking what was seen on the wire to what was found in an image, check that the container at that address runs that image, at the start and the end of the scan.
  7. 07 Take the key that verifies a signed log from somewhere other than the log — A public key stored beside the data it verifies can be replaced along with it; record the key's id and the latest signed checkpoint somewhere the writer cannot reach.
  8. 08 Identify a key in an inventory by the hash of its public key, not by where it was found — "An RSA certificate at this address" cannot tell a renewed certificate from the old one, and an image digest in the location makes every rebuild look like a new estate; put the public key's hash in the identity and keep build identifiers out of it.
  9. 09 Time a file scanner on the bare base image first; symlinks, not size, can set its cost — cbomkit-theia's secrets plugin reads a file's contents once for every symlink that points to it, so a BusyBox-based image costs it about 94 s whatever its size; measure the base before blaming the image.
  10. 10 Count a key-exchange group as accepted only when it is the one negotiated — and sweep TLS 1.2 groups as TLS 1.2 — A handshake can succeed on a group the client did not offer, and fail after the server has accepted the one it did; judge each probe by the group the server chose.
  11. 11 Prove a passive-monitoring script fires on traffic you generated before reading its silence as absence — Zeek ran a handler for an event that does not exist without a word and logged nothing; run every new detection against traffic known to contain the thing it detects.
  12. 12 Check cited evidence against the question it was meant to answer, then derive the conclusion again — That a cited test really ran proves nothing unless it is the test the claim calls for, run after the change, against the thing changed — and the conclusion follows from its raw output.
  13. 13 To bound when a logged event happened, sign the log just before it and just after — A timestamped signature over an event shows it existed by then; only an earlier signature that the event is chained after shows it did not exist before.
  14. 14 Do not switch branches under a running container that bind-mounts the tree; make the health check read the files — A bind mount follows the directory that existed when the container started; when a checkout deletes and recreates that directory, the container keeps an empty one and a liveness check still passes.
  15. 15 Hash every blob in an offline bundle's registry before serving it, and keep the checksum file's own hash somewhere else — A registry serves what is on disk without checking it, a client does not re-fetch what it holds, and a checksum file edited together with what it lists still passes.
  16. 16 Count a change as applied only when the service answers, and put the old configuration back when it does not — The orchestrator reporting a container started is not the service coming up; a configuration the service cannot load leaves it down unless the applier restores the previous one.
  17. 17 In a bundle build, always rebuild what must match the source and record the commit; reuse only what must not change — A build step that skips an image because its tag already exists ships whatever was built first; a test of the bundle then tests old code.
  18. 18 Observe what a service accepts with nothing configured before planning its migration — The same TLS library gives different key-exchange defaults under different servers; with no line set, one already offers the hybrid group and another does not, and both accept RSA key transport.
  19. 19 Label a cause only after changing it and watching the effect go — A reference answer of the form 'this line causes that behaviour' is earned by two observations: the behaviour with the line as written, and its absence with the line changed.
  20. 20 Before reading a configuration, know which occurrence of a setting wins in that software — OpenSSH takes the first value it reads, PostgreSQL the last, nginx the innermost block; the same two lines in a different order, or an include in a different place, give a different listener.
  21. 21 Set a floor per role before comparing two models, and repeat every call before believing it — A model that beats the smaller one is not thereby good enough: each role needs an absolute bar set by what depends on its output, and a reply at temperature 0 is one draw, not an answer.
  22. 22 Deploy from a checkout nobody edits — A running container that bind-mounts a directory from a development tree breaks silently when a branch switch replaces that directory; run a deployment from its own detached checkout, with its state beside it, and move it to a commit on purpose.
  23. 24 A hardware label in a config is a claim; record what served the call — When model calls go through a gateway that can move a lane between machines, the hardware label in the caller's config is a claim that goes stale silently; record the upstream the gateway names on each reply beside the label, and check the label against it before publishing a timing.
  24. 25 Size the scanner network's address range to the parallelism, and record a job that never started as its own failure — When scanners run as containers on a network with a fixed address range, the range bounds how many can run at once; a job that fails because no address was free must be recorded as a runner failure with its reason, never as a scan the target did not answer.
  25. 26 Name the reasoning setting beside the model in every measurement and binding — A hybrid-reasoning model's result depends on its reasoning switch and effort level as much as on its weights, so a measurement, a table row or a tier binding that names the model without its reasoning setting is incomplete, and a gateway lane that pins the setting is part of the model's name.
  26. 27 Before keying a TLS listener, probe each kind of key exchange on its own: named groups, finite-field DHE, RSA key transport — A TLS 1.2 listener can establish keys three ways — a named group, an ephemeral finite-field group it supplies itself, or encryption to its RSA key — and a probe that offers one kind says nothing about the other two; key a listener only after a probe per kind, or a full cipher-suite enumeration.
  27. 28 Read a certificate's CA flag together with its key usage; a self-signed server certificate is usually marked CA:TRUE — openssl req -x509 writes basicConstraints CA:TRUE into every self-signed certificate it makes, server certificates included, so an inventory rule that treats CA:TRUE as 'a certificate authority' misfiles them; a certificate authority's certificate is one with CA:TRUE and keyUsage keyCertSign, and the in-use rules for leaf certificates must not be applied to it.
  28. 29 Give a listener that carries TLS behind a protocol upgrade its own scan profile; a plain TLS scan of its port is silent, not negative — PostgreSQL, SMTP, IMAP, LDAP and others start TLS only after an in-protocol request, so a scanner that opens the port and speaks TLS gets nothing back and reports nothing; the listener's protocol must be named in the scope and bound to a profile that speaks the upgrade, and a scope protocol no profile claims must be visible as unscanned, never as clean.
  29. 31 Confirm every cause an answer key names by changing it, including the ones written as annotations — A cause written into an answer key as an aside — a trace, a hint, a why — is a label like any other and needs the same two observations; one the key's author wrote from reading named a commented-out line as the cause of a default, and the first model trace to reach it was right where the key was wrong.
  30. 32 Ask the protocol stack's runtime what it will negotiate before calling a migration blocked, or not blocked, by its supplier — Whether software can offer a post-quantum algorithm is a property of the protocol stack that negotiates it, not of the cryptographic library underneath; ask that runtime for its own list, with no network, and keep the raw answer.
  31. 33 Read a validated module's certificate for the algorithm you need, and check that the module is active, before calling a system validated — A FIPS 140 validation covers the algorithms its certificate lists, in the module it names, when that module is the one in use; the library's name and version say none of that, and a FIPS provider shipped in an image is not one in use.
  32. 34 Score the retrieval step on its own before scoring a model's answer over it — When a model answers from retrieved passages, record what was retrieved with every answer and score whether the passage that settles the question was among it; a faithful model fails every item retrieval misses, and the failure is not the model's.
  33. 35 Compare two inventories by the identity of each observation and by what it says, leaving out references to the records behind it — A component's reference should be a hash of what was observed, so the same thing seen twice is the same entry; and a comparison should strip the event ids an entry cites, which are new on every scan, or every scan of an unchanged estate looks like change.
  34. 36 When verifying that a listener requires post-quantum key establishment, probe TLS 1.2 on its own; a classical-only TLS 1.3 client is refused, not downgraded — A server that shares no group with a TLS 1.3 client refuses it rather than falling back to TLS 1.2, so a negative probe offering every classical group says nothing about TLS 1.2; a listener restricted to the hybrid group can pass it while still accepting finite-field Diffie-Hellman and RSA key transport over TLS 1.2.
  35. 37 When a probe claims a handshake the enumerating witness does not find, call the verdict inconclusive and say why; neither side settles it — A verifier that lets its witness only lower a verdict will silently turn a misread probe into a false 'not enforced'; when the negative probe reports a key exchange the witness says the listener does not offer, one of the two misread the listener, and the verdict is inconclusive with the reason, until a person reads the raw output.
  36. 38 Before citing or redrawing a standard, read its status on the publisher's page; cite the current revision by its own identifier — A withdrawn publication keeps circulating — in search results, in summaries, in copies saved earlier — so the identifier in hand may not be the one in force; read the status, cite the superseding revision, and say whether the part relied on changed.
  37. 39 Every label in a diagram of what a system does is a claim; fill it from the record and check each against the record before it is shown — A box that says 'signed', 'by rule' or 'reached' reads as fact, and a framework's boxes invite filling them with what the system ought to do; compute each label from the ledger where it can be computed, and check the rest line by line against the ledger before the page is published.
  38. 40 Draw a cryptographic inventory in columns along its dependency chain, not as a force-directed graph — A CBOM already has an order — service, listener or image, asset, file — so draw each link of that chain as a column, one service's chain at a time, and group bulk files by directory; a force layout throws that order away and, unbounded, drifts nodes off the canvas.
  39. 41 Before approving a change that requires post-quantum key establishment, probe each kind of client against a copy with the change; enforced says it landed, not whom it refuses — A require change verified enforced has, by definition, refused every client that cannot offer the hybrid group; measure which kinds those are, against the live listener and a copy with the proposed configuration, and put that table in front of the approver.
  40. 42 Before trusting a discovery tool's silence, show it something it should find; an empty result is a finding about the tool until then — A scanner that reports nothing has either found nothing or cannot see — a hybrid group its TLS library lacks, a library it has no rules for, code it cannot resolve without a build — and only a known positive tells the two apart.
  41. 43 Report a change's time from approval to proof beside its time from policy to proof; the gap is the wait for a person, not the system — Time from the policy decision to the last verdict includes however long the change waited for an approver; shown alone it reads as the system's speed, so headline the approval-to-proof time and give the other as what it is.
  42. 44 Publish a curated export, checked for leaks, not the working repository; and keep the list of what must not leak out of the published tools — A working repository built in a real environment carries that environment in its history, its tests and its notes; publish a fresh tree exported from it, with private passages marked at the source and stripped on export, a scan that refuses the export on any match, and the scan's own patterns kept private.
  43. 45 Score an inventory against a key that knows about changes: an item a verified change removed is remediated, not missed — When the estate an answer key describes can be changed, a scan after a verified change no longer sees what the change removed; count each such item as remediated, by the change event that removed it, and take it out of the denominator, or every successful migration reads as a drop in coverage.
  44. 46 After publishing a repository, read its own checks: they run in an environment the export was never tested in — A repository published from a private working copy carries workflow files written for some earlier state of it; they run on every public push, and a red mark on the front page is the first thing a reader sees. Run the workflows' steps on a clean copy of the export before publishing, and read their result after.
  45. 47 Before a demonstration, open the published page in a browser at each width it will be seen at, and read its network log — A test suite, a link crawl and a leak check all pass on a page whose fonts never load and whose figure collapses on a phone; only a browser, rendering the published copy at desktop and phone width with the network log open, shows what a visitor sees.
  46. 48 Write each CBOM fact in CycloneDX's own field; where the standard has none, name the property as the tools you feed read it — Two valid CycloneDX 1.6 CBOMs of the same estate can share almost nothing a policy engine reads: the standard leaves the TLS key-exchange group and every SSH algorithm without a field, so each tool invents property names, and a tool that also skips the fields the standard does define is judged on nothing.
  47. 49 Before binding a role to an inference engine on a new machine, check four things the engine decides for itself: that it has a profile for the GPU, the context window it will serve, the share of memory it will take, and the model id it answers to — An engine container chooses its GPU profile, its context window, its memory share and its served model id on its own; on a desk-side box with unified memory each of the four can silently make a role unservable, and only a call through the seam with the role's real request shows it.
  48. 50 When a bundle keeps an image from one build to the next, key it to a hash of its build context, never to its name — A bundle that reuses an image by name will carry a stale service for as long as the name stays the same; the kept image must be keyed to what it was built from, and the test that catches it is scoring the bundle-started estate against the answer key.
  49. 51 Where a protocol upgrade can be refused, ask for it once and record the answer before scanning what it would carry: a scanner that cannot represent a refusal records a timeout — A TLS scanner pointed at a PostgreSQL listener that refuses TLS waits out its budget and records a timeout, which reads as a failed scan; one SSLRequest answered N in a millisecond is the finding: the database speaks in the clear.
  50. 52 An inventory read as an ordinary user must list every path it could not open, and the plan must carry the privileged read as a step — Reading a server's files without privileges sees the public half of each key pair and none of the private keys; an inventory that drops the unreadable files silently looks complete and is not, so the reader lists them and the plan asks for one privileged, read-only pass.
  51. 53 An offline install carries the build backend with the wheelhouse and installs outside the lock file; nothing in the runbook calls the package manager's run command — A wheelhouse of runtime wheels is not enough: the project's own build needs its backend, a locked sync fetches from the lock's recorded URLs even with every wheel on disk, and a loader that shells out to uv run re-resolves the project on every call; install with uv pip --offline --no-index and run tooling under the environment's own interpreter.
  52. 54 When a box already serves the engines on its loopback, join their containers to the kit's bridge under the kit's names instead of starting them again — A harness that reaches its engines by container name on a bridge cannot see a port bound to the host's loopback; docker network connect --alias puts the box's own engine containers on the bridge under the names the tier map expects, with the box's tested launch recipe left untouched.
  53. 55 A reply cap on a thinking tier is a thinking budget: set it from the measured tokens of the role's hardest items, and record a cut-off as an empty reply — When a role is bound to an engine with reasoning on, the reasoning counts against the reply's token cap; a cap sized for the answer alone returns nothing on the items that need the most thought, and the only safe reading of a cut-off is a wrong reply.
  54. 56 A signer's first signature over an event is a floor on the span that starts there, never a reading of it; check a ledger's clock against the bracket, not the floor — An independent signer says when an event existed by (the first signature over it) and when it cannot have existed before (the last signature before it); a span measured from the first-seen time is a lower bound, and a ledger whose own span falls inside that bracket agrees with the signer.
  55. 57 When two renderers must show the same header, give them one stylesheet and one markup shape, copied at build time; a second implementation that matches by description drifts — A header that an application renders from a template and a static-site generator renders from a theme override stays identical only when both load the same stylesheet file and emit the same element shape; a second stylesheet written to look the same is a second design, and the reader sees the whole band change when they cross from one to the other.
  56. 58 A model whose chat template thinks by default must be told not to on every plain call, and its reply's shape belongs in the prompt and a validator, not in the engine's grammar — Nemotron's chat template reasons unless the request turns it off, so a short plain call spends its whole budget thinking and returns nothing; turn thinking off in the tier's request block, and with thinking off describe the JSON shape in the prompt and validate it, because the engine's structured-output grammar can run a call to its cap.
  57. 59 Serve a static site that is rebuilt in place with Cache-Control: no-cache; without it the browser keeps old pages for a tenth of their age — A response with Last-Modified and no Cache-Control lets the browser choose its own freshness, typically a tenth of the time since the file last changed, so a page built days ago is reused for hours after a rebuild; send no-cache, and the ETag keeps the check cheap.
  58. 60 Before a component goes in an architecture picture, find the line of code that calls it; a stack drawn from what the box has installed claims parts the system never uses — An architecture drawing is a claim about what the system does, so each box in it needs a call site, and each path through it needs a code path; drawing what is installed beside the system, or what a reference design would use, puts parts in front of an audience that a single question exposes.
  59. 61 Give an animated presentation a snapshot mode that draws each frame's final state at once, and photograph every frame before presenting it — Animated pages hide their defects in motion and in timing, and a headless browser photographs the first frame, not the last; a mode that skips delays and draws the end state lets a machine take a still of every beat, and the stills show text, overflow and errors that a run-through glides past.
  60. 62 Before a container changes the user it runs as, change the owner of the files it appends to in a shared, sticky directory; the kernel refuses even root — With fs.protected_regular set, as Ubuntu sets it, an open that may create a file in a world-writable sticky directory fails when the file belongs to someone other than the opener and the directory's owner, root included; a container switched from one uid to another over a kept volume cannot append to its own earlier log until the file is handed over.
  61. 63 A static copy of a page whose answer comes from a model shows a call made once and labelled, offers only the questions recorded, and runs the rule's check again where it is built — A published, static copy of the workbench has no model to call; its Ask the CBOM page shows the example questions answered once by a real call, labelled with the model, the hardware and the date, and recomputes every citation's verdict against the ledger it is published with, so the verdict a reader sees is never a stored one.
  62. 64 Run the accessibility check in every colour scheme a page ships; a palette that passes in light can fail in dark, and the reverse — WCAG contrast is computed from the colours a reader is shown, so a page with a dark and a light scheme is two pages to the checker; run it once per scheme.
  63. 65 Before making a shared directory's files private, list every process that reads them and the user each runs as — Before making a shared directory private, list every reader and the uid each runs as; where writers and readers differ, make the mode a setting.
  64. 66 Pinning a self-signed certificate by making it the only trust anchor still checks its dates; an expired management-controller certificate fails the pin — Loading the certificate a server served as the context's only trust anchor (with partial-chain verification for a leaf a CA issued) is a sound pin in Python's ssl module and anything built on OpenSSL, but OpenSSL still checks the anchor's validity dates, so a long-expired self-signed controller certificate is refused; renew it before turning the pin on, or the read stops before it starts.
  65. 67 Publish a running system as a recording, a record and notes; never as a static copy of its pages with the buttons disabled — A static copy of a live application's pages costs a fixture, a template branch and a dead-button note per page and grows with the application's features, not with its story; publish a recording, the documents it produced with their hashes, and screenshots in the notes instead.
  66. 68 When two sources describe one asset, keep every claim, put one in force by the grade of its evidence, and show the rest as dissent; never fold two values into a list — An inventory built from several tools gets two values for one field sooner or later; folding them into a list of both changes the field's type and tells the reader nothing, and taking the first silently loses the other. Keep each as a claim with its grade (watched on the wire, read from a host, parsed from a file, reported in a document), project the best-graded one, write the disagreement beside it, and let only a person's recorded resolution override the rule.
  67. 69 A policy pack written from secondary summaries is marked unverified and applies no date; the primary is read, hashed and quote-checked before any of its dates or names counts — Summaries of a standard describe the version their authors read; the standard moves on. A pack built from them carries verified: false, sets no deadline and marks every status provisional until the primary document is read first-hand, its hash recorded and every quote in the pack checked against its text by the loader; the CNSA 2.0 pack's five-category timeline, taken from two summaries that agreed, was not in the FAQ's current version at all.
  68. 70 A number shown on two pages is computed in one place; a page that counts a rule's events and a page that counts the document's entries will disagree — A rule judges each observation and the document folds several observations onto one entry, so a count of the rule's events and a count of the document's entries are two different numbers under one label; every page that shows the figure reads it from the same projection, and a test holds the two readers equal.
  69. 71 An automated keyboard pass counts only the controls that are shown; a control inside a closed disclosure is reached through its summary, and a page that takes focus on load is walked from where it starts — A Tab-order check that compares the controls it reached with every focusable element in the page reports traps that do not exist: links inside a closed details element are not in the tab order until it is opened, and a page that focuses its input on load starts part-way down. Count what is shown, follow the wrap-around, and explain every difference before reporting one.
  70. 72 A recorded model answer belongs to the scan it was asked about; a build that shows a newer scan stops until the answers are recorded again — A static copy has no model to call, so it shows what a model said once, recorded against one scan's record. When a newer scan becomes the one the copy shows, the recordings do not follow it, and the page publishes an empty answer unless the build refuses to run without them.
  71. 73 A demonstration written around one machine goes stale the day the machine leaves; name hardware once, as where a run was recorded, and build the beats on the approach — A stage whose beats name a box, its chips and its model on every screen is true for one day and one machine. Four days later its recording came from a different host with different models, and three machines were named across eight beats with no reconciliation. The fix is structural: the beats describe the approach, and hardware appears once, as the provenance label on the run the copy shows.
  72. 74 A drawing that must fit one screen takes its height from that screen, and shares it among its rows by what each row needs; a constant cap leaves room unused while the rows collide — The stage's opening drew three bands into a height capped by a stylesheet constant: on an 883 px screen it took 443 px, left 250 px empty under itself, and spread eight services 10 px apart in 12 px type. Sized from the screen and divided by what each band's rows need, the same drawing takes 600 px on that screen and nothing overlaps; four screen sizes were rendered to check.

docs.title: When verifying that a post-quantum key exchange is required, offer every classical group, not the ones the server was configured with
The rule
docs.text: To show that a listener requires hybrid post-quantum key establishment, the client that must be refused offers every classical group a client could offer, and any group an enumerating scan finds accepted outside the allowed list rules out "enforced".

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
In TLS 1.3 a server picks a key-exchange group from the intersection of its list and the client's. A hybrid group, such as X25519MLKEM768, pairs a classical exchange with the post-quantum KEM (key-encapsulation mechanism) ML-KEM-768. "Enforced" means no classical-only client can complete a handshake.

A probe can only show that the groups it offered were refused. If the list of groups to refuse is taken from the server's previous configuration — the natural place to look — the probe answers "is the old configuration gone?", not "is every classical exchange refused?". A server configured with the hybrid group and any classical group not on that list passes.

Measured: with ssl_ecdh_curve X25519MLKEM768:secp384r1, a pair of probes that refused X25519 and P-256 reported enforced. A client offering only P-384 connected. The second-witness scan had listed secp384r1 as accepted, and that list was not consulted.

Two independent mechanisms are needed because each has a blind side. A single handshake with a long offer list shows that one of the offered groups was accepted, or none. An enumerating scan tries groups one at a time, but only the groups that scanner knows.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text:
Whenever a check must establish the absence of a class of algorithm on a listener: TLS key-exchange groups, SSH key-exchange methods, cipher suites, signature algorithms. It applies equally in reverse: confirming a rollback to classical means refusing every post-quantum and hybrid group.

It does not apply when the intent is only to enable the new algorithm alongside the old; then the classical probe is expected to succeed, and the result is the distinct state "enabled, not enforced".

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
Keep the refuse list as data, by kind, separate from what any server is configured with:

# policy/crypto-policy.yaml
key_establishment:
  hybrid: [X25519MLKEM768]
  classical: [X25519, secp256r1]          # what the estate is configured with
  every_classical: [X25519, X448, secp256r1, secp384r1, secp521r1,
                    ffdhe2048, ffdhe3072, ffdhe4096, ffdhe6144, ffdhe8192,
                    brainpoolP256r1tls13, brainpoolP384r1tls13, brainpoolP512r1tls13]

The negative probe, one handshake, any protocol version:

openssl s_client -connect HOST:443 -servername NAME \
  -groups X25519:X448:P-256:P-384:P-521:ffdhe2048:ffdhe3072:ffdhe4096:ffdhe6144:ffdhe8192:brainpoolP256r1tls13:brainpoolP384r1tls13:brainpoolP512r1tls13 </dev/null

Enforced requires a handshake failure here, a success for the hybrid-only probe, and an enumerating scan (testssl.sh -f) whose accepted groups are all on the allowed list. Regenerate the list from openssl list -tls-groups when the probe's OpenSSL changes.

docs.title: Give an isolated Docker network no host address, and test for it
The rule
docs.text: A Docker network meant to hold deliberately weak or untrusted containers is created internal and with its IPv4 gateway mode set to isolated, and its isolation test checks that the host holds no address on it.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
internal: true removes the route from the bridge to other networks. It does not remove the host from the bridge. Docker still assigns the bridge's gateway address to the host's side of it, so every service the host binds to all interfaces — SSH, a database, another project's published port — is reachable from every container on that network at the gateway address. Nothing is routed, so a test that looks for a default route, or tries an outside address, passes.

Measured on Docker 29.1.5: a container on an internal bridge reached the host's SSH daemon at the gateway address. An egress probe that checked the routing table and two off-subnet addresses had passed.

For a test estate built to contain old software, or for scanner containers aimed at such an estate, that is the opposite of isolation: the weakest containers have a path to the host.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any bridge network whose purpose is containment: vulnerable-by-design targets, malware or fuzzing sandboxes, rehearsal copies of an estate. It needs Docker 28 or later. It does not apply to a network whose containers must reach the host on purpose.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
# compose.yaml
networks:
  target_net:
    internal: true
    driver_opts:
      com.docker.network.bridge.gateway_mode_ipv4: isolated
    ipam:
      config:
        - subnet: 172.16.106.0/24

Check from the host that it holds no address in the subnet, and from a container that the failure is explicit:

ip -o -4 addr show | grep -F '172.16.106.' && echo "host is on the bridge"
docker exec CONTAINER wget -q -T 6 -O /dev/null http://172.16.106.1:22/
#   want: "Host is unreachable" — not a timeout, and not a missing tool

Write the isolation test so that only an explicit "unreachable" passes. A timeout, or a container image without a tool that can attempt a connection, is not evidence. Then point the test at an address that is reachable and confirm it fails.

docs.title: Carry a registry in an offline bundle; docker save and docker load do not preserve digest references
The rule
docs.text: A bundle that must start with no network, and whose images are pinned by digest, carries a registry with its data directory, filled registry-to-registry with every platform of each image, and is tested by removing every image and starting from the bundle alone.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
Pinning an image by digest (repo@sha256:…) is how a deployment runs exactly the bytes that were tested; a digest names the content, not a place. Three ways of moving images lose it:

  • docker save by digest. The image comes back from docker load as an untagged id. The bytes are present and nothing can start them by the reference that pins them: "No such image".
  • docker save by tag. The tag survives; the repository digest changes, because the saved form drops the multi-platform index the original digest named. Any record of "this service runs digest X" is stale after the load.
  • docker push of an image pulled for some of its platforms. Docker pushes only what it holds and builds a new index for it, under a new digest.

A registry stores manifests and indexes by digest and serves them unchanged, so a reference that resolved when the bundle was built resolves when it is loaded. Two tools fill it without losing a digest: a multi-platform build pushed straight to it (docker buildx build --platform … --push), and a registry-to-registry copy of every platform (skopeo copy --all). Check each digest after the copy; refuse the bundle if one changed.

The registry's own image is the one thing saved with docker save — by tag, which does survive — once per architecture.

Built and tested this way, a bundle of eight images for two platforms was 608 MB; with every image the deployment uses deleted, the system started from it in 8.9 s, every pull the daemon reported came from the local registry, and a live scan through it scored as before.

One more reason to build the bundle early: anonymous reads from Docker Hub are rate-limited, and on a shared lab address they were refused for most of an afternoon. A bundle built ahead of time is also what makes a build repeatable on a bad day.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Air-gapped or offline deployments of anything pinned by digest — scanners, verifiers, services whose image identity is itself evidence. It does not apply to a bundle whose images are referenced by tag and whose digests are never compared; there save and load are enough.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
# build time, online: a registry with its data on disk
docker run -d --name bundle-registry -p 127.0.0.1:15000:5000 \
  -v "$PWD/bundle/out/registry:/var/lib/registry" ghcr.io/distribution/distribution:3.0.0
# your own images, every platform, straight in
docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t 127.0.0.1:15000/agency/portal:m0 --push agency/portal
# third-party images, every platform, digest unchanged
skopeo copy --all --dest-tls-verify=false \
  docker://ghcr.io/testssl/testssl.sh@sha256:DIGEST docker://REGISTRY_IP:5000/testssl/testssl.sh:pinned
# the registry's own image, by tag, per architecture
docker save --platform linux/arm64 -o bundle/out/registry-image.arm64.tar ghcr.io/distribution/distribution:3.0.0

At run time: load the registry image, start it read-only on its data, pull each image by digest from it, start with --pull never. Point the deployment's configuration at the registry-qualified digests and regenerate anything that records image digests after the load. Test by deleting the images first and recording the daemon's image events: every pull should name the local registry. Say what the test did not do — here, the host's own route to the internet was not cut.

The project's scripts: bundle/build.py, bundle/load.py.

docs.title: Believe an identity header only on a connection from the proxy that sets it
The rule
docs.text: An application behind a forward-auth proxy accepts the proxy's identity header only when the connection comes from the proxy's own address, and treats it as absent from anywhere else. With no proxy address configured, it accepts none.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
In forward auth, a reverse proxy asks an identity provider whether a request is signed on, and if so copies the provider's headers — the user name, the groups — onto the request it forwards. A careful proxy also deletes those headers from the incoming request first, so a client cannot supply its own.

All of that protects the path through the proxy. The application itself still listens on an address, and anything else that can reach that address bypasses the proxy and can send any header it likes. On a shared network segment that is every neighbour.

Measured: an application that took the approver's name from the sign-on header the proxy sets on any request. From a neighbouring container, two plain HTTP requests with a made-up name proposed a configuration change and approved it. The change was applied to a running service, and the audit log recorded an approval "authenticated by single sign-on". Every downstream control — a signed checkpoint, a runner that checks for an approval before acting — accepted it, because the approval event was well formed.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text:
Any service that makes an authorization decision from a header set by a proxy: forward auth (Authelia, oauth2-proxy and the like), a service mesh sidecar, a cloud load balancer's identity headers. It matters most where the decision is consequential — approving a change, not rendering a filtered page.

It is a floor, not a full answer. Whoever can originate connections from the proxy's address — the proxy host itself, or an attacker able to take over that address on the segment — can still forge the header. A decision that must survive that needs a credential the application verifies itself: a signed token from the identity provider, or a signature by the approver's own key.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
# the peer address, not a forwarded-for header
TRUSTED = {a for a in os.environ.get("TRUSTED_PROXIES", "").split(",") if a}

def identity(request):
    if request.client.host not in TRUSTED:
        return None
    return request.headers.get(IDENTITY_HEADER) or None

Default to an empty list, so a deployment that forgets to configure it cannot approve anything rather than trusting everyone. Refuse a state-changing request whose Origin is another site. Record in the audit event how the identity was established, in words a reader can check. Then test it from a peer that is not the proxy: the request must fail, and the page must offer no action.

Better still, do not give the application an address neighbours can reach. Where the platform requires one, the peer check is the control.

docs.title: Score an inventory for what it invents, and put a decoy in every layer it is scored on
The rule
docs.text: When an inventory is scored against an answer key, a claim the key does not hold counts against it; each scored layer contains at least one decoy; and a layer nothing scanned is reported as not scanned.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A cryptography bill of materials (CBOM) is scored against an answer key for coverage — how much of what is there it found — and false positives — how much it reported that is not there. If false positives are counted only as "decoys flagged", three things go wrong.

  • Over-claiming is free. With no decoy in a layer, nothing reported there can be wrong. A scanner that asserts every algorithm on every endpoint reaches full coverage with a clean record. Measured: 180 invented components, including "ML-KEM-1024 on a classical web server", cost nothing; they were filed as "outside the key's scope".
  • An untested trap looks like a pass. A decoy in a layer that was never scanned is "not flagged" by every tool. Shown as 0 of 1 in green, it reads as discrimination. It is absence.
  • A decoy is suppressed in part. Scanners emit several components per file: the certificate, its public key, its signature algorithm, its hash. A key that matches the decoy only by one component type credits a tool for avoiding it while the rest remain in the inventory for a reader to find.

An answer key for a planted estate is exact for the class of thing it covers. That exactness is what allows "not in the key" to mean "wrong".

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text:
Any evaluation of a discovery tool against planted truth: cryptographic inventories, vulnerability scanners, secret scanners, software bills of materials. It applies with most force when comparing a tool against baselines, where a lenient scorer flatters whichever column reports more.

It does not apply to findings genuinely outside the key's stated scope — here, symmetric ciphers and hashes — which are counted separately and neither credited nor penalized.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
State the key's scope in its header, then score in four bins:

Bin Counted as Matches a present item covered Matches a decoy, and is reported as in use false positive In the key's scope, on a keyed subject, matches nothing false positive ("unplanted claim"), listed by name Outside the key's scope unkeyed: shown, not scored

Match a decoy by its location, whatever component type the tool emitted. Give every layer a decoy of its own kind: an unserved certificate in an image; a weak cipher in a commented-out line of configuration; on the wire, a group a listener advertises and then refuses to negotiate. Report a layer in which a column holds no component as "not scanned — N decoys untested". Finally, test the scorer itself: feed it an inventory that claims everything, and one that claims nothing, and check that neither scores well.

Write the key, and commit it, before the scanner it scores exists. An honest key includes items the tool cannot reach, kept in the denominator.

docs.title: Record which container a scan reached, and join evidence only when it is the one you think it is
The rule
docs.text: Every network scan records the container that held the target address while it ran and the digest of the image that container runs. Evidence from the network and evidence from an image are joined only when those agree with what the inventory believes; when they do not, each is reported on its own and the disagreement is stated.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A cryptographic inventory joins layers: this certificate, seen in a TLS handshake at an address, is that file in an image. The join is where the value is — it is the first link in tracing a finding to the thing that must change. It rests on an assumption: that the service at the address is running the image that was scanned.

That assumption comes from configuration — a compose file, a deployment manifest, a scope document — and configuration goes stale the moment anything is rebuilt, restarted from a different tag, or loaded from a bundle.

When it is stale, the result is not an error. It is a confident wrong answer. Measured: with one service running a different build than the scope named, the image scan read the old image, found certificates that matched nothing on the wire, and the "is it in use?" rule concluded that the served certificates were unused. The inventory was worse than the raw scanner output it was built from, with no warning.

The same assumption sits under verification. "The change landed" is a statement about a specific container. A probe that reaches a different one — another replica, a stale instance, the wrong service at a reused address — measures something else.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text:
Whenever results from different vantage points are merged about "the same" service: wire and image, wire and source, scan and re-scan, change and verification. It applies to estates the tool can inspect through the container runtime.

Where it cannot — a network someone else operates — the container identity is unavailable. The binding is then the address and the served certificate's fingerprint, and the inventory must say that the join is weaker.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
For each scan, look up the container on the target network by address before and after, and keep both:

"binding": {"address": "172.16.106.10", "container_id": "…",
            "image": "agency/portal:m0", "image_digest": "sha256:…", "stable": true}

Then, as a rule whose result is itself recorded:

  • image digest equals the one the scope names, and stable is true: bound — join freely;
  • anything else: unbound — report the wire findings, link nothing, judge nothing in that image as unused, and show the reason next to the listener.

A negative conclusion needs more than a positive one. "This certificate is not served" is asserted only when every listener of the image was scanned, each is bound, and every certificate they served was found in the image.

For a verification, compare each probe's container with the one the change was applied to, and return "inconclusive" on a mismatch.

Check on each platform how the runtime reports a container's image: the comparison here relies on the container's image id being the repository digest, which holds with Docker's containerd image store and has not been checked on the classic store.

docs.title: Take the key that verifies a signed log from somewhere other than the log
The rule
docs.text: A signed log is verified with a public key, and against a latest checkpoint, that were obtained independently of the log's own files. Verification that used only what sits beside the log reports that plainly.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A tamper-evident log chains each entry to the one before by hash and signs checkpoints over the chain. The signature says: whoever held the private key attested to this state. Two things are needed to use it, and both are easy to keep in the wrong place.

  • The public key. It is convenient to store it next to the log so a reader has everything in one directory. But a party able to rewrite the log can rewrite that file too: alter the entries, recompute the hashes, sign new checkpoints with a key of their own, and replace the public key. Every check then passes, because the log is being verified against itself.
  • The latest checkpoint. A signature covers everything up to a point and nothing after. A log truncated back to an earlier checkpoint is a valid, shorter log. Only someone who knows a later checkpoint existed can tell.

Both were measured on a real ledger. Checked against the signing service's own key and its own list of what it had signed, each tamper failed. Checked from the files alone, a full rewrite with a swapped key passed, and so did a truncation.

This is not a weakness of the signature algorithm. ML-DSA-65 (FIPS 204), a post-quantum signature scheme, did exactly what a signature does. The trust anchor was in the wrong place.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any signed or hash-chained record meant to be checked later by someone other than its writer: audit logs, software attestations, transparency logs, inventories with provenance. It applies with most force when the record is exported — sent to an auditor, archived, moved to another machine.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
Publish two short values out of band each time they change, where the log's writer cannot alter them — a ticket, a printed report, a second system:

  • the key id: the SHA-256 of the public key in its standard encoding;
  • the latest checkpoint: its sequence number and the hash it signed.

Then verify with them:

pqch ledger verify --signed ledger.jsonl \
  --key-id 69d4ea57…16f2 \
  --known checkpoints.json      # [{"through_seq": 12, "head_hash": "…"}]

Have the tool warn, in its output and not only its documentation, when the key was taken from beside the log and checked against nothing. Have the signer keep its own record of what it signed, apart from the log, and refuse to sign a log from which one of its earlier checkpoints has disappeared. Show the key id and the latest checkpoint on screen so a reader can copy them down.

State the limits beside the result: a signature proves the log has not changed since signing, not that what was written was true; entries after the latest checkpoint are unsigned; and nothing here protects against the holder of the signing key.

docs.title: Identify a key in an inventory by the hash of its public key, not by where it was found
The rule
docs.text: An inventory entry for a key or certificate is identified by where it is, what kind of thing it is, and the hash of its public key. Identifiers that change on every build — image digests, container ids — are recorded with the entry and kept out of its identity.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A cryptography bill of materials (CBOM) is re-scanned, and each re-scan is compared with the last to answer "what changed?". That comparison needs a stable identity for each entry: a fingerprint under which the same thing seen twice is one entry and a different thing is another. Two natural choices each fail in one direction.

  • Too coarse. "Wire, this address and port, a certificate, RSA." A certificate replaced by another RSA certificate — a renewal, a larger key, an attacker's substitute — has the same fingerprint. So does a host key regenerated at a different size. The comparison reports no change.
  • Too fine. "Image portal@sha256:d7ba…, this path, a certificate, RSA." The digest changes on every rebuild, and on a save and load. Every entry in the image becomes new, and the comparison reports that everything changed.

The public key is the stable thing. The SHA-256 of its SubjectPublicKeyInfo (the standard encoding of an algorithm identifier and key) is the same wherever the key appears — in a served certificate, in a file, across rebuilds — and different for any other key.

It does a second job. The same hash, computed from a handshake and from a file, is what proves they are the same certificate. That is the first link of a dependency chain, made by arithmetic, with no model and no naming convention.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text:
Asymmetric keys and certificates in any inventory that is compared over time or joined across sources. It applies less cleanly in three cases:

  • A private key file with no public half alongside has no identity a file scanner can compute; a regenerated key there looks unchanged.
  • An SSH host key seen on the wire is commonly identified by its OpenSSH fingerprint, a hash of a different encoding of the same key. Convert to one form before comparing across layers.
  • Algorithms with no key — a negotiated group, a hash — have no identity, and place plus name is their whole fingerprint.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
"subject": {"kind": "file", "image": "agency/portal", "path": "/etc/nginx/tls/portal.crt"},
"source":  {"subject_digest": "sha256:d7ba…"},
"asset":   {"type": "certificate", "role": "signature", "name": "RSA",
            "identity": "spki-sha256:e028e2ea…"}

Fingerprint = SHA-256 of the canonical form of {layer, subject, type, role, name, identity}, with identity null when there is none. Compute the key hash with any X.509 library:

spki = cert.public_key().public_bytes(Encoding.DER, PublicFormat.SubjectPublicKeyInfo)
identity = "spki-sha256:" + hashlib.sha256(spki).hexdigest()

Test both directions: swap a key for another of the same family and confirm the fingerprint changes; rebuild the image with the same keys and confirm no fingerprint does. Settle this before anything compares re-scans; changing the meaning of an identity later invalidates every record that used the old one.

docs.title: Time a file scanner on the bare base image first; symlinks, not size, can set its cost
The rule
docs.text: Before tuning or budgeting an image scanner, time it on the bare base image the estate is built from, and on a synthetic image of the same size. If the base alone is slow, the cost is in the base's structure — usually its symlinks — not in anything the estate added.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A file scanner reads every file in an image and matches its contents against patterns. Its cost should follow the bytes it reads. In cbomkit-theia 1.1.2, the plugin that looks for secrets and private keys took 94.8 s of a 94.6 s scan of a 4.6 MB image — every other plugin together took about three seconds — and it was CPU-bound on one core the whole time.

The image's size did not explain it: 4 MB of random files took 1.6 s. A bare alpine:3.22, with nothing added, took 93.7 s. The difference is structure. Alpine's command-line tools are one BusyBox binary of about 800 KB with 304 symlinks pointing to it, one per command. The plugin reads the target's contents once per symlink. Measured directly: one 800 KB file took 1.1 s alone, 18.4 s with 50 symlinks to it, 69.8 s with 200 — linear in the number of links. 304 links × about 0.3 s each is the 94 s.

So every Alpine-based image costs this plugin about a minute and a half before the scanner reaches anything the estate put there. Its --ignore patterns did not change the time.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text:
Any scanner that walks a container filesystem: secret scanners, SBOM and CBOM tools, malware scanners. Bases that link many names to one binary — BusyBox (Alpine), toybox, multi-call Go binaries — or that keep many alternatives symlinks are where to look. It does not apply to scanners that read package databases rather than files.

Under emulation the effect multiplies: the same scans took 633 to 837 s per image as arm64 under qemu-user.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
docker save alpine:3.22 -o base.tar
time docker run --rm --network none -v "$PWD:/scan:ro" \
  ghcr.io/cbomkit/cbomkit-theia:<pinned> image -p secrets docker-archive:/scan/base.tar

Then run each plugin alone (-p certificates, -p secrets, …) on the real image to find which one carries the cost. Count symlinks per target:

docker run --rm IMAGE sh -c 'find / -xdev -type l -exec readlink {} \; | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head'

Where image results change only when an image does, scan once per image digest and replay the result, which is what this project does. Report the finding upstream with the synthetic reproduction: one file, N symlinks.

docs.title: Count a key-exchange group as accepted only when it is the one negotiated — and sweep TLS 1.2 groups as TLS 1.2
The rule
docs.text: When probing which key-exchange groups a TLS server accepts, offer one group at a time and count it as accepted only when the server's key share is in that group — not when the handshake succeeds, and not only when it completes. Groups that exist only in TLS 1.2 are probed with TLS 1.2.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
"Did the handshake work?" answers a different question from "does the server accept this group?", in both directions:

  • Success on another group. Offered only brainpoolP256r1 in TLS 1.2, a Postgres server whose groups exclude it completed the handshake anyway — with finite-field Diffie-Hellman (DHE) at 2048 bits, because the client also offered DHE cipher suites and the server chooses DHE parameters itself. Counting that success as "Brainpool accepted" is wrong.
  • Failure after acceptance. Offered the same curve, a RabbitMQ server did accept it and sent its key share; the OpenSSL client then aborted with "wrong curve", because in TLS 1.2 the offered curves also limit the certificate's curve, and the server's ECDSA certificate was on P-256. Counting that failure as "Brainpool refused" is also wrong.

Two version traps sit beside these. Brainpool curves have TLS 1.2 codepoints that cannot be used in TLS 1.3; offered beside TLS 1.3 they are silently ignored, so a sweep that does not force TLS 1.2 never sees them. And OpenSSL 3.5.7 prints a TLS 1.3 finite-field group as Temp Key: DH, 3072 bits, so a sweep that matches on the group's name misses it.

Each of these made one tool look wrong in this project's scanner comparison, and in each case the fault was the comparison's probe. Once the probe judged by negotiated group and swept TLS 1.2 names as TLS 1.2, testssl.sh and the OpenSSL sweep agreed on every target: a hybrid web server, Postgres, RabbitMQ, Kafka, and a client-certificate listener.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any active TLS probe that reports which groups a server accepts: inventory scanners, verification probes, compliance checks. It matters most for "refused" results, which a verifier uses to say a classical exchange is gone.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
# one group, its negotiated name compared with the one offered
openssl s_client -connect HOST:PORT -groups X25519 </dev/null 2>&1 \
  | grep -E 'Negotiated TLS1.3 group|Temp Key'
# TLS 1.2-only curves, forced to TLS 1.2
openssl s_client -connect HOST:PORT -tls1_2 -groups brainpoolP256r1 </dev/null 2>&1 | grep 'Temp Key'
# finite-field groups: compare the size, since OpenSSL prints "DH, <bits> bits"
openssl s_client -connect HOST:PORT -tls1_3 -groups ffdhe3072 </dev/null 2>&1 | grep 'Temp Key'

A key share in the offered group means accepted, whatever happens after it. A completed handshake in another group means not that group. Compare finite-field groups by size: tools name the same group by RFC 3526, RFC 7919 or bit count.

docs.title: Prove a passive-monitoring script fires on traffic you generated before reading its silence as absence
The rule
docs.text: A new detection script for a passive monitor is run first against traffic generated for the purpose and known to contain what it detects. An empty log counts as "not present" only after that.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
Passive monitoring — watching traffic rather than probing it — is the only way to see what a service offers when it connects out, its client-side posture. Its output is a log, and an absent log line reads naturally as an absent finding.

In Zeek, a script reacts to named events. Zeek 9.0 accepted a script that handled ssl_extension_supported_groups, an event it does not define — the TLS "supported groups" extension is still delivered as ssl_extension_elliptic_curves, after its older name. The script loaded, Zeek raised no error, and the handler never ran. Zeek's own TLS log recorded the same connections, so the capture was working; only the detection was not. Renamed, the same capture logged every client hello and the groups it offered, including codepoint 4588, the hybrid group X25519MLKEM768.

Without the generated traffic, the conclusion would have been "these clients offer no post-quantum groups".

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any passive or event-driven detection: Zeek and Suricata scripts, log-based SIEM rules, eBPF probes. It applies with most force where the thing detected is new — post-quantum codepoints, new extensions — because names and numbers for it are least settled in the tools.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
Run a known client beside the monitor and assert the detection fires:

# a client that offers the hybrid group every few seconds
openssl s_client -connect TARGET:443 -groups X25519MLKEM768:X25519 </dev/null
# Zeek in the client's network namespace, with the script under test
docker run --network container:CLIENT --cap-add NET_RAW zeek/zeek:lts \
  zeek -C -i eth0 groups.zeek LogAscii::use_json=T

Check the script's own log has entries, and that the expected value — here 4588 — is in them, before using it on traffic of unknown content. Keep the generator and the check with the script, and rerun them when the monitor is upgraded. Event names and codepoint tables change between versions.

docs.title: Check cited evidence against the question it was meant to answer, then derive the conclusion again
The rule
docs.text: When a conclusion cites evidence held by an independent party, check four things, not one: that the evidence exists as cited; that it is the evidence the question calls for; that it was taken after the event it speaks to, from the thing that event changed; and that the conclusion follows from the raw material when it is read again.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A common design for a trustworthy result has one component run the tests and keep its own log, and another write the conclusion and cite the tests by id. The reader looks each id up in the log and compares what the conclusion says about it — output hash, start and end time, target — with what the log says.

That comparison proves the cited tests ran. It does not prove they were the right tests. Whoever writes the conclusion can usually also ask for tests, and can ask for one that is bound to come out the way they want. A listener that accepts two classical key-exchange groups will still refuse a third it was never configured with; a probe offering only that third group is a real job, in the log, fresh, against the right container, with a truthful "refused". Cited as the negative probe of a check that should have offered every classical group, it supports a verdict that is false.

The same comparison passes evidence lifted from another occasion, if the conclusion copies the old test's details faithfully: the log does hold that test, with exactly that hash and those times.

And it leaves the reading of the evidence to the writer. A log that confirms a scan ran says nothing about whether the scan's output lists two more groups than the conclusion admits.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text:
Wherever one party attests and another summarizes: test reports that cite CI jobs, compliance findings that cite scans, change records that cite verification runs, an agent's report that cites tool calls. It applies with most force when the summarizer can also start the tests.

It does not replace separating the two parties. If the summarizer can write the log, none of these checks means anything.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
Have the party that runs tests log, for each one, what it was asked — the profile and every parameter — as well as what happened. Then, when reading a conclusion:

Check Catches The test is in the log with the same output hash, times and target Invented or altered evidence No other conclusion cites it One test used twice Its profile and parameters are exactly what the pre-stated check prescribes A genuine test of an easier question It started after the logged end of the change it verifies, against what that change produced Evidence from another occasion The raw output, parsed again by the reader, gives the recorded result, and the results give the conclusion A misreading, honest or not

Fix the check before the change, so "what the question calls for" is a matter of record. Make the decision from parsed results a pure function, so the reader can call the same code the verifier did. Show nothing as verified when any row fails, and say "unchecked" for a conclusion that cites nothing.

docs.title: To bound when a logged event happened, sign the log just before it and just after
The rule
docs.text: An interval measured from a log is trustworthy on a second clock only if each end is bounded on both sides. Have the timestamping signer sign the chain immediately before the event that starts the interval is written, and again immediately after. Report the interval as "no more than" the span from the earlier signature to the first signature over the end event.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A hash-chained log is signed at checkpoints by a service with its own clock, which puts its time inside the signed message. It is tempting to read that time as "when the event happened". It is weaker than that, and the weakness is one-sided.

A signature over an event proves the event existed when the signature was made. It is an upper bound on the event's time. It says nothing about how long the event existed before the signer saw it — the writer can hold it — and nothing stops the writer stamping it earlier still, if no signature precedes it. For the end of an interval an upper bound is what is wanted. For the start it is the wrong bound: a late start makes the interval look short.

The lower bound comes from the chain, not from the signer's clock rule. Each event is hashed onto everything before it, and a checkpoint is itself an event containing a signature nobody could have produced earlier. So an event that follows a checkpoint in the chain was written after that signature was made. A checkpoint just before the event and one just after pin it between two times on the signer's clock.

A signer that also refuses events stamped far from its own time catches gross errors, but only between checkpoints. Before a log's first checkpoint, nothing is bounded from below.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text:
Any log from which durations are read and shown as a result: time to deploy, time to remediate, time to respond. It matters when the writer benefits from the duration being short, or when the reader will quote it.

What it does not bound: the gap between something happening in the world — a person deciding — and the writer creating the event. Only a signature made by that person, with a time, closes that.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
• Write a checkpoint immediately before each event that starts a measured interval, and immediately after. Start the log with one, over its first event.
  • Compute the second-clock interval from the last signature before the start event to the first signature over the end event, and label it an upper bound.
  • Show both readings. When they differ by more than the tolerance allows, show neither as a result.
  • Have the signer refuse to sign backwards: never a point at or before one it has signed, never a time earlier than its last.
  • When a log lacks the earlier signature, say so beside the number.

docs.title: Do not switch branches under a running container that bind-mounts the tree; make the health check read the files
The rule
docs.text: A deployment that bind-mounts directories from a working tree must not share that tree with branch switching. And a health check must open the files the service needs, not only answer.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A bind mount attaches a directory by identity, not by path. When git checkout moves to a commit in which a directory does not exist, git removes it; coming back, git creates a new directory with the same name. The container still holds the old, now deleted, one — and sees it empty. A directory that exists in both commits survives, which is why the fault touches some mounts and not others.

Nothing restarts and nothing logs. The service fails only when it next reads a file from the lost mount, which may be minutes into a long operation. A health endpoint that returns a constant reports a process, not a service.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text:
Development and lab deployments run straight from a repository checkout: Compose files with ./config:/app/config style mounts. It applies equally to any tool that replaces a directory instead of changing it in place — some editors, rsync --delete with a rename, unpacking an archive over a tree.

It does not apply to named volumes, or to files copied into the image.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
• Deploy from a checkout nobody works in, or copy read-only configuration into the image and mount only what must change at run time.
  • In the health endpoint, check that each file the service will need is readable, and answer 503 naming the missing one:
# src/pqch/ui/app.py
missing = [str(p) for p in (KEY, POLICY, Path(os.environ.get("PQCH_POLICY", "policy/pq-algorithms.yaml")))
           if not p.is_file()]
if missing:
    return JSONResponse({"ok": False, "missing": missing}, status_code=503)
return {"ok": True}
  • After any branch switch on a host with running containers, compare ls inside the container with ls on the host for each mounted directory, and recreate the container if they differ.

docs.title: Hash every blob in an offline bundle's registry before serving it, and keep the checksum file's own hash somewhere else
The rule
docs.text: An offline bundle that carries a container registry's data directory is checked in two steps before use: every blob is hashed and compared with the SHA-256 it is named by, and the bundle's checksum file is compared with a hash that did not travel with the bundle.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
Three behaviours, each reasonable alone, add up to no check at all.

  • The registry trusts its disk. Blobs are stored under their SHA-256, and the registry serves the file at that path. It does not hash it on the way out.
  • The client trusts its store. A client verifies the digest of what it downloads — and downloads nothing it already holds. On a machine that has seen the image before, a pull "succeeds" without reading the damaged blob. The damage surfaces later, on another machine, or after a prune.
  • A checksum file beside the data is self-consistent, not authentic. Anyone who can change a listed file can change its line. This is the same mistake as keeping a public key beside the log it verifies (lesson 07).

Content addressing makes the first check free of any extra file: the name is the checksum. Only one value needs to be carried separately.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Air-gapped delivery of images by registry directory, mirrored registries restored from backup, any content-addressed store moved as files. It applies whether the concern is a failing disk, a truncated copy or deliberate change; the second step is for the last.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
# bundle/load.py — before the registry is started
for data in sorted(registry.glob("docker/registry/v2/blobs/sha256/*/*/data")):
    if sha256_of(data) != data.parent.name:
        raise SystemExit(f"registry blob {data.parent.name[:16]}… does not hash to its name")
  • At build, print the SHA-256 of the checksum file and record it where the bundle's carrier cannot reach: a ticket, the receiving team's notes, a signed message.
  • At load, require it: bundle/load.py --expect-sums <hash>. Without it, print that the bundle was checked against nothing but itself.
  • Test the loader on a machine with an empty image store before relying on "every image came from the bundle"; on a warm machine a pull event names the registry and may have fetched nothing.

docs.title: Count a change as applied only when the service answers, and put the old configuration back when it does not
The rule
docs.text: An automated configuration change is applied when the service answers on the new configuration. If it does not, the applier writes the previous configuration back, brings the service up on it, and records a failed attempt — not an apply.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
Three checks can all pass on a file that takes a service down. A shape check confirms the file holds only the directives the tool is allowed to write. A diff check confirms the file is what was approved. The orchestrator confirms it created and started a container. None of them loads the file as the service will. A value the service's own libraries reject — a curve name, a cipher string, a path — is found only by the service, at start, and the service's answer is to exit.

An applier that handles only the orchestrator's errors treats that as success. The verifier that runs next reports inconclusive, because its probes cannot connect, and the record says a change was applied when what happened is an outage with the bad file still in place.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text:
Any tool that edits configuration and restarts a service: policy-driven TLS settings, feature flags in files, generated proxy configuration. It matters most where the change is to cryptographic settings, because the valid values depend on the library the service was built with, which the tool writing the file may not share.

Where the service has a configuration test command (nginx -t, sshd -t), run it first; the rule still holds, because a file can pass the test and fail under the service's real environment.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
