1. Keep the previous file in memory before writing the new one.
  2. Recreate the service, then wait for the listener — a TCP connect to the service's own address and port, with a deadline.
  3. If the deadline passes: write the previous file back, recreate again, wait again, log apply-failed with whether the service came back, and return an error to the caller.
  4. Log an apply only on the other path, and include the new container's id, so a later check can tell the two apart.

docs.title: In a bundle build, always rebuild what must match the source and record the commit; reuse only what must not change
The rule
docs.text: A packaging step decides, per artifact, whether reuse is correct. Artifacts that must equal the current source are built every time and stamped with the commit they came from. Artifacts that must stay the same from one package to the next are reused, on purpose and by name.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
"Skip it if it already exists" is added to a build to save time, and it is keyed on a tag. A tag says nothing about what is behind it. The first build populates the registry; every later build finds the tag and moves on. The package's manifest gets a fresh timestamp, the test of the package passes, and the code inside is from the first build.

The same build may hold artifacts for which reuse is the requirement. Test targets that generate keys and certificates when built become different targets on every rebuild; an answer key or a recorded scan then describes something that no longer exists. Treating both kinds with one flag is the error — whichever way the flag is set, one kind is wrong.

A layer cache already makes the always-rebuild path cheap: unchanged dependency layers are reused by content, which is safe, where reuse by tag is not.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Offline bundles, release archives, base images for a lab, any build with an "if not present" shortcut. It applies whenever a package will be tested in place of the source it is supposed to contain.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
• Build source-derived images unconditionally and let the builder's cache do the saving.
  • Write the commit, and whether the tree was clean, into the package's manifest:
# bundle/build.py
commit = sh("git", "rev-parse", "HEAD")
if sh("git", "status", "--porcelain", "--", "src", "Dockerfile", "pyproject.toml", "uv.lock"):
    commit += "-dirty"
  • Reuse fixtures explicitly, with a flag that rebuilds them when that is what is meant.
  • Before testing a package, compare the commit in its manifest with the one under test. A test report names both.

docs.title: Observe what a service accepts with nothing configured before planning its migration
The rule
docs.text: Before writing a change to a service's key establishment, start it with no key-exchange, protocol or cipher line and probe it. Plan from what it accepts then, not from the library it links.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
Hybrid key exchange — a classical exchange and a post-quantum key-encapsulation mechanism (KEM) run together, such as X25519MLKEM768 — arrives in a TLS library as a group the library can negotiate. Whether a server offers it is the server's decision, and servers decide differently.

Two servers on the same OpenSSL 3.5 show it. nginx passes no group list unless told to, so it inherits the library's default list, which includes the hybrid group: an unconfigured nginx is already "enabled". PostgreSQL sets its own default list, X25519 and P-256, so an unconfigured Postgres is not. A plan that says "add the hybrid group" is a no-op for the first and the whole change for the second.

The defaults also include what a migration has to remove. Both servers, unconfigured, accept RSA key transport over TLS 1.2 — the client encrypts the session secret to the server's RSA key, with no group involved — and Postgres accepts finite-field Diffie-Hellman as well. None of that appears in a configuration file, because nothing set it.

And some runtimes cannot offer the hybrid group whatever is configured. That is a supplier dependency, and it is found by asking the runtime what it lists, not by reading its configuration reference.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Planning any change to cryptographic settings on software you did not configure from scratch: inherited estates, container images from a vendor, anything whose configuration is short. It applies again after every library upgrade, because the defaults move with the library.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
1. Start the service with its key-exchange, protocol and cipher lines removed.
  2. Probe one group per handshake, with TLS 1.3 and TLS 1.2 forced separately, and probe RSA key transport and finite-field DHE on their own (lesson 10):
openssl s_client -connect host:443 -tls1_3 -groups X25519MLKEM768 </dev/null
openssl s_client -connect host:443 -tls1_2 -cipher kRSA </dev/null
openssl s_client -connect host:443 -tls1_2 -cipher kDHE </dev/null
  1. Sort the result three ways: already offered by default; offered only when configured; not offered by this runtime at all. The third list goes to the supplier, not to the change queue.
  2. To require the hybrid group, set the group list to it alone and restrict the protocol to TLS 1.3: TLS 1.2 cannot carry it, and leaving TLS 1.2 on leaves RSA key transport and DHE on with it.

docs.title: Label a cause only after changing it and watching the effect go
The rule
docs.text: When a test set's reference answer names a cause — the configuration line behind a behaviour, the commit behind a regression — do not write the answer from reading. Run the system twice: once as it is, to see the behaviour, and once with the named cause changed, to see the behaviour go. Keep the item only if both hold, and keep both raw outputs with it.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A label written by reading is an expert's prediction, and it carries the expert's model of the software. Precedence rules, defaults and silently ignored files are exactly where that model is wrong, and they are also exactly what such a test set exists to probe. A model under test that shares the labeler's misconception will then be scored correct, and one that knows better will be scored wrong.

Two observations remove the labeler's beliefs from the label. The first shows the behaviour is real. The second is a small controlled experiment: change one thing and see whether the effect follows. It also catches the subtler error where the named line is a setting of the behaviour and not the one in force — deleting it changes nothing, because another line or the default supplies the same value.

"No line causes it" is a claim too, and it has its own experiment: remove every live line that names the setting, and the behaviour must remain.

"The evidence cannot decide" is the hardest label to defend by argument and the easiest by construction: build two systems that produce the same evidence and behave differently, and observe both.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text:
Building evaluation items, regression tests or training examples about causes: configuration tracing, root-cause attribution, "which change fixed it". It applies whoever writes the labels — a person, a script or a language model — and matters most when a model writes them, because the label then needs to stand without trusting its author.

It does not apply to labels that are definitions (a name maps to a standard name by a registry); those need a citation, not an experiment.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
• Mark the cause in the fixture and state the change that should remove the effect; have the builder apply it mechanically.
  • Choose a change of value, not a deletion, when the default would restore the same behaviour.
  • Fail the item, loudly, when either observation disagrees with the label.
  • Store the two raw outputs and their hashes beside the label.

docs.title: Before reading a configuration, know which occurrence of a setting wins in that software
The rule
docs.text: Tracing a behaviour to "the line that sets it" requires the software's own precedence rule. State the rule for each kind of server before reading its files, and resolve includes in the order the server does.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
Configuration grows by accretion: a hardening pass appends a line, a policy tool drops a file into a directory, a base image ships defaults. The result is a setting that appears more than once. Which occurrence takes effect is not a convention shared across software.

Software A setting given twice Included files OpenSSH (sshd_config) The first value read is used; later ones are ignored Read at the point of the Include line: an include at the top beats the main file, at the bottom it loses PostgreSQL (postgresql.conf) The last value read is used Read at the point of the include: after the main file's line it wins, before it loses nginx The innermost block that sets it wins: server over http Inlined where the include stands; a file the pattern does not match is not read at all

The same two lines, three winners: first value, last value, innermost block.

A reader — or a tool, or a language model — that carries one rule to all three will name the wrong line with confidence, and a change made to that line will apply cleanly and alter nothing. The verifier then reports that the change did not land, which is the right answer to the wrong edit.

Two things that are never the cause: a commented-out line, however recent it looks, and a file left in a configuration directory under a name the include pattern does not match.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any step that maps observed behaviour to configuration: a migration plan, an audit finding that cites a line, an automated change. It matters most on servers configured in layers — distribution defaults, drop-in directories, generated files.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
• Ask the server for its effective configuration where it can tell you: sshd -T, SHOW ssl_groups; in PostgreSQL, nginx -T for the inlined text.
  • When proposing an edit, edit the occurrence that wins, and say why it is that one.
  • Confirm by observation: change that line's value and probe (lesson 19).

docs.title: Set a floor per role before comparing two models, and repeat every call before believing it
The rule
docs.text: Before running a model bake-off, write down for each role the accuracy below which its output cannot be used as designed, and how many harmful errors it may make. Decide "use model B" only when A misses the floor, B clears it, and B is better on the same items by a stated margin. And score an item by the majority of several calls, because one call is one draw.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A comparison answers "which is better". The question a build needs answered is "is this good enough to act on", and the two come apart in both directions. A role whose output goes straight into an inventory — a name, a classification — has to be nearly always right, because nothing downstream catches a wrong entry; the larger model's 27 of 30 on normalization beat the smaller model's 23 and still fails that role. A role whose output is rehearsed and verified before anything depends on it can tolerate more, because the rehearsal is the check; 24 of 30 change plans verified on the wire is enough when every plan is rehearsed first.

Without a floor the bake-off always says "use the bigger one", and on a machine where the bigger one costs a swap and a queue, that answer is expensive and sometimes wrong. With a floor, the outcome set gains the two that matter: "neither — redesign the role" and "the small one with reasoning on is enough".

The repeat is for a different failure. A temperature of 0 is read as determinism, and it is not: serving engines batch, kernels reorder, and the same prompt comes back different. On single calls a role's score moves by several items from one run to the next; on majority-of-three it does not. A pipeline that acts on one reply without a verifier is acting on noise some of the time.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Choosing a model per task in any pipeline where tasks differ in what checks them: inventory fields, classifications, plans, explanations. It applies with most force on a single machine where the larger model cannot stay resident. The floors are set by the pipeline, not by the models: a role with a verifier behind it gets a lower floor than one without.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
1. For each role, write the floor and the harmful-error allowance from what consumes the output, and commit them before any model runs.
  2. Score a reply against a label or a verifier, never against a model's reading of it.
  3. Call each item three times; count it correct on a majority; report the items whose calls disagreed as a number of its own.
  4. Decide per role from the floors first and the pairwise comparison second; name the outcome from a closed list that includes "neither".
  5. Treat a role that lands "neither" as a design question — a rule, a table, a person — not as a reason to try a third model.

docs.title: Deploy from a checkout nobody edits
The rule
docs.text: Run a deployment from a checkout that exists only to be run — a detached worktree or a clone pinned to a commit — with its state in a directory of its own beside it. Never from the tree where code is edited and branches are switched. Deploying a change is an explicit step: move the checkout to the commit, rebuild, recreate.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A container's bind mount is bound to a directory's inode, not its path. When a branch switch deletes and recreates a directory that the running container mounts — a policy directory, a configuration directory — the container keeps the deleted one and sees it empty. Nothing restarts, nothing logs an error, and a health check that only asks "is the process up" keeps answering yes. In this project the page's scan and propose buttons were broken for an hour that way, and the commit that recorded the page as working was made in the same second as the switch that broke it (lesson 14 is the mechanism; this lesson is the practice that avoids it).

A separate checkout also makes "the build being shown" a fact: the deployed commit is whatever the checkout is at, and git worktree list says what that is. Numbers shown on a page can then be tied to a commit without trusting memory.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any deployment that bind-mounts files from a source tree: compose projects run from a repository, a static site served from a build directory, a configuration directory mounted into a service. It applies doubly where a coding agent works in the same tree, because an agent switches branches to review and compare, and does so without the pause a person might take.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
• One checkout per deployment, detached at a commit; a worktree of the development repository is enough and shares its objects.
  • State — ledgers, raw output, scope files, generated configuration — in a directory the checkout points at by configuration, not inside the checkout, so a change of commit never moves the record.
  • Git-ignored working files the deployment needs (environment, overlays, rendered configuration) copied into the checkout and listed, so the next person knows what is there that the repository does not hold.
  • A health check that reads the files the service depends on and names the one it cannot read, so the silent case cannot recur unnoticed.
  • The deploy procedure written down as three commands: move the checkout, rebuild, recreate.

docs.title: A hardware label in a config is a claim; record what served the call
The rule
docs.text: Every timing taken through a gateway carries two facts: the hardware label the caller's configuration asserts, and the upstream the gateway actually routed to. Record both on every call. Before a timing is published with a machine's name on it, the label is checked against the upstream; where they disagree, the upstream wins and the label is corrected.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A gateway exists so that callers do not know where a model lives — and so that the operator can move it. The caller's configuration names a machine because a number without one is worthless; but nothing updates that name when the operator rebinds the lane. In this project a bake-off's fast arm was labelled as running on a four-GPU fleet; the lane had been moved to a desk-side box the day before the bake-off ran. Every latency in the result was a number from the wrong machine until the live reply's headers were read, four days later. The accuracies were unaffected; the hardware column of a table that exists to say what hardware brings was wrong.

Most gateways name the upstream on each reply. LiteLLM sends x-litellm-model-api-base; others send their own. A caller that records it has provenance per call, not per configuration file.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any measurement of latency, throughput or cost taken through an inference gateway, a load balancer or a model router — anything that can choose or change the backend without the caller's configuration changing.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
• The inference seam records the upstream named in the reply's header as served_by on every completion and on the ledger actor of every event a model contributed to, beside the config's hardware label.
  • A result file for a measurement carries both; a report reads served_by and treats hardware as the claim it is.
  • A deployment's configuration says what each label means on what date, and a lane move in the gateway is a dated line in that file.
  • Where the gateway sends no such header, the measurement names the gateway as the hardware and says the machine behind it is not recorded.

docs.title: Size the scanner network's address range to the parallelism, and record a job that never started as its own failure
The rule
docs.text: A network that scanner containers join for the duration of a job has at least as many free addresses as jobs may run at once, plus the runner's own, plus a margin for a container that is being torn down while the next starts. A job whose container could not be created or started is recorded with the daemon's reason and a status that says the runner failed, distinct from a scan that ran and found the target unreachable.

docs.title: Why
docs.text: A scanner container on a macvlan or any network with an address pool takes an address when it starts and gives it back when it is removed. With eight jobs in flight and seven free addresses, the eighth container fails to start, and every job that starts while the pool is empty fails the same way in under a second. Those fast failures look, from the harness's side, like thirteen listeners that refused to talk: the same status, no raw output, nothing in the ledger that a reader could tell apart from a host firewall. The daemon's message — no available IPv4 addresses — was in the runner's stderr tail and nowhere a page would show it. Widened past the parallelism, the same pool lets every reachable listener answer.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any runner that launches one container per job onto a network with an explicit address range: macvlan legs into a VLAN, bridges with a small subnet, anything with --ip-range. The tighter the range was drawn for firewall reasons, the more likely it binds.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
• Set the pool from the runner's worker count: workers + 1 for the runner + a margin of a few; /28 for eight workers.
  • Or cap the workers from the pool, and say so in the runner's log.
  • Give a job that never ran its own status, carry the daemon's message into the ledger event, and show it on the page beside the target, so "the runner could not start a scanner" is never read as "the target did not answer".
  • When a targeted scan reports many failures of a few hundred milliseconds each, read the runner's log before reading anything into the targets.

docs.title: Name the reasoning setting beside the model in every measurement and binding
The rule
docs.text: Wherever a model is named — a benchmark row, a tier binding in the inference seam, a gateway lane, a journal claim — name its reasoning setting with it: thinking on or off, and the effort level if the model has one. Two numbers for the same model at different settings are numbers for two different engines. A gateway lane that pins the setting is part of the model's name, and a change to the lane's default is a rebinding that calls for a new measurement.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A hybrid-reasoning model emits a deliberation before its answer, and a flag in its chat template turns that deliberation on, off or down to a budget. The flag changes how many tokens the model writes by two orders of magnitude and changes its accuracy on any task that needs more than one step. In this project, the same 120B-A12B weights on the same machine at the same memory share traced a wire finding to its configuration line on 9 of 30 items with thinking off, 26 at medium effort and 21 with full thinking, where a quarter of the calls ran past a 900 s timeout. On conflict resolution the spread was 9 to 23 of 29. The gap between two different 120B models at one setting was two items; the gap between one model's settings was seventeen. The completion lengths tell the same story: a median of 21 tokens off, 904 at medium, 3,695 on full.

The setting is also where the gateway can change the engine without changing its name. A lane that pins thinking off for one caller's benefit serves every caller on that lane; a default moved from full to medium effort changes the result of every role bound to the tier. A row that says "the 120B" has not said which of three engines it measured.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text:
Any model with a reasoning switch or an effort level: the Nemotron 3 and 3.5 families, Gemma 4 with thinking, GPT-OSS and its effort levels, Qwen3, and the hosted models that expose a thinking budget. Through a gateway it applies twice, because the lane's configuration may pin or override the setting the caller asked for.

It does not apply to a model with no such switch, but the record still says so: "reasoning: none" is a setting.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
• The inference seam's tier definition carries a reasoning block (on or off, and the effort or budget) and a role is bound to a tier with that block, never to a model name alone; the frozen pqch.inference/1 does this and every actor on the ledger records the reasoning setting beside the model id and the engine.
  • A bake-off arm is named for its setting (-think, -nothink, -medium) and the setting is in the arm's configuration file, so a result file is self-describing.
  • A table row that compares models states the setting in the same cell as the model, and a successor model is compared with the incumbent at the same setting before it is compared at its own default.
  • When the gateway's lane changes its default reasoning setting, the roles bound to that lane are re-measured against their floors before the change is relied on (lesson 21), and the measurement records what served the call (lesson 24).

docs.title: Before keying a TLS listener, probe each kind of key exchange on its own: named groups, finite-field DHE, RSA key transport
The rule
docs.text: Write a listener's key-establishment entries only after three separate probes, or one full enumeration of its cipher suites: a handshake that offers named groups only, one that offers finite-field ephemeral Diffie-Hellman suites only (-cipher kDHE), and one that offers RSA key-transport suites only (-cipher kRSA). A listener that answers "no" to one kind has not answered for the others.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
TLS 1.2 establishes a session key in three different ways, and a server's configuration names at most one of them explicitly:

Kind What the server contributes Where it is configured What a group list shows Named group (ECDHE, or TLS 1.3 FFDHE and KEM groups) a key share in a group both sides name ssl_groups, ssl_ecdh_curve, jdk.tls.namedGroups the group Ephemeral finite-field DHE (TLS 1.2) parameters the server supplies itself, built in or from a file ssl_dh_params_file, ssl_dhparam, or nothing nothing: the group has no name on the wire RSA key transport its RSA certificate's key; the client encrypts the secret to it the cipher list, by its default nothing: no group is involved

Three kinds of key exchange, and the two a probe that offers groups cannot see.

A probe offering only named groups exercises the first row. PostgreSQL 18 with ssl_groups = 'X25519MLKEM768:X25519' refused secp256r1, which reads as a listener that does exactly what its configuration says; the same listener completed a handshake on a 2048-bit finite-field group it supplied itself (RFC 3526 group 14, PostgreSQL's built-in default when no parameters file is set) and another on RSA key transport. Both are key establishment a quantum computer breaks, and both were invisible to the probes that wrote the first version of the listener's answer key. The missing item was found by testssl.sh's cipher-suite enumeration, which reports the DHE suites and the size of the group behind them.

The failure is quiet: a probe that offers only -groups X25519 and succeeds proves X25519 is accepted and proves nothing else, and the person reading "X25519MLKEM768 and X25519 accepted, secp256r1 refused" believes the list is complete.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any TLS 1.2 listener, and any TLS 1.3 listener that also accepts 1.2. Servers whose cipher list is a default — PostgreSQL, Java, Erlang, older nginx builds — are the ones most likely to carry a DHE or key-transport path their group configuration never mentions. A TLS 1.3-only listener has no RSA key transport and no server-supplied DHE; a named-group probe is complete there.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
• Hand probes, OpenSSL 3.5, each on its own:
openssl s_client -connect HOST:PORT -groups X25519MLKEM768 </dev/null   # named groups, one at a time
openssl s_client -connect HOST:PORT -tls1_2 -cipher kDHE  </dev/null   # finite-field DHE only
openssl s_client -connect HOST:PORT -tls1_2 -cipher kRSA  </dev/null   # RSA key transport only

Read the negotiated cipher and Server Temp Key lines; a DH, 2048 bits temp key is a server-supplied group, and Cipher is AES256-GCM-SHA384 with no temp key is key transport. - In the harness the wire profile runs testssl.sh with -f (groups) and -E (every suite per protocol), and the normalizer reads DH_groups and the TLS_RSA_WITH_* suites beside the group lists (lesson 10 for what counts as accepted). - An answer key's listener is complete when it has an entry, present or decoy, for each of the three kinds; a decoy is right where the listener looks as if it would and refuses (M0B review F-62).

docs.title: Read a certificate's CA flag together with its key usage; a self-signed server certificate is usually marked CA:TRUE
The rule
docs.text: Call a certificate a certificate authority's only when it has basicConstraints CA:TRUE and keyUsage with keyCertSign. Record the bare CA:TRUE flag separately. Apply the rules that judge a leaf certificate — "no listener serves it, so it is not in use" — only to certificates that are not authorities by that reading; an authority's certificate is in use through what it issued or what names it, never by being served.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
openssl req -x509 makes a self-signed certificate, and since OpenSSL 1.1.1 it adds basicConstraints = critical, CA:TRUE to it by default. That is how most self-signed server certificates in the world are made, so most of them claim to be certificate authorities. A reader that takes the flag at its word puts a web server's certificate, a database's and a long-retired one in the same class as the organisation's internal CA.

The distinction matters because the two classes are judged by different evidence. A leaf certificate is in use when a listener serves it; one that no listener serves, in an image whose listeners were all scanned, can be marked not in use — that is what keeps a retired certificate left in an image out of the inventory (lesson 05). An authority's certificate is never served as a leaf: the records database's ca.crt is what it verifies client certificates against, the partner CA's certificate is what the API's partner listener requires a client to chain to. The same rule marks both not in use and is wrong both times, and on the first scan of the M1 estate it cost the workbench three keyed items its baselines kept.

RFC 5280 section 4.2.1.3 is the ground: when a certificate carries the keyUsage extension and is used to verify signatures on certificates, keyCertSign must be set. A CA that issues anything carries it; openssl req -x509 does not add it unless asked. The exception is an authority without any keyUsage extension, which the standard permits; such a certificate reads as a leaf here, and the inventory errs toward "unknown" rather than toward inventing an authority.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any inventory of certificate files on hosts or in images, and any rule that judges a certificate by whether it is served. It applies with particular force to internal PKI, where self-signed authorities and self-signed servers come from the same command.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
• The harness's own reader records both fields on every certificate finding: is_ca (CA:TRUE with keyCertSign) and basic_constraints_ca (the bare flag). The parser is pqch.scout.keys.parse_certificate_pem; the reader is pqch image-files.
  • The in-use rule skips every finding read from a file whose certificate has is_ca; its basis says why. An authority's in-use status is a question for the issuer links (M1, dependency chains) and the configuration that names it, which the reader records as referenced_by.
  • When writing an answer key, key the authority's certificate file as present with kind: certificate-authority, and expect a scanner that reports it as "self-signed, CA" to have read only half of it.

docs.title: Give a listener that carries TLS behind a protocol upgrade its own scan profile; a plain TLS scan of its port is silent, not negative
The rule
docs.text: Name the protocol of every listener in the scope — tls only for TLS from the first byte, otherwise the protocol whose upgrade carries it (postgres, smtp, imap, ldap). Bind each such protocol to a scan profile that speaks the upgrade, and let the plain TLS profile refuse those listeners. A listener whose protocol no profile claims is shown as not scanned; it is never shown as having no cryptography.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
Several protocols begin in the clear and switch to TLS when the client asks: PostgreSQL's SSLRequest, SMTP's and IMAP's STARTTLS, LDAP's StartTLS extended operation. A scanner that opens the port and sends a TLS ClientHello is speaking the wrong language. The server answers in its own protocol or closes the connection, the scanner finds no TLS, and — because "no TLS" is a legitimate result for a port — it reports nothing wrong. Nothing distinguishes this from a listener with no cryptography. The records database in this project, which accepts RSA key transport and a server-supplied DHE group as well as the hybrid group its configuration names, is exactly the listener an inventory most needs to see, and the plain profile saw none of it.

The fix is not a smarter scanner but an honest scope. The scope says what each listener is; the runner binds a profile per protocol and refuses a mismatch, so the silent case cannot occur by accident; and the scan plan skips a protocol no profile claims and says so, so the gap is on the page rather than in a column of zeros.

The same port, two profiles: the one that speaks the upgrade sees everything, the other sees nothing and says nothing.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL's own upgrade), mail (SMTP, IMAP, POP3), directories (LDAP), XMPP, FTP with AUTH TLS, and any service whose TLS is "optional" in its protocol. It does not apply to listeners that are TLS from the first byte on a dedicated port (HTTPS, AMQPS, LDAPS, SMTPS), which the plain profile scans.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
• In the estate's compose file, the x-pqch.endpoints entry names the protocol: {port: 5432, protocol: postgres}. The scope generator carries it; the runner's profile tls-starttls-postgres claims it and tls-targeted refuses it.
  • testssl.sh speaks the upgrades with --starttls postgres|smtp|imap|ldap; OpenSSL's s_client -starttls does the same for hand probes. Every handshake repeats the upgrade, so budget about twice the time of a plain scan.
  • A wire finding carries the listener's protocol as the scope names it, so the rules and the answer key meet it at the same subject.
  • Check for the silent case the way lesson 11 checks a monitor: scan a listener you know carries TLS behind an upgrade, and confirm the plain profile is refused rather than returning an empty result.

docs.title: Confirm every cause an answer key names by changing it, including the ones written as annotations
The rule
docs.text: An answer key's labels are what it is scored on, and a careful author confirms each one by observation. The key also tends to carry asides — the line a finding "comes from", a hint for a future scorer, a reason — written from reading because nothing is scored on them yet. Treat each of those as a label the moment anything reads it: confirm it by the same test as the labels, the behaviour with the named line as written and its absence with the line changed (lesson 19), or mark it unconfirmed. When a model's answer disagrees with an annotation, read the annotation before scoring the model.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
The labels of a test set are checked because a score rests on them; the annotations beside them are not, because nothing does. That changes the day a new role is built that reads them. Here the key's trace field, written at M0 and M1 as a note of where each planted weakness came from, became the check on the investigator's trace, and three of its entries had never been tested: two named the file that includes the cause rather than the one that holds it, and one named a commented-out line as the cause of a value the server supplies by default. The item's own comment, written by the same author on the same day, stated the default correctly. The two statements sat a few lines apart in one file and no test compared them.

A model under test that knows the software better than the annotation is then scored wrong, which is the failure lesson 19 exists to prevent — and it is more likely on exactly the cases that matter, since defaults, precedence and included files are where a reader's model of the software is weakest.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any reference data with fields that are not scored today: a why, a trace, a source, an expected location. It applies with particular force when the reference is the key for a planted estate, because the author who planted the weakness is confident about it and writes from memory. It does not mean every comment must be tested; it means a field becomes a label when code reads it, and must be confirmed then, not after a disagreement.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
1. When a new consumer of a reference field is written, list the field's values and confirm each by observation before the first scored run; record the observation beside the item as the labels' provenance is recorded.
  2. Where confirmation is a mutation (change the line, watch the behaviour go), reuse the harness that labelled the scored items — here spikes/s3/build_r5.py's method — rather than reading.
  3. A disagreement between a model and a reference is a question for both. Record the model's answer as its claim, re-derive the reference from the software's documented behaviour, and correct the key with a dated comment when the key was wrong, as records-kex-dh-2048 now carries.
  4. Where no live line sets a behaviour, write the reference as cause: default, so that a trace naming any line is scored wrong and a trace saying default is scored right.

docs.title: Ask the protocol stack's runtime what it will negotiate before calling a migration blocked, or not blocked, by its supplier
The rule
docs.text: Before recording that a system's change is blocked on its supplier — or that it is not — run the system's image with no network and ask the component that negotiates the protocol for its own list of algorithms: the TLS stack's supported groups and signature algorithms, the SSH daemon's key exchange and host-key algorithms. Keep the raw output and its hash. Do not infer the answer from the version of the cryptographic library the image contains.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A protocol stack offers only what it implements on top of the library. The library may implement ML-KEM while the TLS layer above it does not list the group, because the group, its code point and its key-share handling are the TLS layer's to add. Erlang/OTP's TLS is its own implementation: OTP 27 with OpenSSL 3.5.9 underneath has ML-KEM in the library and none in the negotiation. The reverse also happens: OpenSSH implements its ML-KEM hybrid itself, so its key exchange is post-quantum on a library that would not say so, while its host keys are not post-quantum at all. A package list gives the wrong answer both ways.

Asking the runtime with no network is cheap and leaves nothing running: the image's entry point is replaced, nothing listens, nothing is reached. The answer is the software's own, not the tool's or the reader's.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any assessment that says a change cannot be made by configuration: a supplier blocker, a "needs an upgrade" ticket, a replacement priority under OMB M-26-15 §3.C.3. It does not replace a wire check of what a running listener accepts, which depends on configuration too; it answers what the software could accept if configured. Where an image ships no tool that can list its algorithms, say so, and use the same build observed on the wire, or record the state as unknown.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
# tools/probe_capabilities.py runs these and keeps the output
docker run --rm --network none --entrypoint sh IMAGE -c 'openssl list -kem-algorithms'   # OpenSSL 3.x
docker run --rm --network none --entrypoint sh IMAGE -c 'ssh -Q kex; ssh -Q key'           # OpenSSH client
docker run --rm --network none --entrypoint sh IMAGE -c \
  "erl -noshell -eval 'io:format(\"~p~n\", [ssl:groups()]), halt().'"                      # Erlang/OTP TLS

Record the date, the image ID and the raw output's SHA-256 with the result; the result is a snapshot of that image, and a rebuilt image is measured again.

docs.title: Read a validated module's certificate for the algorithm you need, and check that the module is active, before calling a system validated
The rule
docs.text: To say a system uses a validated module for an algorithm, three things must hold and each must be checked: a FIPS 140 certificate exists whose list of approved algorithms includes that algorithm; the module the system loads is that certified module; and it is active, not merely present. Read the first from the certificate page, not from the library's name or release notes. Read the other two from the running image.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A validation certifies a module, not a library family. Many vendors validate their own builds of the same open-source provider, at different times and with different algorithm lists, and a newer release of the library may add an algorithm its validated build does not yet cover. On 2026-10-20 the OpenSSL project's own validated provider listed neither ML-KEM nor ML-DSA, while one vendor's validated build of the same provider listed both. "We use OpenSSL, which has a validated module" says nothing about post-quantum algorithms.

Presence is not use either. An image can carry a FIPS provider, built and installed, with the configuration that activates it commented out; every handshake then runs on the default provider, which is not the validated one.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any claim that a system meets a validated-module requirement, and any blocker that says a post-quantum change waits for one. It applies per algorithm: a module validated for ECDH and RSA is not thereby validated for ML-KEM. It does not settle whether a given build matches the certified version; that is in the certificate's Security Policy, which a full check reads too.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
1. Take a dated snapshot of the active certificates for the libraries the estate runs, with each certificate page's list of approved algorithms and the page's hash (tools/cmvp_snapshot.py).
  2. In each image, list the loaded providers and read the configuration that activates them (openssl list -providers; the .include of fipsmodule.cnf and its activate line).
  3. Record one of three states per item and algorithm: in-use (the certified module is loaded and active), available-not-in-use (a certificate covers the algorithm for this library; the system does not use it), or none-validated (no active certificate in the snapshot covers it).

docs.title: Score the retrieval step on its own before scoring a model's answer over it
The rule
docs.text: When a model answers from passages a retriever chose, record the retrieved passages, with their scores, on every answer, and score the retrieval separately: for each item, was the passage that settles it among those retrieved. Read the answer's score only alongside that one. Fix whichever step failed, and measure the fix on items the first round did not see.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A model that cites only what it is given — the behaviour a design wants — can answer no better than its retrieval. If the settling passage is missing, a faithful model either refuses or settles on the nearest passage it has, and a nearby passage can be a plausible wrong answer. Scored only on the final answer, that looks like a weak model; a larger model would be bought to fix a ranking problem. Here the item descriptions named algorithms, the pack's table rows named algorithms, and the queue passages named dates and functions; retrieval ranked the table rows first for 11 of 14 items, and the model, given no queue, named none — or, once, the wrong one it was handed.

Recording the retrieval on the event costs a few integers and makes the diagnosis a query over the ledger rather than a re-run.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any retrieval-augmented model job with a checkable answer: an explanation checked against a rule, a citation checked against a source, an answer checked against a key. It applies most where the query and the settling passage use different words for the same thing.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
1. On each answer, record the query and the retrieved passage ids with their scores (as integers if the record is hashed).
  2. Score two numbers per round: retrieval recall of the settling passage, and answer accuracy where retrieval succeeded.
  3. Change the retrieval — the query's wording, a filter by the item's function, a second index for the passages that settle — and measure it on a fresh set of items, against the same floor written before the first round.

docs.title: Compare two inventories by the identity of each observation and by what it says, leaving out references to the records behind it
The rule
docs.text: Give each inventory entry a reference derived from what was observed — the layer, the place, the kind of asset, its name and the key — so the same observation in two scans has the same reference. Compare two inventories by that reference, and compare each entry's content with every reference to the record behind it removed: event ids, run ids, timestamps of the scan.

docs.title: Why
docs.text: An entry that carries its evidence names the events it rests on, and a new scan writes new events for the same observation. Those ids are correct, and they are noise to a comparison: they change on every scan whether or not anything in the estate did. Left in, they turn every scan into a report of change, and a watch mode built on it re-examines everything or nothing useful. A reference made from a counter or from the order of discovery has the opposite fault: the same observation gets a new reference when anything before it changes, and an unchanged entry looks removed and re-added.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any comparison of two snapshots of an inventory or a bill of materials whose entries cite their evidence: change detection, drift reports, "what changed since yesterday". It does not apply to an audit of the evidence itself, where the event ids are the point.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
1. Make the reference a hash of the observation's identity fields, and test that two scans of the same estate produce the same references.
  2. Before comparing content, drop fields that only point at evidence (evidence lists, *-evidence properties, event keys inside structured values), recursively.
  3. Test the comparison on two scans of an estate known to be unchanged: the expected result is no change, and anything else is a bug.

docs.title: When verifying that a listener requires post-quantum key establishment, probe TLS 1.2 on its own; a classical-only TLS 1.3 client is refused, not downgraded
The rule
docs.text: A check that a listener requires hybrid post-quantum key establishment includes a TLS 1.2 handshake that must be refused, separate from the probe that offers every classical group. An accepted TLS 1.2 handshake means classical key establishment is still possible, whatever the other probes said.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
The negative probe of a paired check offers every classical group and allows any protocol version, on the idea that a server which would accept classical key exchange will do so. Against a TLS 1.3 server that is not what happens. The client offers TLS 1.3 and TLS 1.2; the server picks TLS 1.3, finds no group it shares with the client, and ends the handshake. It does not go back and offer TLS 1.2. So the probe is refused, and the check reads that as "classical refused".

TLS 1.2 is still there for a client that asks for it. In TLS 1.2 the key exchange is chosen by the cipher suite: ECDHE uses a group, but DHE uses the server's finite-field parameters, and RSA key transport uses no group at all. Restricting the groups leaves both open. And TLS 1.2 cannot carry the hybrid group, so any TLS 1.2 handshake that completes is classical key establishment.

This is the change most easily written for "require the hybrid group": set the groups, and stop. It is the plan that looks right, and on PostgreSQL it leaves RSA key transport in place, the weakest key establishment the listener had.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any verification of require on a TLS listener whose software supports TLS 1.2: nginx, PostgreSQL, Java, Erlang and most others. It does not apply to enable, where classical key establishment is still allowed. A listener that is TLS 1.3 only passes it by construction.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text: Add a fourth probe for require: openssl s_client -tls1_2 with the client's default suites (and -starttls postgres, or the protocol's own upgrade, where there is one). It must be refused; an accepted handshake caps the verdict at enabled-not-enforced and names TLS 1.2 among what the listener also accepts. On the server the matching change is a minimum protocol of TLS 1.3, beside the groups.

docs.title: When a probe claims a handshake the enumerating witness does not find, call the verdict inconclusive and say why; neither side settles it
The rule
docs.text: When the probe that must be refused reports a key exchange that the enumerating witness does not find the listener accepting, record the verdict as inconclusive, with that contradiction as the reason. Do not let either side win.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A verifier of this kind has two sorts of evidence: probes that sample one handshake each, and a witness that enumerates what the listener accepts. The witness is allowed to lower a verdict — if it finds a classical group accepted, the change is not enforced whatever the probes said — and not to raise one, because a witness that missed something must not turn a failure into a pass. That asymmetry is right, and it has a blind side: a probe misread as accepted lowers the verdict to enabled-not-enforced, the witness cannot correct it, and the result looks like a careful, conservative answer.

A probe can be misread in exactly that way. OpenSSH, offered no key exchange it shares with the server, logs kex: algorithm: (no match) and then gives up; a parser that takes the first kex: algorithm: line as the negotiated one reads a refusal as acceptance. The verdict said the listener still accepted classical key exchange; the witness said it offered only the hybrid. Both could not be true.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any verifier that combines sampling probes with an enumerating witness and lets the witness only lower the result. It does not apply when the witness errs or lists nothing; that is its own failure, already inconclusive.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
1. When the negative probe is accepted, compare what it negotiated with the witness's list. If it is not on the list, the verdict is inconclusive, and the reason names the algorithm and the disagreement.
  2. Read the raw output. Fix whichever reader was wrong, with a test built from that raw output.
  3. Re-derive every past verdict from its raw outputs with the change, and check that no honest verdict moves.

docs.title: Before citing or redrawing a standard, read its status on the publisher's page; cite the current revision by its own identifier
The rule
docs.text: Before a standard, guideline or white paper is cited, quoted or redrawn, read its status where the publisher keeps it. If it has been withdrawn, cite the publication that supersedes it, by that publication's own identifier, and say whether the part relied on changed.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
Publishers withdraw and supersede documents without removing the old copies. The old PDF stays in search results, in secondary summaries and in files saved before the change, and its title is often identical to the new one's. NIST marks a withdrawn publication by prefixing a notice page and by giving the replacement a suffix such as -upd1 or r1. A citation of the old identifier points the reader at a document the publisher no longer stands behind, and for a federal reader that undoes the credibility the citation was meant to give.

The change may be small. CSWP 39's update rewords one paragraph on the 2031 security-strength transition and leaves the rest, including Fig. 3, as it was. Saying so is part of the citation: a reader who knows the update exists will ask whether the figure moved.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text:
Every citation of a standard, a mandate or a guidance document, and in particular any figure or table redrawn from one, where a reader will compare the drawing with the source. It applies equally to a document read weeks earlier and saved: the status is a property of the day it is cited.

It does not replace reading the document. A status page says what is in force, not what it says.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
• Open the document from the publisher (for NIST, the DOI or csrc.nist.gov) on the day it is cited; read the first page for a withdrawal notice.
  • Cite the identifier in force, with its date and any update date, and the DOI.
  • In docs/SOURCES.md, record the date read, the PDF's hash, the superseded identifier, and what the update changed in the part relied on.

docs.title: Every label in a diagram of what a system does is a claim; fill it from the record and check each against the record before it is shown
The rule
docs.text: Treat every label in an architecture or capability diagram as a factual claim. Compute it from the record where it can be computed; where it is prose, check it line by line against the record before the page is shown, and mark what is partial or absent as such.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A diagram reads as a statement of fact, and its words are short enough that nobody stops to ask for the evidence. A framework's diagram adds a pull of its own: its boxes name what a complete system has — libraries, enforcement, vulnerability management — and a box left empty looks like a failure, so it gets filled with what the system ought to do or nearly does. The result is the brochure the project exists to avoid.

Prose labels drift in a second way. The author knows what the system does on the estate it was built on and writes that, and a second estate on the same page — the lab, where the system observes and changes nothing — inherits words that are true only of the first.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any page or slide that says what a system does, part by part, and in particular one laid over a published framework, where the framework's own labels set the expectation. It applies to the selection of an example too: "the last change that landed" was, on the record, a review's deliberate rollback; the example must be filtered for the kind it is meant to show.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
• Compute counts and states from the ledger at render time; never type a number into a label.
  • For every prose label, name the event, rule or file that makes it true. If none can be named, the label is partial or off, and the page says so: the overview dims a framework label an estate does not reach and says why on hover.
  • Select examples by the property they illustrate (here: a landed change toward post-quantum, every verdict re-deriving from its raw output), not by recency.
  • Render the page for each estate it covers and read every box against that estate's record.

docs.title: Draw a cryptographic inventory in columns along its dependency chain, not as a force-directed graph
The rule
docs.text: Draw a CBOM as columns that follow its dependency chain — the system a person knows, the service, its listeners and images, the cryptographic assets, the files they come from — with one service's chain shown to the end at a time, and group a directory's files into one entry when there are more than a few.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A CBOM is not a general graph. Its dependencies run one way, and that direction is the explanation a reader needs: this row of the spreadsheet is this service, which listens here, negotiates this key exchange, and is served from this file. A force-directed layout places nodes by repulsion and attraction, so it discards the direction, and a reader has to rebuild it by tracing lines. Without a force that keeps nodes inside the canvas it also scatters them out of view, and the figure reads as isolated dots.

Volume hides the chain in a second way. A base image carries a package manager's signing keys; each is real cryptographic material and a CBOM entry, and none is served by anything. Listed one per row they outnumber everything the service actually uses.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any view of an inventory whose relations have a direction: a CBOM, an SBOM's dependency tree, a data-flow inventory. It does not apply where the relations have no order, such as which clients talk to which servers, where a network layout is the honest picture.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
• One column per link of the chain, with a heading saying what it is.
  • Order the first column by what the reader brings (the spreadsheet's rows), and keep rows with no evidence visible and marked.
  • Show every service; draw the assets and files of the one in focus, and let a click move the focus.
  • Group files no asset points to by directory above a small threshold, and list them in the detail panel.
  • Position by column and row; never simulate a layout for structured data.
  • Where the estate has no spreadsheet or service names — a network observed, not built — start the chain from where the listener is: subnet, host, listener, then its entries. The columns change; the direction does not.
  • Put the view where the CBOM is opened, for every estate, not inside one walkthrough.

docs.title: Before approving a change that requires post-quantum key establishment, probe each kind of client against a copy with the change; enforced says it landed, not whom it refuses
The rule
docs.text: Before a require change is approved, run one handshake per kind of client against the listener as it runs and against a copy with the proposed configuration, and show the approver which kinds the change shuts out.

docs.title: Why
docs.text: Enforcement is refusal. A listener that requires the hybrid group refuses a TLS 1.3 client offering only classical groups outright — it does not fall back — and refuses TLS 1.2, which carries no hybrid group at all. The verifier's enforced verdict is exactly that refusal, so it can only confirm the breakage, never warn of it. The warning has to come from asking each kind of client before the change, against a copy, where a refusal costs nothing.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Every change that moves a listener from enable to require, and any change that removes an algorithm. It does not apply to enable, which adds a choice and refuses no one — though the matrix shows that too, as "unchanged".

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
pqch change matrix <change-id> --run <change-run>

The runner starts the copy in the twin network with the proposed file and probes it and the live listener with the same client profiles; the result is a matrix.completed event beside the rehearsal, shown on the change. Map the profiles onto real clients from the estate's own evidence: on a network with passive capture, the clients that never offered a hybrid group are the ones a require change would refuse.

docs.title: Before trusting a discovery tool's silence, show it something it should find; an empty result is a finding about the tool until then
The rule
docs.text: Run every discovery tool first against a target holding what it is meant to find — a planted estate, a labelled repository — and treat an empty or partial result elsewhere as unknown until it has passed that test.

docs.title: Why
docs.text: A tool's output is bounded by what it can speak and what it has rules for, and it rarely says where that boundary is. A TLS scanner whose library predates ML-KEM cannot offer the hybrid group, so a listener that requires it looks like no TLS at all. A source scanner covers named libraries; code that hashes with the standard library or signs tokens with another package is outside it, and the report says "no cryptography assets were detected". A Java analyser that resolves types from compiled classes finds nothing in source alone. Each of these is silence that reads like a clean result.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Choosing a scanner, comparing vendors, and reading any inventory a tool produced on an estate no one has labelled. It matters most for post-quantum work, where the newest algorithms are the ones older tools cannot see.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
• Score the tool against a planted estate with an answer key (here, pqch import … --key agency/answer-key.yaml), including decoys it should not report.
  • For code, use a repository with labelled call sites in the libraries the target actually uses, and check the tool's library coverage against them.
  • Record the tool's version and image digest with every result; coverage changes between releases.

docs.title: Report a change's time from approval to proof beside its time from policy to proof; the gap is the wait for a person, not the system
The rule
docs.text: Headline a change's time from approval to its last verdict; give the time from the policy decision beside it, labelled as including the wait for a person.

docs.title: Why
docs.text: Time-to-change is measured from ledger timestamps: the policy event, the approval, the verdicts. The span from policy to proof is the honest end-to-end number, but most of it can be a proposal sitting in a queue — overnight, over a weekend. Shown alone it reads as the speed of the machinery and buries the measurement that says how fast an approved change is carried out and proved. Shown alone, the other hides how long decisions take. Both are true; each answers a different question.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any page, report or talk that quotes how long a change took, whenever a person is in the loop.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
• From intervals(): approval_to_verdict_ms is the headline; policy_to_verdict_ms follows, labelled.
  • Use units a reader can take in: seconds for the machinery, minutes or hours for the wait.

docs.title: Publish a curated export, checked for leaks, not the working repository; and keep the list of what must not leak out of the published tools
The rule
docs.text: Make the public repository a fresh tree exported from the working one: leave out the private files, strip passages marked private at the source, scan the result for anything that must not leak and refuse to write it on any match — and keep that list of patterns out of the published tools.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A repository built against a real environment absorbs it: addresses in test fixtures and configuration examples, hostnames as measurement labels, a domain in a plan, findings in notes, and all of it again in every commit of the history. Turning such a repository public publishes the history too, and rewriting history to clean it is error-prone. An export with one fresh commit has no history to leak.

A scan only finds what it is told to look for, so the scan's list names the very things it protects: an internal domain, a username, a product the environment runs. Published with the tool, it would leak them itself.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any project developed against a private environment and then shared: a proof of concept built in a lab, a tool tested against production-like data, a write-up drawn from a real estate.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
• Mark private passages where they are written (here <!-- lab --> blocks, # lab claim markers and lab_only: true entries), so the export does not depend on someone remembering them.
  • Export from a commit, not the working directory (git archive), so what is published is what is committed.
  • Scan the exported tree and every built page; any match refuses the export. Keep the patterns in a private file the tools read.
  • Remap private addresses in tests to ranges the environment does not use, keeping their relationships, so the tests still mean the same thing.
  • Build any public site from the exported tree, so it can hold nothing the repository does not.

docs.title: Score an inventory against a key that knows about changes: an item a verified change removed is remediated, not missed
The rule
docs.text: When a scan follows a verified change, count each answer-key item the change removed as remediated, citing the change, and take it out of the denominator; count it as missed only if nothing removed it.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
An answer key (the list of everything planted in a test estate, written before any scan) describes the estate as built. A migration is meant to make the estate stop matching it: once a listener requires a post-quantum hybrid key exchange (one that combines a classical and a post-quantum algorithm), the classical groups it used to accept are gone, and no scan can find them. Scored naively, the scan "missed" them, and the inventory's coverage drops at the very moment the migration succeeds. That inverts the measurement: the better the estate gets, the worse the scanner appears.

The opposite shortcut is as wrong: dropping every unfound item from the denominator hides real misses. The distinction has to come from evidence: a change that was approved, applied, and verified by probes (a client offering only the new algorithm connects, one offering only the old is refused) on that listener, before the scan.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any evaluation of discovery against a known truth in an estate that can be changed: a test range, a lab, a staging copy. It does not apply to items no change touched, to changes that were enabled but not enforced (the old algorithm is still accepted, so it should still be found), or after the estate is reset to its built state, when the key is true again.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
• Key the rule on the change record, not on the absence: the item's listener, a verified change with intent require before the scan, and no reset after that change.
  • Report remediated items separately and by the change that removed them, so the score reads "35 of 35 found, 3 remediated by change X", not "35 of 38".
  • Give the estate a reset to its built state, recorded like any change, so a run can start from the key's truth again.

docs.title: After publishing a repository, read its own checks: they run in an environment the export was never tested in
The rule
docs.text: Before publishing, run each workflow's steps on a clean copy of the exported tree; after publishing, read the repository's check results.

docs.title: Why
docs.text: A working repository accumulates continuous-integration workflows (the automated checks a hosting service runs on every push) written for the state it was in when they were added. In private, a failing one is easy to stop seeing. Published, every push runs it in a fresh machine against the export, which differs from the working copy: files are left out, passages stripped, another branch serves the site. A failure there is shown beside every commit, and it is the first signal a reader gets of whether the project works.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any repository published as an export or a fresh history from a private copy, and any first push of a repository to a new host. It matters less for a repository developed in public, where the checks already run on every change.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
• List the workflows the export carries; delete any that duplicate the publish step (here a Pages workflow, where Pages is published from a branch).
  • Run each remaining step on a clean copy of the export, with a fresh environment: uv sync --group dev, the linter, the tests, the strict site build.
  • After the push, read the result (gh run list -R owner/repo) before telling anyone where the repository is.

docs.title: Before a demonstration, open the published page in a browser at each width it will be seen at, and read its network log
The rule
docs.text: Before showing a page, render the published copy, not the source tree, in a real browser at every width it will be seen at, with the network log open, and look at it.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
The checks a project runs are blind to how a page looks. A test suite renders templates and asserts on text. A crawler follows links and reports status codes, but a stylesheet's url() references are not links, so a font that fails to load is invisible to it. A leak check reads words. None of them notice that a figure's columns overlap on a phone, that a page scrolls sideways on a laptop, or that every heading is in a fallback face because the fonts were named by a root-absolute path and the site is served under a base path. A visitor notices all of it in the first second.

The published copy differs from the development copy in exactly the ways that break these things: another base path, another mode (a static snapshot instead of a live server, so a message about a missing sign-on reads as an error), another viewport.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any page served at a base path other than /, any page served from a static build of a dynamic one, and any page that will be opened on a phone from a link. It matters most before a demonstration, when the page will be seen by people who will not report what they saw.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
• Render the published address, not the source, at 1440 px and 390 px, in the dark and the light scheme. Headless Chromium through Playwright does it in a script; keep the script.
  • Record every failed request and every console error on each page; a font or a script that fails to load is a failed request, not a broken link.
  • Measure document.documentElement.scrollWidth against the viewport on every page; anything wider scrolls sideways. Find the element that overflows its parent; the fix is usually minmax(0, 1fr) in a grid, overflow-x: auto on a table, or a media rule that a later rule overrides.
  • Name assets relative to the stylesheet (url(fonts/x.woff2)), never by a root-absolute path, so one stylesheet works at any base.
  • Read every message the static copy shows that a live server would not: a form's absence, a sign-on notice, "live state" on a snapshot.

docs.title: Write each CBOM fact in CycloneDX's own field; where the standard has none, name the property as the tools you feed read it
The rule
docs.text: A CBOM (cryptography bill of materials: an inventory of the algorithms, keys, certificates and protocols an estate uses) is only as useful as the tools that can read it. Write every fact that CycloneDX defines a field for in that field. Where the standard has no field, choose the property name deliberately, after reading how the tools that will consume the CBOM name it, and write it down as a decision.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
CycloneDX 1.6 is a schema, not a vocabulary for everything a scanner sees. It defines:

Asset Standard fields that a policy can judge Protocol type (tls, ssh, ipsec, ike, …), version, cipherSuites (name, IANA identifiers, algorithm references), ikev2TransformTypes, cryptoRefArray (references to the algorithms in use, without their roles) Certificate subject, issuer, validity dates, signatureAlgorithmRef, subjectPublicKeyRef, format, extension Algorithm primitive, parameter set, curve, mode, padding, functions, classical and NIST quantum security levels Key and other material type, size, state, dates, algorithmRef

It has no field for two facts that matter most in a post-quantum inventory:

  • The key-exchange group a TLS server selected (X25519MLKEM768 or plain X25519, for example), which is where post-quantum key exchange shows. A cipher suite in TLS 1.3 does not name it.
  • Any SSH algorithm: key exchange, host key, encryption. IKEv2 has its own transform list; SSH has nothing.

Each tool fills those gaps with free-form properties, under names it chose. Two tools that both write valid CycloneDX therefore agree on the envelope and disagree on where the facts sit, and a policy engine reads only the places its own tool writes. A tool that also keeps the facts the standard does define in its own properties, as this workbench does with its pqch: properties, leaves a consumer nothing to judge at all.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text:
Whenever a CBOM leaves the tool that wrote it: imported into another scanner, a policy engine, an asset system, or handed to an auditor's tooling. It does not apply to a field only the workbench reads (its ledger links and evidence), which can stay in pqch: properties.

It does not mean adopting one vendor's names as the standard. The names for the missing fields are a choice between consumers, and writing a fact twice (the workbench's property and a consumer's) is legitimate while the standard is silent.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
1. For each fact the CBOM writer emits, check the CycloneDX schema (src/pqch/cbom/schema/bom-1.6.schema.json, definitions.cryptoProperties) for a field before writing a property.
  2. Link by reference where the schema does: a certificate to its signature algorithm and public key, a key to its algorithm, an endpoint's cipher suites to their algorithms.
  3. For a fact with no field, list the property names the target consumers read, choose one, and record the choice and the alternatives in an ADR. That includes whether a certificate is in use.
  4. Name an algorithm so that it can be judged alone. A consumer may read the algorithm's name and nothing else, so a name that carries the size or curve (RSA-2048, ECDSA-P-256), or a filled parameterSetIdentifier and curve, is safer than a family name with the size kept elsewhere.
  5. Test the result in the consumer: import the CBOM and confirm that a planted weakness is reported.

Steps 1 to 4 are applied in the workbench's writer since 2026-11-09 (ADR-0007 records the names chosen and the alternatives); step 5, the re-upload to a consumer, is still to be done with the next access to one.

docs.title: Before binding a role to an inference engine on a new machine, check four things the engine decides for itself
The rule
docs.text: Before a role is bound to an engine on a machine it has not run on, call the engine through the inference seam with the role's own request and read what comes back. Four things the engine chooses without asking, and a fifth about how it answers, decide whether the role can run at all: whether the container holds a profile for that GPU; the context window it serves; the share of the machine's memory it takes at start; and the model id it answers to. Only the role's real request exercises all four. A health check or a one-line chat shows none of them.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A packaged engine (a NIM, a vLLM image, an ollama container) ships for many machines and chooses at start what to do on this one. Each choice is sound for a dedicated data-centre GPU and wrong, or merely different, on a desk-side box whose 128 GB is one pool shared by the CPU, every engine and every container.

What the engine decides Default behaviour What it did on the DGX Spark, 2026-11-04 GPU profile The container carries built engines per GPU family and picks one that matches; none matching is a start failure The Nemotron 3 Super 120B NIM found no profile and exited. The retrieval NIM matched only an ONNX fp16 profile (every TensorRT profile, compute capability 8.6 to 12.0, marked incompatible) and that profile failed on its first request inside ONNX Runtime. The two images tagged -dgx-spark (Llama 3.1 8B, Nemotron Nano 9B v2) matched and served Context window The profile's own maximum sequence length, not the model's The 8B NIM served 8,192 tokens; the harness's roles ask for up to 16,000 completion tokens (a reasoning model thinks in the budget), so every call was refused with 400 in under 60 ms. NIM_MAX_MODEL_LEN=40960 removes the limit Memory share 0.7 of the GPU at start (vLLM-based NIMs), refused if less is free The Nano NIM wanted 85.14 GiB with 55 free and exited. On unified memory the share counts against every other tenant: NIM_MAX_GPU_MEMORY_UTILIZATION_STARTUP=0.2 for the small engine, 0.55 for the 120B under vLLM, and the harness, the estate and the page in what is left Thinking under structured output A reasoning model thinks before the typed reply only when a reasoning parser separates the two; a NIM without one, asked for a JSON schema, is held to the schema from the first token The Nano NIM's "thinking" arm matched its plain arm item for item (32 to 35 completion tokens a reply); the same request without the schema thought for 280 to 338 tokens, in the content. The roles that need thinking (call-site read, classification: spike S3) cannot get it from this container; under vLLM with --reasoning-parser the same model family can Model id The id baked into the profile, visible at /v1/models nvidia/nemotron-nano-9b-v2, while the image is nvidia-nemotron-nano-9b-v2-dgx-spark; a tier map with the image's name drew 404 on every call

None of these is a defect of the engine. Each is a choice an engine makes for a machine it cannot see whole, and the seam is the only place the four meet the role's request.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text:
Whenever an engine moves to a machine or an image it was not measured on: a new box, a new container tag, a profile change, a second engine placed beside it. It applies with any OpenAI-compatible engine; the variable names above are NVIDIA NIM's, vLLM takes --max-model-len and --gpu-memory-utilization, ollama takes neither and sizes itself.

It does not replace the measurement that binds the role (spike S3's floors): a call that comes back is necessary, not sufficient. And it says nothing about which engine is faster or better; it says only whether the role's request can be served at all.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
1. list-model-profiles (a NIM) or the engine's start log: is there a profile for this GPU, and which backend is it?
  2. GET /v1/models: the served id and max_model_len. Put that id, not the image name, in the tier map; make the window larger than the role's prompt plus its completion budget.
  3. Set the memory share before the engine starts, from the budget of everything that will be resident, and check free -g and the engine's "available KV cache" line after it loads.
  4. Run the role's own request through the seam (spikes/s3/run.py --set dev on six items) and read the recorded error field, not the HTTP status alone.
  5. For a role that needs reasoning, compare completion tokens with and without the thinking switch under the role's schema; equal counts mean the switch did nothing, and the arm must not be labelled "thinking".

The kit's kit/engines.sh carries these settings per tier in kit/engines.env, so the next box starts from what this one measured.

docs.title: When a bundle keeps an image from one build to the next, key it to a hash of its build context, never to its name
The rule
docs.text: A bundle builder that reuses an image already in the bundle must decide "already built" by a hash of the image's build context (every file's path and content), recorded in the manifest beside the image, and rebuild when the hash differs. The image's name and tag say nothing about what it was built from.

docs.title: Why
docs.text: Keeping images is right for a test estate whose every build makes new keys and certificates: rebuilding it needlessly changes the estate under the answer key. But "keep if the name exists" keeps forever. The mini-agency's api service gained a second listener on 2026-10-19; the bundle, first built on 2026-10-05, kept the api image by name on every build after, and a scan started from that bundle could not find what the source had added. All of its jobs reported ok: a scanner that cannot connect to a listener that does not exist records a finding of its own, not a failure. The defect showed only as a lower score against the answer key, which is the one check that knows what should be there.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any build that caches an artefact across runs by a stable name: a bundle, an image cache, a wheelhouse, a generated fixture. It does not apply to artefacts that must be rebuilt every time (the harness image, which must be the source as it stands) or to artefacts fetched by digest, which are keyed already.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text: bundle/build.py records source_hash per built image in manifest.json and keeps an image only while the hash of its context matches; --rebuild forces every slice image. After any bundle build, start the estate from the bundle and run one scan: the answer-key score (wire, host, posture, false positives) must match the score of the estate built from source. A bundle whose score is lower carries something stale.
