docs.title: Where a protocol upgrade can be refused, ask for it once and record the answer before scanning what it would carry
The rule
docs.text: When a protocol reaches TLS through an upgrade the server may refuse (PostgreSQL's SSLRequest, STARTTLS in SMTP, IMAP or LDAP), send the request once, record the answer as a finding, and run the TLS scan only if the answer is yes. A refusal is a result, and the plainest one: the connection continues in the clear, credentials included.

docs.title: Why
docs.text: A TLS scanner is built to describe TLS. Given a server that declines the upgrade, testssl.sh waits for a handshake that never comes, and the runner's budget ends it: the record says timeout, with no findings. A timeout and a refusal look alike in a list of jobs, and only one of them is a fact about the server. PostgreSQL's answer to SSLRequest is a single byte, S (TLS follows) or N (it does not); reading that byte takes a millisecond and states the fact.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any listener whose TLS is negotiated inside another protocol. It does not apply to a listener that starts with a TLS handshake; there a refusal is a failed handshake the scanner already reports.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text: The runner's postgres-tls-offer profile sends the SSLRequest and records the byte; a system scan runs it first for every PostgreSQL listener and scans TLS only where the answer is S. The finding is a protocol entry with tls_offered: false, and a plan puts "turn on TLS" ahead of any key-exchange step on that listener.

docs.title: An inventory read as an ordinary user must list every path it could not open
The rule
docs.text: When a server's files are read without privileges, record each path that could not be opened beside what was read, carry the list into the CBOM, and put one privileged, read-only pass in the plan. Never let an unreadable file disappear from the result.

docs.title: Why
docs.text: On a Unix system a key pair's public half is world-readable and its private half is not: an SSH host's .pub files can be read by anyone, its private keys only by root. A reader running as an ordinary user therefore finds every public key and no private one, and an inventory built from it counts the server's keys correctly while missing what they protect: which private keys exist, in what format, of what size, and whether any sits outside the expected places. Leaving the unreadable files out makes the partial picture look whole.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any inventory of files read with less than full privilege: a scan as a service account, a container without the host's root, a read of a mounted volume. It does not apply where the reader is root on the system, where nothing is unreadable to it.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text: The runner's packer lists every path it cannot open in the archive's manifest; the reader reports the list; platform.observed carries it with the user the read was made as; the CBOM's device component shows it; and the server's plan adds "read the paths an unprivileged read could not open" as a step for today.

docs.title: An offline install carries the build backend with the wheelhouse and installs outside the lock file; nothing in the runbook calls the package manager's run command
The rule
docs.text: To install a Python project on a machine with no package index, carry three things beside the runtime wheels: the build backend the project's pyproject.toml names and its dependencies, the editable-install helper if the install is to be editable, and a requirements list exported from the lock without the project itself. Install with uv pip install --offline --no-index --find-links <wheelhouse>, the requirements first and then the project with --no-deps. Every tool the runbook then runs starts with the environment's own interpreter (.venv/bin/python), never with uv run.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
Three mechanisms, each enough on its own to stop an offline install.

A wheelhouse built by downloading the lock's runtime requirements holds what the project imports, not what builds it. uv sync builds the project itself from source, which needs the backend pyproject.toml names (here hatchling, with packaging, pathspec, pluggy, tomlkit and trove-classifiers), and an editable install needs editables as well. None of these is a runtime dependency, so none is in the lock's export.

A lock file records, for every package, the URL it was resolved from. uv sync --frozen installs from those records; a --find-links directory is an extra source, not a substitute, and when the locked distribution is not matched there uv fetches the recorded URL. On a box whose policy is "no downloads" that is a silent policy breach: the download hook watched for curl, not for the package manager.

uv run <command> is "sync, then run". It resolves the project against the box's own index configuration on every call, and on a box whose configuration says no-index it cannot see the carried wheelhouse and fails before the command starts. A loader or a runbook step that shells out to uv run therefore fails on exactly the machine the offline bundle exists for. The environment's interpreter runs the installed package without resolving anything.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any install on a host with no package index, or with a local index that does not hold the project's pins: an offline bundle, an air-gapped rehearsal, a venue machine. It does not apply where the index is reachable and allowed; there uv sync --frozen is the right command and the lock is the point.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
On the build host, with the lock as it stands (an aarch64 target from an x86_64 host):

uv export --frozen --no-dev --no-hashes -o requirements.txt
grep -v '^-e \.$' requirements.txt > req-noself.txt
pip download -r requirements.txt -d wheelhouse --platform manylinux2014_aarch64 --platform any \
    --python-version 3.12 --implementation cp --abi cp312 --abi abi3 --abi none --only-binary=:all:
pip download hatchling editables -d wheelhouse --platform any --python-version 3.12 --only-binary=:all:
rm wheelhouse/<project>-*.zip      # pip's source archive of the project tree, not a wheel

On the target, in the checkout:

uv venv --clear
uv pip install --offline --no-index --find-links wheelhouse -r req-noself.txt
uv pip install --offline --no-index --no-deps --find-links wheelhouse .
.venv/bin/python -c "import <package>"

Tooling in the repository that runs the package (bundle/load.py) calls sys.executable -m <package>; the runbook writes .venv/bin/python tools.py, never uv run. Where uv run cannot be avoided, UV_NO_SYNC=1 UV_OFFLINE=1 makes it use the environment as it stands.

docs.title: When a box already serves the engines on its loopback, join their containers to the kit's bridge under the kit's names instead of starting them again
The rule
docs.text: If the machine the kit lands on already runs the inference engines in containers of its own, published on the host's loopback, do not start the kit's engine containers beside them. Attach the box's containers to the kit's bridge with docker network connect --alias <kit name> <bridge> <container>, point the tier map at the container's own listening port, and leave the box's launch recipe as it is.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
The kit's UI service runs on a bridge with an explicit subnet and reaches each engine by a name the tier map gives (pqch-engine-fast, pqch-engine-embed). A port published on 127.0.0.1 is the host's loopback, which a container on a bridge cannot reach; host-gateway reaches the host's bridge address, not its loopback. Starting the kit's own engine containers would work but would double the GPU residency and discard a recipe the box's operators have tuned and tested for that hardware (on the demo GB10, Lightning under vLLM 0.27.1 with DSpark speculative decoding, flags the kit's launcher does not carry). A Docker container can belong to several networks; an alias on the second network is a name only that network resolves. The engine is then one process, reachable by the box's tools on the loopback and by the kit on the bridge.

Two consequences follow. The tier map names the port the container listens on, not the host's published port (8000 inside, where the host sees 8001). And the attachment lives on the container: whatever recreates the container, such as the box's own up and down, drops it, so the two connect commands are part of any restart.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: A machine with its own container stack for inference that is tested on that hardware: a workshop image, a shared lab box, a vendor's demonstration unit. It does not apply to a bare host, where kit/engines.sh starts the engines on the bridge directly, nor to engines that run outside Docker, which need a relay on the bridge or a bind to the bridge's address.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
docker network create --subnet 172.16.108.0/24 pqch-kit-inference
docker network connect --alias pqch-engine-fast  pqch-kit-inference <llm container>
docker network connect --alias pqch-engine-embed pqch-kit-inference <embed container>
docker run --rm --network pqch-kit-inference <any local image> getent hosts pqch-engine-fast pqch-engine-embed

In kit/inference.yaml, each tier's base_url uses the container's listening port and its served model id; the roles stay unmeasured on that engine until spike S3's dev set has run against it (lesson 49).

docs.title: A reply cap on a thinking tier is a thinking budget: set it from the measured tokens of the role's hardest items, and record a cut-off as an empty reply
The rule
docs.text: When a role is bound to a tier whose engine reasons before it answers, the reply's max_tokens is the budget for the thinking and the answer together. Set it from the measured token use of that role's hardest items on that engine, at or above the largest value seen, and never from the length of the answer alone. A reply that stops at the cap is an empty reply: record it with its finish reason, score it as wrong, and never retry it silently or raise the cap for one call.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
An OpenAI-style completion has one token cap. With a reasoning parser on, the engine writes its thinking into the same budget before it writes the typed answer, and the parser only separates the two afterwards. When the budget runs out during the thinking there is no answer at all: the body is empty and the finish reason says length. The thinking is longest on exactly the items that matter, the ambiguous conflict or the plan with a constraint, so a cap that fits the median item fails the hard ones. Measured on one engine: conflict resolution thinks for a median of 11,600 tokens and one call in nine runs past 16,000, so a 4,000-token cap sized for the answer returns nothing on every item; classification's 90th percentile sits at 4,136, just over the same cap, so one call in ten would vanish. A cut-off is a wrong reply, not a missing one: the rule that the model only interprets still stands, the rule's own answer is shown, and the empty reply is on the record with its cause.

The budget is for the role's worst call, not its typical one, because the same input does not think the same length twice: one Ask the CBOM question on the same engine used 2,790 completion tokens on one run and ran past 16,000 on another, with the same passages shown.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Every role bound with reasoning: true in the tier map, on any engine that thinks inside the completion (vLLM's reasoning parsers, a NIM's reasoning mode). It does not apply to a tier with thinking off, where the cap bounds the answer alone, nor to a gateway lane that holds the thinking outside the completion's budget.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
Each role's call site sets max_tokens with the measurement beside it. Spike S3's development set gives the distribution per role and engine, a cut-off counted at its cap:

for r in r1 r2 r3 r4 r5 r6; do f=spikes/s3/results/dev/<arm>/$r.jsonl; cap=16000; [ $r = r6 ] && cap=20000
  jq -s --argjson cap $cap 'map(if .finish_reason=="length" then $cap else (.usage.completion_tokens // 0) end)
     | sort | {n: length, p50: .[length/2|floor], p90: .[(length*0.9)|floor], max: .[-1]}' -c $f; done

The harness's caps are 16,000 for call-site read, classification, conflict resolution, trace-to-cause and Ask the CBOM, and 20,000 for change plans, the spike's own envelope. A role whose p90 approaches its cap on a new engine is re-measured before it is bound there; the cap moves only with a row in the BRIEF's table.

docs.title: A signer's first signature over an event is a floor on the span that starts there, never a reading of it; check a ledger's clock against the bracket, not the floor
The rule
docs.text: A signed checkpoint says two things about an event: the first checkpoint whose sequence covers it says the event existed by that signing time, and the last checkpoint before it says the event did not exist before that time. A span between two events therefore has, by the signer's clock, a floor (first seen of the end minus first seen of the start) and a ceiling (first seen of the end minus the signature before the start). The ledger's own span, from its stamped timestamps, is consistent with the signer when it lies inside that bracket, each end within the allowed skew. A check that compares the ledger's span to the floor alone reports a disagreement whenever an event waited for its first signature.

docs.title: Why
docs.text: A checkpoint is signed when the writer asks for one, not when each event is written. A proposal that drafts a change through a model holds its run open for minutes between the policy event and the first checkpoint, so the signer's first sight of the policy event is late by exactly that wait, and a span measured from it is short by the same amount. The ledger's timestamp, stamped when the event was written, is not wrong, and neither is the signer: the two measure different things. The ceiling from the signature before the event is what bounds a backdated stamp, and that is the end of the bracket a backdating would cross. The floor catches a stamp set in the future. Both are needed; neither alone is a reading.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any ledger with an independent signer whose checkpoints are not one per event: an append-only run ledger with periodic signatures, a transparency log with batched signed tree heads. It does not apply where every event is individually countersigned at write time, where first-seen and the stamp coincide.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text: pqch.migrator.intervals computes, per change, the ledger span, the signer floor (signer_policy_to_verdict_ms) and the signer ceiling (signer_policy_to_verdict_max_ms), and reports clocks_disagree_ms only when the ledger span falls below the floor or above the ceiling by more than twice the skew allowance. The resolution page shows the time-to-change with both signer readings beside it; a disagreement replaces the time with the size of the breach. When reading a span from any signed ledger, quote the bracket, and say which end the stamped value sits near.

docs.title: When two renderers must show the same header, give them one stylesheet and one markup shape, copied at build time; a second implementation that matches by description drifts
The rule
docs.text: Where an application and a static site are meant to read as one place, the header is one file: one stylesheet, which the application serves and the site build copies in, and one element shape, which the application's template and the site's theme override both emit. The site's own theme styles the page below the header and nothing above it. Nothing about the header is written twice.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A header described twice — "boxed on the left, the notes on the right, the same two rows" — is implemented twice, and two implementations agree only on the day they are written. Each later change lands in one of them: a date line under a label, a tighter gap, a kraft box. The reader does not see two stylesheets; they see the band at the top of the page change colour, face and height the moment they click from the demonstration into the notes, and read that as leaving one site for another. That is the opposite of what the shared header is for.

The static-site generator cannot read the application's stylesheet at serve time, since it is served from another path and, on a published copy, from another host. So the build copies the file in, beside the fonts it needs, and the generator lists it before its own theme. Fonts referenced by a relative path resolve in both places when a fonts/ directory sits beside the stylesheet on each side. The generator's own additions — the search box, the drawer that opens the index on a narrow screen — are styled in the site's own file in the header's colours, which the header stylesheet carries as custom properties on the header element itself, so the site needs no copy of the application's palette.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any application that serves a documentation site beside itself and wants the two to share a header: a server-rendered app with a mkdocs or similar site under a sub-path. It also holds for a published static copy of both, where the copy must carry the file. It does not apply where the two are meant to look different, and it does not make the generator's chrome (sidebar, search, footer) part of the shared file; those stay the site's own.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
• The header's rules live in one file the application serves (src/pqch/ui/static/header.css), imported first by the application's stylesheet. The palette it needs is declared on the header element, not on :root.
  • The site build copies that file in (tools/build_site.py, copy_header), beside the fonts, into site_src/stylesheets/; the copy is generated and git-ignored, and mkdocs.yml lists it before the site's theme.
  • The application's template (src/pqch/ui/templates/_header.html) and the site's override (site_overrides/partials/header.html) emit the same elements with the same classes; the site's override adds the generator's tools inside the brand row, and the site's stylesheet styles only those.
  • After a change, open the application's page and a site page side by side at each width the demonstration will be seen at and compare the header's rows; a difference in height or face means something was written twice.

docs.title: A model whose chat template thinks by default must be told not to on every plain call
The rule
docs.text: When an engine serves a model whose chat template reasons by default, as Nemotron 3 and 3.5 do, put chat_template_kwargs: {enable_thinking: false} in the request block of every tier meant to answer plainly, and let a role that should reason turn it back on. With thinking off, do not rely on the engine's structured-output grammar. Write the reply's JSON shape into the prompt, parse and validate the reply in the inference seam (the one module every model call goes through), and retry once.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A reasoning template writes its thinking first, inside the same token budget as the answer (lesson 55). A plain call sized for a one-line answer therefore ends during the thinking: the content is empty and the finish reason is length, every time. Measured on Nemotron 3.5 Lightning under vLLM 0.27.1, five of five 120-token calls came back empty. The same calls with thinking off answered in 46 to 78 tokens in about a second. On a stage, an empty narration looks like a broken demo, not a budget problem.

Structured output constrains each token to a grammar. With thinking off on that engine, the grammar let one call in five run on to its cap without closing the object. The same happened once in five with thinking on, at 4,000 tokens and 27 s. A prompt that shows the shape, plus a validator and one retry, gives the same guarantee to the caller. A failure costs one more short call, not a stalled one: with that arrangement the ask-cbom role passed every citation check on 12 of 12 items at a median of 2.8 s.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any model whose template thinks unless told otherwise, on any OpenAI-compatible engine that passes chat_template_kwargs through (vLLM, SGLang, a NIM built on either). It does not apply to a model without a reasoning template, or to an engine that keeps the thinking outside the completion's budget. Whether a grammar stalls depends on the engine and its version, so measure it on each new engine before relying on it.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
In the tier map, the request block rides on every plain call to that tier (kit/inference.promax.yaml):

tiers:
  fast:
    request: {chat_template_kwargs: {enable_thinking: false}}
    structured: false          # the shape goes in the prompt; the seam validates, one retry
    reasoning:
      request: {chat_template_kwargs: {enable_thinking: true}}
      structured: true

To check an engine, send five plain calls at a small cap and five with the schema, then count the length finishes: spikes/s3/results/2026-11-05-promax-thinking-default-and-grammar.json records the four arms.

docs.title: Serve a static site that is rebuilt in place with Cache-Control: no-cache
The rule
docs.text: When an application serves a static site from a directory that is rebuilt in place, have it send Cache-Control: no-cache with every file. A page whose header or content must change together with the application's pages should never be left to the browser's own freshness guess.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A file server such as Starlette's StaticFiles sends Last-Modified and an ETag but no Cache-Control. With no stated expiry, HTTP lets a browser choose a heuristic freshness, typically a tenth of the time since the file last changed (RFC 9111, section 4.2.2). During that time the browser does not ask the server at all. A page built three days ago is therefore reused for about seven hours after a rebuild. The server is right, the reader sees the old page, and a reload shows the old page again. Here the result was a site header that still had a removed tab and lacked a new one, on some pages and not others, depending on which pages the reader had opened before.

no-cache does not stop caching. It makes the browser ask before reusing its copy. With an ETag the answer is a 304 Not Modified with no body, so the cost is one round trip per page.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any static content the reader expects to change with the application: documentation served beside a demonstration, a preview of a build, a generated report. It does not apply to fingerprinted assets (file names that carry a content hash), which can be cached for a long time because a new build gives them new names.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
Subclass the static handler and set the header (src/pqch/ui/app.py):

class _Revalidated(StaticFiles):
    def file_response(self, *args, **kwargs):
        response = super().file_response(*args, **kwargs)
        response.headers["Cache-Control"] = "no-cache"
        return response

Check it with curl -sI <url> | grep -i cache-control. Copies that a browser saved before the change carry no such header and stay until they expire. Clear them once, with a hard reload of each page or by clearing the browser's cache.

docs.title: Before a component goes in an architecture picture, find the line of code that calls it
The rule
docs.text: Draw a component in an architecture picture only when you can point to the code that calls it, and draw a path through the picture only when a request follows that path in the code. Write the call site next to each box in the drawing's source. A component that is installed on the machine but not called stays out, or is drawn apart and labelled as available.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A picture is believed more readily than a sentence and checked less often. A box tends to arrive because it belongs to the platform, sits on the machine, or appears in a reference design. Milvus and the rerank NIM were on the demonstration box, part of its RAG stack, and a retrieval-augmented system "usually" has both. Retrieval here is an embedding call, a cosine over a few hundred cached vectors inside the application, and a rule that follows the CBOM's dependencies. That is enough at this size, and it is easier to explain. The picture claimed more than the system does. One question from a technical judge ("what is in your vector store?") would have exposed it, and the honest answer would have cost the drawing its credibility.

The same holds for paths. The question journey was drawn ending at the deliberate tier after Ask had moved to the fast tier without thinking by measurement (lesson 58). A drawing is not updated when a role moves unless the role's binding is what the drawing reads.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Every architecture picture shown to someone who may act on it: a demonstration, a design review, a proposal. It does not apply to a picture labelled as a target or reference design, as long as the label is in the picture and not only in the speaker's words.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
Before showing the picture, search for each box's call site:

for c in milvus rerank embed vllm signer runner; do printf '%-8s ' $c; grep -rli "$c" src/pqch --include=*.py | head -1 | grep . || echo NONE; done

A box with no call site comes out. A path is checked against the role bindings in the tier map. The field notes' drawing of the stack (tools/draw.py, sketch_arch_five_layers) states the check in its docstring, with the date it was made.

docs.title: Give an animated presentation a snapshot mode, and photograph every frame
The rule
docs.text: A page that presents in beats, with counters that climb, panels that fade in and graphs that settle, needs a mode in which every beat draws its final state at once. Use that mode to take a still of every beat at the resolution it will be shown at, then read each still before the presentation.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A run-through watches motion, and the eye forgives what passes quickly: a placeholder that is replaced a second later, a number that is wrong only while it is counting, a panel that never arrives because the one before it threw an exception. A headless browser's screenshot is taken when the page has loaded, which is the first frame of each animation, not the last. So without a snapshot mode neither a person nor a machine sees the state the audience will be left looking at.

The snapshot mode does three things: the data is inlined in the page, so nothing waits on the network; every delay is zero and every transition is finished; and a page error is written into the page, so the still shows it. Each beat then renders the same way every time, and a defect is in the picture. The stills here caught an object printed as [object Object], an elapsed time of ×Infinity measured from an event the change did not have, and a beat drawn half-way.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any presentation built as a web page with animation or live data: a demonstration, a dashboard shown on a screen, a walkthrough. It does not replace a run-through at full speed, which tests timing and pace; it tests what is drawn.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
The demonstration takes ?snap=1. Each beat is a fragment:

firefox --headless --no-remote --profile <scratch>/prof --window-size=1920,1080 \
  --screenshot beat.png "http://127.0.0.1:8080/demo?snap=1#scan"

A fresh profile renders the light colour scheme. To shoot the dark scheme, put user_pref("ui.systemUsesDarkTheme", 1); in the profile's user.js. Inside the page, the snapshot flag zeroes the delay helper, sets every counter and gauge to its end value, and catches each panel's errors separately, so one failure cannot hide the rest of the beat.

docs.title: Before a container changes the user it runs as, hand over the files it appends to in a sticky volume
The rule
docs.text: When a service that keeps a log or a state file in a shared, world-writable, sticky directory is moved to another user (a container's user: changed, from the operator's uid to root or back), change the owner of those files to the new user before it starts. Do not assume root can write anything.

docs.title: Why
docs.text: A sticky directory (mode 1777, like /tmp) lets anyone create files in it but lets only a file's owner remove or rename it. Linux's protected_regular setting goes further, against a class of attacks in which a file is planted where a privileged program will open it. An open with O_CREAT of an existing file in such a directory is refused when the file belongs to neither the process nor the directory's owner. Appending with "create if missing" (Python's open(path, "a"), the shell's >>) uses O_CREAT. Ubuntu sets the value to 2. So a runner that wrote jobs.jsonl as uid 1001 and then restarts as root is refused on its own log, with EACCES. That reads like a permissions bug in the runner and is the kernel working as intended.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: A volume or bind mount whose directory is world-writable and sticky, a file in it owned by the previous user, and a new user that is neither that owner nor the directory's owner. It does not apply to a directory owned by the new user, or to a volume created fresh after the change.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
Hand the files over before the first write as the new user:

docker exec <container> chown 0:0 /var/pqch-runner/jobs.jsonl     # to root
docker exec <container> chown 1001:1001 /var/pqch-runner/jobs.jsonl  # and back

Better still, give each service a directory owned by the user it runs as, so the sticky bit is not needed. The kit's compose.system.yaml records the step beside the setting that changes the user.

docs.title: A static copy of a model page shows a recorded call and checks it again
The rule
docs.text: When a page whose answer comes from a model is published as a static copy, show answers recorded from a real call, labelled as recorded with the model, the hardware and the date. Offer only the questions that were recorded. Store the model's reply, never the verdict on it, and run the check again where the copy is built.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A static site cannot call a model, so there are three honest options. A page can go dark, which is what a link rewritten to "in the live workbench only" amounts to. A page can be removed, which hides the feature. Or a page can show a real call and say exactly what it is. A recording is evidence of what one engine said once. Dressed as a live answer, it would claim a capability the copy does not have.

The check is a different kind of thing. In Ask the CBOM, a rule decides whether each cited ledger event exists and was among the passages the model was shown (CBOM: the cryptography bill of materials, the estate's inventory of algorithms, keys, certificates and protocols). The rule is code. It costs nothing to run again, and it reads the ledger the copy actually publishes. A stored "passes" would still read "passes" if the published ledger were later trimmed or rebuilt. A recomputed one shows "fails" instead. So the reply is stored and the verdict is computed where the reader reads it.

The hardware is the same kind of claim. A page that says "on this box" is true where it is served live. In a copy it must name the hardware the runs themselves recorded, read from their ledger, and say that the architecture drawn is the design rather than the machine that produced these numbers.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any page that shows a model's output beside a rule's check of it, published where the model cannot be reached: a static demonstration site, an offline handout, a screenshot set for a talk. It does not apply to the running workbench, where every question is a live call. It does not make a recorded answer a measurement. The role's binding still comes from the evaluation set with its floors and repeats, and the recording is one call per question.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
Record against the scan run the copy will publish, on the profile whose binding was measured:

# the deployment's runs, the lab's profile; the key from the app container's environment
PQCH_VAR=/path/to/var PQCH_INFERENCE_CONFIG=/path/to/inference.yaml \
  uv run python -m pqch.cli ask record            # writes var/ask/<run>.json

The public build (tools/build_public.py) copies the recording for each run it publishes and renders the Ask page and one page per recorded question in snapshot mode. There the route reads the recording, calls no model, and passes the stored reply through pqch.ask.check against the run's ledger. A run with no recording gets a page that says so, and a question that was not recorded is answered with "only the example questions are answered in this copy". Record again whenever the published scan run changes. A recording is keyed to its run and is ignored for any other.

The demo stage follows the same rule. pqch demo record narrates each row of the scan's plan once through the call the live stage makes and keeps the lines in var/demo/<run>.json. In the public build the stage inlines its whole document: the test agency only, never a server read whole; every CBOM entry the entry panel shows; the recorded narration; and the Ask beat pointed at the recorded answer pages. The scan replays from its ledger, the change from the latest change run in which a change landed (a run left waiting for an approval has nothing to prove), the buttons that would start a scan or approve a change say they need the running workbench, and the hardware is the label the scan jobs wrote on the ledger.

docs.title: Run the accessibility check in every colour scheme a page ships
The rule
docs.text: When a page follows the reader's colour scheme (prefers-color-scheme), run the automated accessibility check once per scheme, and fail on a serious violation in either. The check here is axe-core (Deque's open-source accessibility rule engine, run in headless Chromium) against WCAG 2.1 (the W3C's Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, version 2.1), whose success criterion 1.4.3 sets the contrast minimum for text.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A contrast ratio is computed from the two colours the reader actually sees. A page with a dark and a light scheme is two pages for this purpose: every text colour, every tinted background and every translucent colour is a different pair in each. A checker running in a headless browser sees whichever scheme the browser reports, which is light unless it is told otherwise, so one pass checks half of what ships.

Translucent text is where the two diverge most. A colour such as rgba(196,207,221,.56) is blended with whatever is behind it: the same declaration gives 4.48:1 on the page and 4.41:1 on a card, both under the 4.5:1 that SC 1.4.3 asks of normal text; at .62 it gives 5.22:1 and 5.13:1. The light scheme's dim text is opaque and passes for that colour; its own failure is a different opaque grey (--classical, 4.31:1 on the page background), which the checker finds only in the light pass. Each scheme fails on a colour the other never shows.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any page with more than one colour scheme, a high-contrast mode or a theme switch. It applies to the public copy of a page as well as the served one when they share stylesheets. It does not replace a person checking with a keyboard and a screen reader: axe-core finds what can be computed from the page, not whether the page makes sense read aloud.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
Open one browser page per scheme and run the same check in each (Playwright's color_scheme):

# tools/a11y_check.py
for scheme in ("light", "dark"):
    page = browser.new_page(color_scheme=scheme, reduced_motion="reduce")
    ...
    res = page.evaluate("tags => axe.run(document, {runOnly: {type: 'tag', values: tags}})",
                        ["wcag2a", "wcag2aa", "wcag21a", "wcag21aa"])

Fix a failing colour at its definition, not at each use: here one variable in each scheme's block of style.css and header.css. Keep the check as a test (tests/test_accessibility.py) so a new colour is measured before it ships.

docs.title: Before making a shared directory's files private, find every reader
The rule
docs.text: Before a change makes the files under a shared directory 0600 and its directories 0700, list every process that reads them and the user each one runs as. If they are not all one user, make the private mode a setting, and turn it on per deployment once they are.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A file's mode decides who may read it by user and group. 0600 leaves only the owner. That is the right mode for a ledger, raw scanner output or a CBOM, which together map an estate's weakest cryptography. But a pipeline split across containers often writes as one user and reads as another. In the workbench's kit, the system runner runs as root so it can read host keys only root can read. It writes its raw output under var/raw, and the app reads that output as the operator's uid. Written 0600 by root, it is unreadable to the app (uid 1000 is neither root nor in group 0), so the server scan would stop at the read. The uids are read from kit/compose.system.yaml and compose.yaml; the failure was reasoned from them, not exercised.

Two writers, three readers, three uids: the file a private mode would close is the one the app needs.

Two shortcuts make it worse:

  • A process-wide umask. It also governs files written for other audiences. The runner renders the test estate's configuration, which the estate's services read as their own users.
  • A group-readable mode (0640). Root's files carry group 0, which the reader is not in.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any shared volume, bind mount or network share written by more than one service. It does not apply where one user writes and reads everything; there, private modes cost nothing.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
Change modes at each writer, not with a umask, behind a setting. The workbench's version is PQCH_VAR_PRIVATE=1 (src/pqch/varmode.py), with a sweep for what was written before:

PQCH_VAR_PRIVATE=1   # on every service that writes under var/
pqch var harden      # once: directories 0700, files 0600, symlinks not followed

Write down which readers you checked, including any that read from the host outside the containers: here tools/build_public.py --var, which runs as the invoking user and, after pqch var harden, has to run as the files' owner. The data-handling page (site_src/data-handling.md) states why the setting is off by default.

docs.title: Pinning through OpenSSL checks the anchor's dates
The rule
docs.text: Before pinning a management controller's certificate (or holding a session to the certificate just observed), check that the certificate is within its validity dates. If it is not, issue the controller a new certificate first. Otherwise the pinned read fails before any credential is sent.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A management controller (iDRAC, iLO, a BMC) usually serves a self-signed certificate. No CA vouches for it, so the usual choices are no verification or a pin: the fingerprint seen once, required ever after.

With Python's ssl module and anything else on OpenSSL, the simplest sound pin is a context that trusts only the served certificate:

  • load the served certificate as the context's only trust anchor
  • turn hostname checking off (controllers are reached by address)
  • for a leaf a CA issued, add partial-chain verification so the leaf alone can anchor

OpenSSL then checks the chain it builds, and that check includes the anchor's validity dates. A baseboard management controller (BMC, the service processor that manages a server out of band; Dell's is the iDRAC) ships with a self-signed certificate issued at first boot with a fixed lifetime, and in our experience it is rarely renewed, so an expired anchor is the common case rather than the exception (the lab's one controller; not a survey). The failure is correct: an expired certificate is not trustworthy by its own terms. But it surprises an operator who expected the pin to compare fingerprints only.

docs.title: Where the measurement stops
docs.text: Measured with a self-signed P-256 certificate carrying the CA bit (BasicConstraints: CA), as the test generates it. Not measured: a CA-issued leaf used as the anchor through partial-chain verification, and a self-signed certificate without the CA bit, which is what a controller usually serves; both go through the same OpenSSL date check by its documentation, and the test asserts the refusal names expiry.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any pin, trust on first use, or hold-to-observed-certificate built by loading the served certificate into an OpenSSL trust store. It does not apply to a pin that compares a fingerprint after an unverified handshake. That pin accepts an expired certificate, and the credentials are sent before the comparison unless the code is careful.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
Read the controller's certificate dates from an observing handshake first. The workbench's reader records them with no credential sent. Renew the certificate if it has expired, then turn the pin on in the controller's secrets file:

# PQCH_CONTROLLER_SECRETS/<host>.env
REDFISH_TRUST=observed       # the session held to the certificate this read observed; or: pin, with
                             # REDFISH_PIN_SHA256=<the fingerprint an earlier read recorded>

The read records its mode and fingerprints in the controller's platform.observed event. When the session does not verify, it records why and stops before the login.

docs.title: Publish a recording, a record and notes, not a facsimile
The rule
docs.text: When a system that runs in one place has to be shown where it cannot run, publish three things and nothing else: a recording of it doing its work, labelled as a recording; the record it produced, as documents with their hashes; and notes, with the system's own screens as screenshots. Do not publish a static copy of its pages with the controls disabled.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A static copy of a live page is a facsimile: it looks like the application and is not. It costs, for every page, a recorded fixture to render it from, a branch in the template for what must be hidden or disabled, a note under each dead control saying so, and a check that nothing private reached the render. That cost grows with the application's features, so the public copy becomes a second rendering target for the whole application, maintained in step with the first. And the facsimile misleads exactly the reader who matters most: the one who checks. A button that does nothing teaches that reader to distrust the pages that are honest.

The three audiences of such a site want different things, and none of them wants the facsimile. A person shown the project on a machine that cannot run it wants a walk-through: a recording gives it, with its date and the hardware it ran on. A person who checks wants the output and the method: the documents, their hashes and the notes give it, and a verifier they can run gives more than any page. A reader wants the explanation: the notes, with the screens shown as they were captured, so a picture never has a dead button.

Three things to publish, and the one not to: the facsimile is the only one whose cost grows with the application.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any system that runs behind a door, on an owner's hardware or on data that cannot leave, and has to be shown outside it: a demonstration published to a static host, a screenshot deck for a restricted laptop, a paper's artefact. It applies most where the audience includes people who will check. It does not apply where the public copy is the system, served live with its own data, and it does not forbid one honest viewer over published documents (here, the CBOM opened entry by entry), which is a document reader, not a facsimile.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
Name the pages the public copy renders in one list, and test that the shared header offers no other. Generate the record page from the published run at build time, so a document's hash is never typed by hand. Capture screenshots with a tool from a curated workspace that holds only what may be published, at a fixed width and scheme, and recapture when a page changes. Write the decision down, so the next feature is given a beat, a row or a picture, and not a page.

# the workbench's version (ADR-0006)
tools/build_public.py      # PUBLIC_PAGES: the stage, the CBOM viewer, the recorded answers, About; record_page()
tools/screenshots.py       # the other screens, captured from the curated runs into docs/journal/img/pages/ (the site build copies them in)
site_src/pages.md          # the captions beside them

docs.title: When two sources describe one asset, keep every claim, put one in force by the grade of its evidence, and show the rest as dissent; never fold two values into a list
The rule
docs.text: Every finding about an entry is a claim, and the inventory keeps all of them. Each claim carries the grade of its evidence, from a small ordered table kept as data: observed on the wire (a handshake or probe the harness made or watched), observed on the host (a running system's firmware or controller answered), parsed from a file (a certificate, key or configuration read), reported (a document someone else produced: an imported CBOM, a supplier's statement). The entry's values come from the best-graded claim, the earliest on the ledger at equal grade, and the entry says which claim that was and what decided it. A parameter two claims give different values for is written as dissent beside the entry, every value with its grade, tool and event; it is shown, not resolved. A person may set a field by a recorded resolution event, which outranks the rule until a recorded revocation cites it. No value is ever folded into a list of both, and no field changes type.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
Two tools that read one estate will disagree: a certificate's expiry in a stale export, a key size one parser reports and another does not, a group spelled three ways. The two easy answers are both wrong. Folding the values into a list of both keeps the information but changes the field's type, so a rule that reads a key size as an integer breaks on the next entry, and a reader is told only that two values exist, not which to believe. Taking the first finding loses the other without a trace, so a stale document imported after a fresh scan can silently overwrite the scan, and nobody can tell afterwards which tool said what.

Precedence by grade rather than by tool is what makes the order defensible: a handshake the harness watched is better evidence about a listener than any document's description of it, whoever wrote the document; and the order is a handful of rows in a versioned file, not a judgement about vendors buried in code. Writing the dissent beside the entry is what makes the merge auditable: the reader who checks sees both values, who said each, and which rule chose, and can overrule it in the open with an event that names its basis.

Identity is handled the same way: a claim that carries no key identity (an imported entry whose document had no field for the public key's hash) joins the one identified entry in the same place with the same kind, role and name; with two or more such entries it stays apart as a possible match, never an identity assumed.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text:
Any inventory, cryptographic or not, assembled from more than one source, and any single source that reports one thing twice. It applies with special force when documents from outside are brought in: an imported CBOM, a supplier's statement, a vendor's export. The one exception is a list-valued field that is a set by nature (the names a tool used for one algorithm), which unions. It does not apply to presence: a claim that an entry exists which no other source saw is not a disagreement about a value but a question of whether the thing is there, and is settled by a fresh scan where the thing is reachable, not by precedence.

Two claims on one entry: the better-graded one in force, the other kept as dissent; the list and the silent overwrite crossed out.

docs.title: A policy pack written from secondary summaries is marked unverified and applies no date; the primary is read, hashed and quote-checked before any of its dates or names counts
The rule
docs.text: A policy pack is a standard or memorandum as data: the dates it sets, the algorithms it names and the systems it governs, each with the words it is written in. A pack is written from the primary document only. Its source block records the document's URL, version marking, the SHA-256 of the file read and the date it was read, and the loader refuses the pack if any quote in it is not found, in order, in the text extracted from that file. When the primary cannot be obtained, the pack may still be written from secondary sources so that the scope rule is real (which pack governs which system), but it says verified: false, the assessor applies none of its dates as a deadline, and every judgement it yields carries provisional into its basis and onto the page. The flag is dropped only by rewriting the pack from the primary, not by finding a third summary that agrees with the first two.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
Secondary sources describe the version their authors read, and a standard that is being transitioned to is revised. The CNSA 2.0 FAQ was published in September 2022 as Ver. 1.0, revised in April 2024 (2.0), December 2024 (2.1) and October 2026 (2.2). The two summaries this project's pack was first written from agreed with each other on a five-category timeline with dates from 2025 to 2033, and were both right about the version they described. Ver. 2.2 does not contain that table. It gives three dates for all of national security systems and, in the same revision, states positions a summary from 2022 could not have carried: that a hybrid is compliant only where NSA identified one (IKEv2, not TLS), that SHA3-384 and SHA3-512 are allowed for a hardware's internal integrity checks only, that HashML-DSA is not allowed and that no further NIST standard is planned for the suite. A pack that had applied the summaries' dates as deadlines would have planned migrations against a table that no longer existed, with no event on the ledger to say where the dates came from.

Agreement between summaries is not verification. Two summaries that cite the same version agree because they share a source, not because the source is current.

The timeline two summaries gave, and the one the primary gives; the first was never applied because the pack said so.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Whenever a tool encodes a standard, a memorandum, a vendor's deprecation schedule or a certification list as data that will set a date or a verdict: a compliance rule, a migration queue, a compatibility tag. It applies with more force when the primary is hard to obtain, because that is when a summary is most tempting; a site that refuses an automated client will usually serve a person with a browser, and the person's download, hashed, is the record.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
1. Write the pack from the primary. Extract its text (pdftotext -layout), keep the text beside the pack, record the file's SHA-256, its version marking and the date read, and quote the passage behind every date and every name.
  2. Make the loader refuse a quote that is not in the text. A pack that cannot quote its source is not a pack.
  3. If the primary is refused, write the pack anyway for the scope rule, mark it verified: false, apply no date from it, and carry provisional into every judgement it produces, visibly. Record each refusal with its date.
  4. When the primary arrives, rewrite the pack from it rather than patching the summaries' version, and write down what changed between the two: that difference is the measure of what the summaries would have cost.
  5. Never rewrite the ledger's earlier judgements. The next assessment of the same evidence gives the final statuses; the provisional ones stay on the record with their flag.

docs.title: Where the claim stops
docs.text: Checked on one pack and one standard. The FAQ's own version history is read from its page footers and its revision notes, not from NSA's site index, which the harness could not reach. The advisory that announced the suite (September 2022, Ver. 1.0) is kept beside the FAQ as a second source; the FAQ is the later text and governs where they differ.

docs.title: A number shown on two pages is computed in one place; a page that counts a rule's events and a page that counts the document's entries will disagree
The rule
docs.text: Every figure a reader sees under one label is computed by one function over one projection. Where the record holds both the judgements a rule made and the document those judgements are written into, the figure is counted from the document, because the document is what the reader holds, and the second page calls the first page's function instead of counting again. A test asserts the two readers give the same numbers.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A projection is a document rebuilt from the record: here the cryptography bill of materials (CBOM), an inventory of every cryptographic asset, rebuilt from the ledger of findings. A rule that judges compatibility runs once per observation. The projection then folds observations onto entries: a certificate seen on the wire and the same certificate found in a file are one entry, and an imported claim with no key identity joins the one entry it describes. So the rule's event count is the number of things observed, and the document's count is the number of things that exist. Both are true. Under the label "not compatible" on two pages they are a discrepancy, and a reader who finds 189 on one page and 183 on another has no reason to trust either.

The defect is invisible to tests that check each page alone. Each page was right about what it counted. It was found by reading a number off a screenshot of one page while writing it down from a note built on the other.

Six judgements fold onto entries that already exist; the figure a reader is shown is the document's.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Wherever a system keeps an event log and a document derived from it, and shows counts from either: findings and assets, alerts and incidents, test results and requirements, log lines and sessions. It applies with most force after a deduplication or merge step is added, because that is the moment the two counts part and nothing fails.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
1. Name the unit a figure counts in the function that computes it: entries, not judgements; assets, not findings.
  2. Give each figure one function, and have every page, export and command call it. A second page never re-derives the count from the events.
  3. Write a test that holds the readers equal on recorded data, and one that states the inequality that is expected (judgements are at least as many as entries), so the difference is documented and not rediscovered.
  4. When a written number is checked against a page, check it against every page that shows that label.

docs.title: Where the claim stops
docs.text: One figure on two pages of one system. The same event-against-entry difference may sit behind other counts the pages show; only the compatibility counts were compared.

docs.title: An automated keyboard pass counts only the controls that are shown; a control inside a closed disclosure is reached through its summary, and a page that takes focus on load is walked from where it starts
The rule
docs.text: A keyboard check presses Tab and records what takes focus. Compare that with the controls a keyboard is meant to reach, not with every focusable element in the page: leave out anything inside a closed <details> other than its <summary>, anything hidden or inert, and anything disabled. Keep pressing through the browser's own wrap-around until every counted control has had focus, so a page that starts with focus part-way down is still walked in full. Report a difference only after each missed control has been explained.

docs.title: Why
docs.text: A disclosure (<details> with a <summary>) hides its content until the summary is activated, and the browser leaves that content out of the tab order while it is closed. That is correct behaviour: the summary is reachable, and opening it makes the rest reachable. A check that counts the hidden links as focusable reports a page where half the controls cannot be reached, which is false, and a false alarm in an accessibility report costs the report its credibility for the real findings. The same holds for a page that sets autofocus: the first Tab moves on from the focused field, and a check that stops when focus leaves the document has seen only the controls below it.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any automated check of keyboard reach: a test in CI, an audit script, a crawler. It does not replace a person walking a task with a keyboard, or a screen reader; it shows that each control can take focus and shows that it has, and nothing about whether the order makes sense.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
1. Build the list of expected controls in the page: focusable, not disabled, laid out, no hidden or inert ancestor, and no closed <details> ancestor unless the control is in that element's summary.
  2. Note whether the page already has focus on one of them when it loads.
  3. Press Tab up to twice the list's length, recording each control by its position in the list, and stop when all have been seen.
  4. For each focused control, read the computed outline and box shadow; neither means no visible focus.
  5. Before reporting a shortfall, classify every missed control. An unexplained one is a finding; an explained one is a correction to the check.

docs.title: Where the claim stops
docs.text: Headless Chromium at one width. Focus order, pointer-free completion of a task and what a screen reader announces were not tested and need a person.

docs.title: A recorded model answer belongs to the scan it was asked about; a build that shows a newer scan stops until the answers are recorded again
The rule
docs.text: A static copy of a system is a set of files with no service behind them. It cannot call a model, so anything a model says on it was said once, recorded, and is shown from the recording. A recording is made against one scan's record and cites that record's events, so it is stored under that scan's id and is valid for no other. The build of the copy checks that the scan it is about to show has its recordings and stops, naming the commands that make them, when it does not. Publishing without them is a deliberate setting, never the default.

docs.title: Why
docs.text: The step that makes a new scan the latest one and the step that records a model's answers are separate, and only the first happens on its own. Nothing fails when the second is skipped: every page builds, every link resolves, no private name leaks, and the page that should show an answer shows a sentence saying there is none. Checks that ask whether pages exist cannot see it; only opening the scene and reading it does. The reader of the published copy is the one who finds it.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any published snapshot that carries generated content keyed to the data it was generated from: recorded model answers, cached summaries, rendered charts, thumbnails. Whenever the data's identity moves, what was generated for the old identity is missing for the new one.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
1. Store each recording under the id of the record it cites.
  2. In the build, compute the id the copy will show and require a recording for it; fail with the exact commands to run.
  3. After a build, open the page that shows model output in a browser and read it. A count of pages is not a check of their content.
  4. Run the recording where it can write. Here the app's container mounts the runs and the raw output only, so the recording is made into a scratch folder and copied to the deployment's state.

docs.title: Where the claim stops
docs.text: One copy and two kinds of recording. The narration lines are a model's words recorded once; their accuracy is not checked by a rule the way the answers' citations are.

docs.title: A demonstration written around one machine goes stale the day the machine leaves; name hardware once, as where a run was recorded, and build the beats on the approach
The rule
docs.text: A recorded demonstration names the machine it ran on once, as the provenance of the run it shows, read from that run's own events. Every other screen describes the approach: what is collected, what judges it, who approves, what proves it, and where a model is allowed to speak. A screen that needs a box's name, chip or model to make its point is making a point about that box, and it will be wrong the first time the recording comes from somewhere else.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A demonstration built for a day on one machine borrows that machine's specifics for its drama: the chip, the memory, the model served, the path up to bigger boxes. Those specifics are true that day. The recording the published copy plays is then remade whenever the estate is re-scanned, on whatever host did the scan, with whatever models the inference seam bound that week. Nothing checks that the words on the screens still match the recording, because the words were typed into the page and the recording is data. The result here was three hosts named across eight beats, two model names for the same role, and a hardware roadmap on the closing screen of a project whose header says it is not a product.

The structural fix is cheaper than a review: let the page read the host from the run (scan.completed carries the hardware label on every job), the model labels from the recording's engine block, and the counts from the same projection every other page uses. Then a new recording cannot disagree with the stage, because the stage has nothing of its own to say about hardware.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any recorded or static demonstration, deck or page that will outlive the machine it was first shown on: a demo-day stage, a conference recording, a published static copy of a dashboard, a README with a screenshot. It applies with more force when the project's claim is an approach rather than a product, because every hardware name on a screen reads as a recommendation.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
1. Keep one provenance line per copy, filled from the data: the host the run's events name, the engines the recording names, the date it was made.
  2. Strip hardware and brand names from every other screen; where a layer of the architecture is hardware, say what it must provide (a container runtime, images by digest, a local model behind one seam), not which box.
  3. Draw the architecture from the run: the packs loaded, the rule's counts, the gap queue, the tiers and roles the config bound. A box with a fixed string in it is a box that will go stale.
  4. Name a specific deployment only as one option, with its proof and its limits, in the notes it links to.
  5. After each new recording, open the copy and read the screens that still carry typed words against the data beside them.

docs.title: Where the claim stops
docs.text: One stage, rebuilt once. The architecture beat still carries typed words for what each component does; only its counts and labels come from the run. A typed sentence can still go stale, and lesson 72's rule, read the copy after every recording, still applies.

docs.title: A drawing that must fit one screen takes its height from that screen, and shares it among its rows by what each row needs; a constant cap leaves room unused while the rows collide
The rule
docs.text:
A figure built to fill one screen without scrolling is sized by the script that draws it, from the room the screen actually leaves it: the viewport, less what sits above the figure and what must stay visible under it. The figure then gives each of its rows the height that row's content needs, and splits only the remainder by proportion. A stylesheet constant can neither see what is above the figure nor know how many rows are in it, so it is always wrong in one direction: too tall and the page scrolls, too short and the labels collide while the screen stays half empty.

The same screen twice: a constant cap leaves a quarter of it empty while the rows collide; measured from the screen, the same drawing has room.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
The opening beat's drawing was given a height in the stylesheet: the viewport less 440 px, kept between 440 and 780. The 440 was a guess at the heading above and the sentence and bar below, made at one window size and never measured again. Above the drawing the heading grew to a 46 px title and two lines of outcome; below it the sentence took two lines; and the drawing's three bands were cut by fixed fractions that gave the chain, with its eight service labels and nine listener labels, less than a third of whatever was left. On the owner's screen the drawing came out at 443 px: eight services in 80 px, step boxes taller than the lanes they sat in, listener labels written over one another, and a quarter of the screen blank underneath. The owner's two captures, the live stage and the published copy, showed the same crowding, because both run the same script against the same rule.

The script already measured the drawing's width from its box. It now measures its top too, takes the viewport height less that top and less the fixed room for the sentence and the bar, and draws into the result. Inside, the sheet band is given the height its rows need (six rows, 20 px each, plus its headings), and the chain and the plan share what remains, the plan a little more because its step boxes are taller than a service label. Listener labels are pushed apart to a 12 px minimum down their column, and the plan's stray dots and its count line share a footer row instead of the last lane. The heading shrank to 38 px and the sentence to 15.5 px, which is what the room above and below the drawing actually needs.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: Any figure meant to stand on one screen without scrolling: a demonstration beat, a dashboard panel, a kiosk page, a slide drawn by script. It applies whenever the figure's content is a list whose length the data decides (services, lanes, rows) and the room around it is set by text whose length the copy decides.

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
1. Let the script measure: the figure's top from its bounding box, the viewport's height, and a fixed allowance for what must stay visible under the figure. Give the figure that height, with a floor under which the page may scroll rather than crush its rows.
  2. Give each row-bearing band the height its rows need, from the data's count and the type size; split only the remainder by proportion.
  3. Where labels ride on data positions, push them apart to a minimum pitch in a pass after layout; move the label, never the mark.
  4. Keep counts and stray marks in their own row; a label placed at the figure's last pixel will meet whatever else was placed there.
  5. Render at the sizes people use (here 1813 × 883 with and without the site header, 1440 × 900, 1280 × 720) and look, before shipping: the collisions were visible in any screenshot and in no test.

docs.title: Where the claim stops
docs.text: One figure, one script, four sizes rendered. The floor of 560 px means a short window (under about 760 px with the site header) scrolls; the figure does not yet drop a band or its labels for small screens. The published copy takes the change only when it is rebuilt and published.

docs.title: Technical notes
docs.text:
One question per note, answered with measured or cited evidence.

  1. 00 What is the CBOM workbench, and what has it shown so far? — A working example of how a cryptographic inventory, built from evidence and kept on a signed ledger, carries an organization from not knowing what it runs to changing an algorithm and proving the change landed.
  2. 01 What is a CBOM, and what is in one? — A CBOM is a CycloneDX bill of materials whose components are cryptographic assets — algorithms, certificates, protocols and key material — with their properties and dependencies; the format is an Ecma standard, the content an agency must put in one is not yet fixed, and the practice of building and using one is where the field is still improvising.
  3. 03 What does federal policy require, and by when? — Executive Order 14412 and OMB M-26-15 require an inventory now, post-quantum key establishment on prioritized systems by the end of 2030 and signatures by the end of 2031 — and the minimum elements of the inventory itself are not published until 2027-03-19, which is why this project builds a record and projects the CBOM from it.
  4. 05 What can be seen on the wire, on a host and in code — and what cannot? — A targeted wire scan shows what one listener accepts; passive capture shows what every client offers and every server chooses across an estate, but not a TLS 1.3 certificate; host and code evidence show what is installed and written, not what runs. Each layer answers a different question, and a cryptographic inventory needs all three.
  5. 06 How does a finding become a dependency chain? — A finding becomes a chain when each link above it — the certificate it rides on, the service that serves it, the mission function and data lifetime behind that service — is either a rule's assertion resting on named ledger events or a fact the owner typed in and the record labels as supplied; the chain is complete when no link is missing, and it never counts a supplied link as something discovered.
  6. 07 How is a migration priority computed? — A migration priority is computed, not chosen: a rule reads the memo's own criteria against the owner's facts to decide whether a system is prioritized, reads the memo's table to decide which of its algorithms are quantum-vulnerable, and places each system's key establishment and signatures in the queue the memo names with its date — and two more rules, each resting on a dated measurement, say whether the change is blocked on a supplier or on a validated module.
  7. 08 What does "verified" mean for a cryptographic change? — A change is verified when a client offering only the new algorithm succeeds and a client offering any old one is refused, on the container the change was applied to, after it was applied, and again after a restart.
  8. 12 What does an auditable record of agent work contain? — An append-only event log in which each event names its actor, its inputs and its evidence, is chained by hash, and is checkpointed with a post-quantum signature by a party that is not the writer — plus a plain statement of what that does not prove.
  9. 13 Where do language models belong in this pipeline, and where not? — Measured on 216 labeled items across fifteen arms of every model the lab holds: a 31B model on four L4s reads call sites and classifies algorithms, and drafts change plans better and 27 times faster than the largest model; tracing a wire finding to the configuration line behind it is the one role that needs a 120B model; naming a tool's spelling and resolving a conflict between layers are better done by rules; and no model decides whether a change worked.
  10. 15 What do the open-source scanners cover, and what is built on top? — Three free scanners together find everything within reach on the wire and about two thirds of what sits in images; what they cannot do is read every key format, say which findings are the same key, which are in use, or what a listener's posture is — and that is what the harness adds.
  11. 16 What does a CBOM make possible once it exists? — A CBOM whose entries carry their evidence and their chain can be projected into any field list without a new scan, compared between scans to see what changed, read against a policy to say what comes first, and handed to a model as the context for its work — and because the same entry is what the result is checked against, the model can draft the change and a verifier, not the model, can prove it landed.
  12. 17 How does a CBOM become a migration plan, and why can't a list of systems? — A migration plan is an order, and the order comes from what the estate shares — a certificate authority whose leaves must follow its root, a library build several services run, one key on two listeners, clients the agency does not control — which a CBOM records and a list of systems does not; on the mini-agency the CBOM yields 26 steps, 15 of them waiting on another, from six rows that say nothing about each other.
  13. 18 What is the workbench built from, why each part, and what would an enterprise run in its place? — Every part of the workbench is a standard or an open source tool chosen because it can be checked; each has an enterprise equivalent that changes the scale, the support and the audit story, not the method.
  14. 19 How is a question to the CBOM answered, and how is the answer checked without asking a model? — A question is embedded, the nearest components and their chains are handed to a model as passages with their ledger event ids, the typed reply names components and cites events, and a rule checks every citation against the ledger and against what the model was shown; retrieval and the answer are measured apart against floors written first.
  15. 20 How is one server inventoried as an estate, below its operating system as well as on the wire, and planned from its CBOM? — A server's cryptography sits in four places that change on four different clocks — its listeners, its own files, its firmware's trust databases and its management controller — and a scan that reads all four into one signed ledger yields a CBOM with the server as a device and its firmware as components, and a plan that separates what the owner can set today from what waits for the vendor.
  16. 21 What does a federal authorization ask of a CBOM tool itself, and where does the workbench stand? — An agency authorizes a CBOM tool as a system of its own, against the same controls as any other; the workbench's foundation (a signed ledger, the CBOM projected from it, a scope the runner enforces, images by digest, models by measurement, verification by probe) is what an assessor looks for, and the three things that would stop an authorization today are all in the shell around it: one owner with no roles, its own cryptography in no validated module, and plain HTTP to the page and the models.
  17. 22 What does "compatible" mean for one CBOM entry, and what cannot be told from the evidence? — Every entry in the CBOM carries one of four statuses under the policy pack that governs its service — compatible, not compatible, unknown, outside the pack — judged by a rule from the pack's own table and the entry's algorithm, with unknown counted on its own so that a gap in the evidence is never reported as a pass, and every status from a pack not read first-hand marked provisional; both packs shipped are read first-hand, so none is.
  18. 23 What can a supplier's attestation stand in for in a CBOM, and what can it not? — The hardware half of an inventory — what signs a firmware image, which modules a controller carries, whether the installed version has a route to post-quantum algorithms — is the supplier's to state; the workbench takes such a statement in as reported evidence on a ledger of its own, joins it to a scanned server by model and firmware version, shows the two beside each other with every disagreement visible, and never lets it become a finding or outrank what the server showed.
  19. 24 What does a later phase need from a discovery phase, field by field, and where does each field come from? — A phase that deploys is planned from a register the discovery phase hands over: one row per step, grouped into the buckets the later phases are scoped by, each row carrying the system, interface, mission thread, owner and classification the owner supplied, the priority and deadline the rules computed, whether the step waits for a supplier, the vendor's path and the owner's cost with its basis, and the CBOM entries the step moves by fingerprint; the workbench writes it from the plan, labels every owner-supplied column as the owner's, and estimates nothing.
  20. 25 How much of an estate's cryptography can a tool reach, by asset class, and how is the rest kept from disappearing into a coverage figure? — Every gap a discovery leaves — a key file not opened, a listener no scan reached, a service nobody described, a path unreadable to the scan's user, a controller certificate whose key the controller does not report, a model no supplier has attested — is written on the ledger as its own event with a stable id, the asset class it falls in, the reason and what would fill it; a person closes one by citing evidence, and coverage per asset class is counted from reached against reached plus open gaps, so the figure can only rise by evidence.
  21. 26 What does a discovery-and-planning phase ask of a CBOM tool, and what does this one answer, measured? — The phase most organisations start with discovers every piece of cryptography, records it in a CBOM, tags each entry against the policy that governs it, maps what is not compatible to its system and owner, prices the risk and hands a plan to the phases that deploy; against that list the workbench answers nine of ten asks from the ledger on the mini-agency (313 components, 183 not compatible, 10 gaps recorded, 25 steps in three buckets), and the one it does not, a proof in a commercial consumer, is named and waiting.

docs.title: What is the CBOM workbench, and what has it shown so far?
The answer
docs.text:
cbom-workbench (its command is pqch) is a worked example, in running code, of what a cryptographic inventory is for. It builds a cryptography bill of materials (CBOM) — a structured list of every algorithm, key, certificate and protocol an organization runs, with where each one was found — from three kinds of evidence, and then uses that inventory to do the thing the inventory exists for: change an algorithm across an estate and prove, by re-scanning, that the change landed. Every finding, decision, approval and verification is an event on an append-only, signed ledger, and the CBOM is rebuilt from that ledger. Its first page draws NIST's crypto-agility plan (CSWP 39-upd1, Fig. 3) with what the workbench does in each part: the CBOM is the plan's information repository, between the tools that fill it and the engine that ranks what to change (note 16). Its centre is the plan the CBOM makes possible: what depends on what, what comes first, and in what order the changes have to go (note 17). The whole of it, with its inference engines, runs on one desk-side machine from an offline bundle (note 18), and the CBOM can be asked questions whose answers cite ledger events, each citation checked by a rule (/ask). A single server is read the same way, below its operating system as well as on the wire, and planned from its own CBOM (note 20).

It is an exploration shared freely, not a product.
