Its three arguments are that the inventory is the tool the migration is made from and checked against, not a report to file; that the place of a language model in that work is something to measure role by role, not assume; and that this work can run on hardware an organization holds, because a map of where its cryptography is weakest is not something to send elsewhere. It is being built now because federal policy requires the inventory now, and the minimum elements of a federal CBOM are not published until 2027-03-19 (note 03): a record built with its evidence can be projected into whatever is asked for later.

So far it has shown the path end to end on a small test estate: scan, inventory, score against an answer key, change policy, apply, verify on the wire — and, since 2026-10-19, the inventory half on an estate twice the size, with a database that still accepts RSA key transport, a broker, a legacy Java service, a post-quantum gateway and an internal certificate authority. The numbers are below, with what each one does and does not establish.

docs.title: The concept: five rungs
docs.text:
Post-quantum migration means replacing the public-key algorithms a large quantum computer could break — RSA, elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman, ECDSA — with the algorithms NIST standardized in 2024: ML-KEM (FIPS 203) for key establishment, and ML-DSA (FIPS 204) for signatures. Key establishment is urgent first, because traffic recorded today can be decrypted later once the key exchange is broken ("harvest now, decrypt later"). United States federal policy sets dates: OMB M-26-15 puts key establishment on prioritized systems in a phase ending 2030, and digital signatures in 2031.

An organization cannot migrate what it cannot see. The project is organized around a maturity ladder in which each rung is a question the organization can now answer:

Rung What the organization has The question it can answer Opaque A hand-kept spreadsheet None reliably Enumerated Scanner output Where is quantum-vulnerable cryptography? Structured A CBOM with dependencies What depends on it? Managed Owners, priorities, approvals What first, what is blocked, what changed? Agile Change as routine If policy changes, how fast can we respond, and did it land?

Crypto agility — the top rung — is the ability to change an algorithm by changing policy, without re-engineering each system. The project treats it as something to measure: the time from a policy change to a verified result.

The five rungs, what each one has, and the question each one can answer.

docs.title: The mechanism
docs.text:
Three ideas hold the design together.

Agents propose, verifiers dispose. Scanners, rules and, where interpretation is needed, a language model produce findings and proposed changes. Whether a change worked is never a model's judgement. It is decided by a verifier that re-scans: one client that offers only the new algorithm must succeed, and one that offers only the old ones must be refused. A listener that accepts both has the new algorithm enabled, not enforced, and that is recorded as its own state.

The ledger remembers. Every event is one line in an append-only file, each line carrying the hash of the one before it. Checkpoints over the file are signed with ML-DSA-65 by a separate signer service. The CBOM, the score and every screen are computed from the ledger and can be deleted and rebuilt.

Models earn their place by measurement. Six roles, a floor per role written before the run, every call repeated, fifteen arms across every model the lab holds: one role needs a 120B model, three run on a 31B model on four L4s (one of them with reasoning on), two went back to rules because no arm reached the floor (note 13). What each step up in models or hardware changes is a measured row or is marked not measured.

The parts, as built today:

Part What it does Uses a model Scope A file listing the only addresses, ports and images that may be touched No Runner The one container that holds the Docker socket; runs named scan profiles and approved changes, and refuses anything outside the scope No Scout Runs testssl.sh (through PostgreSQL's TLS upgrade where the scope says so) and ssh-audit against listeners, cbomkit-theia and the harness's own reader of key material against images; normalizes their output to one finding format No Rules Link a certificate seen on the wire to the file that holds its key; link a listener and its image to the service the scope names, on the runner's record of the container it found; judge whether a certificate in an image is served, leaving a certificate authority's alone; state each listener's posture; name the verifier that could confirm a change to each class of entry; settle each conflict between a file and the wire No Owner's facts Mission function, data lifetime and high-value status per service, typed into one file and recorded as supplied links with a human actor; labelled supplied in the CBOM, never coverage No Managed rules Read OMB M-26-15, carried as quotes the loader checks against the memo, to decide which algorithms are quantum-vulnerable, which systems are prioritized, which queue each system's key establishment and signatures wait in and by when, and whether TLS 1.3 is offered; record supplier and validated-module blockers from two dated snapshots No Watch Records each scan's configuration manifest and what changed since the previous scan; sends only new findings and changed items to the model jobs No Investigator Traces a wire finding to the configuration line that causes it, through three typed tools over the service's build files under step and token budgets; recorded as the model's claim with the engine, the settings and the time Yes — the one role that needs the 120B Scorer Compares a CBOM with an answer key, by layer, beside two baselines No Migrator Renders a central policy into a service's configuration and proposes the difference as a change No Verifier Paired probes and a second witness; issues enforced, enabled-not-enforced, not-landed or inconclusive No, by rule Signer Signs ledger checkpoints; holds the key where nothing else can read it No Inference seam One place that knows where a model lives; code asks for a tier or a role, never a model Yes — the investigator's trace; a typed classification, used by no rule; a conflict explanation where a deployment binds the role (the lab does not)

docs.title: The estate at M1: eight services, scored
docs.text:
On 2026-10-19 the estate grew to eight services and nine listeners: the slice below, a PostgreSQL 18 records database reached through its TLS upgrade, a RabbitMQ 4 queue, a Tomcat 8.5 application on Java 8, a gateway with an ML-DSA-65 certificate and the hybrid group only, a client-certificate listener on the API, and an internal certificate authority that issued three of the certificates. The answer key holds 73 items; every wire claim was probed by hand before the key was committed. The scanners alone and the workbench, by layer:

Layer Keyed Scanners alone Workbench What differs Wire 40 (2 out of reach) 38, no false positive 38, no false positive nothing: the wire is the scanners' Image 20, 2 decoys 14; both decoys flagged 20; no decoy flagged the harness's own file reader (an ML-DSA certificate and key, a PKCS#12 keystore, DSA and Ed25519 host keys) and the rules (two unserved certificates marked not in use, two CA certificates left alone) Posture 9 listeners not stated 9 of 9 a rule over both layers

The delta over the scanners is where the design said it would be: the host layer and the structure, not the wire. The one listener that accepts RSA key transport, the records database, is found only because its scan speaks PostgreSQL's upgrade and enumerates cipher suites; a plain TLS scan of its port reports nothing (lesson 29).

docs.title: Worked example: the four-service slice
docs.text:
The test estate is a "mini-agency" in which every weakness is planted, so an answer key can say exactly what a perfect inventory holds. The first slice is four containers on an isolated network:

Service Listener Planted posture portal TLS Classical: X25519 and P-256 key exchange, RSA-2048 certificate api TLS Mixed: the hybrid group X25519MLKEM768 offered, X25519 still accepted, ECDSA P-256 certificate sftp-legacy SSH Classical and old: OpenSSH 6.6, key exchange down to 1024-bit Diffie-Hellman, a DSA host key bastion SSH Mixed: OpenSSH 10.0, hybrid ML-KEM key exchange first, X25519 still accepted, classical host keys

A hybrid group combines a classical exchange with a post-quantum one, so the session is safe if either holds.

The answer key holds 36 items: 22 on the wire and 10 in images that a good inventory should find, 2 decoys that look like findings and are not, 1 real item no scan can reach (what a service offers when it connects out), and 1 fact that can only be typed in. It was committed before any scanner code was written.

The full test estate is eight services, these four among them, with a key of 74 items (58 to find, 9 decoys, 2 out of reach, 5 supplied); the demo's test agency page shows each service and what was planted in it. The slice's key is kept, frozen, in eval/answer-keys/mini-agency-m0.yaml, and the scores below are the slice's.

Enumerated and Structured. One scan, scored (measured 2026-10-03, xr7620, x86_64):

Layer CBOMkit's image scanner alone All scanners, no harness Workbench Wire 0 of 23 22 of 23 22 of 23 Host (images) 7 of 10, decoy flagged 7 of 10, decoy flagged 7 of 10, decoy not flagged Listener posture not stated not stated 4 of 4

The denominators count the unreachable item, so the wire layer cannot reach 23 of 23 by design. A targeted wire scan takes 27 to 46 s for a TLS listener and 2 to 3 s for an SSH one; an image scan takes 71 to 96 s.

Agile. The portal's key-exchange groups come from one policy file. Changing that file from "classical" to "require hybrid" produces a proposed change with its diff and the exact check that will count as verified. After approval the runner applies it, and the verifier probes the listener, then probes it again after the service is recreated. Measured on the same machine: 63.4 s from the policy event to the last verdict, 62.9 s from approval, with the verdict enforced both times. With a person approving through the page, 69.4 s and 65.6 s. Nearly all of that time is the second-witness scan, 21 to 31 s per verdict; the paired probes take about one second each.

Time to change on the four-service slice: about a minute, nearly all of it the witness that enumerates every group.

Each interval is reported twice: from the harness's own timestamps, and as an upper bound from the times a separate signing service puts inside its signatures — the last signature before the policy event to the first over the verdict (55.6 s and "no more than 55.6 s" on a later change). A change is shown as verified, with a time, only when the runner's own log of its jobs and applies bears the ledger out; the three changes above predate that log and are shown as unchecked.

Off the network. Everything above — the slice, the harness, the scanners — starts from an offline bundle: thirteen images (the whole mini-agency, the harness, three scanners, the registry) by digest, in a local registry on disk; 1.5 GB for both x86_64 and arm64, 756 MB for arm64 alone. With the bundle's images deleted first, it started in 8.7 s, every image came from the bundle, a live scan scored as above, and a policy change was applied and verified with the bundle's registry stopped. The rehearsal on a second host is done: on 2026-11-04 the arm64 bundle, a wheelhouse of 45 wheels and a git bundle of the tree, carried as one 771 MB archive, were installed on a second DGX Spark-class machine (a Dell Pro Max GB10) with no package index and no image pulled from outside; the bundle verified and started in 4.5 s and the live scan scored wire 38 of 40, host 20 of 20, posture 9 of 9, no false positives, in about 2.5 minutes (lesson 53, lesson 54). On the same box the kit reads the machine it runs on as a server, with a second runner of its own and its own signer (note 20). Ask the CBOM answers there on the fast tier with thinking off, every citation passing on 12 of 12 evaluation items at a median of 2.8 s a call (note 19, lesson 58). In the lab, Nemotron 3.5 Super VL through the gateway reaches both answer floors, 12 of 12 each at a median of 55 s, and the public demo shows its answers to the six examples, recorded and checked again when the site is built (lesson 63). The public demo carries the eight-beat stage the same way: the test agency only, replayed from its ledgers, the plan's narration recorded once, and the hardware named as the runs recorded it.

docs.title: What follows
docs.text:
• At the first rung, a harness adds structure, not coverage. On this estate the workbench finds exactly what the scanners find. What it adds is the link from a wire finding to the file holding the key, the judgement that a certificate sitting in an image is not served, and a stated posture per listener. Anyone presenting this work should say so in those words.
  • The baseline matters. Measured against CBOMkit alone, any tool that scans the network looks transformative, because CBOMkit does not scan networks. The honest bar is all the open-source scanners run together with no harness.
  • Verification is where the value concentrates. An inventory can be approximately right and still be useful. A statement that a change landed cannot. Most of the engineering effort, and most of the defects found in review, were in the verifier and in who is allowed to write what.
  • Time-to-change is a measurable property. About a minute on one service is a starting figure for one estate, not a benchmark.
  • The tool is judged before the estate. An agency authorizes the workbench as a system of its own. Reviewed against those controls, its foundation holds and the three blockers are in the shell around it: roles and separation of duties, its own cryptography in a validated module, and TLS (note 21). What can change without changing the demo has: every deadline assessed from now on names the document that set it (M-26-15 or NIST IR 8547), a model-set fact in the CBOM names its model, the checkpoint algorithm is a setting, the scope carries who authorized it and until when, and TLS to the models, origin checks, file modes and a release signature are settings a deployment turns on.
  • Every entry is tagged, and unknown is a count. Each CBOM entry carries its status under the pack that governs its service, compatible, not compatible, unknown or outside the pack, judged by a rule from the pack's own table; on the four-service slice, 2, 39, 1 and 5 under M-26-15. A gap in the evidence is a number of its own, never a pass; both packs, M-26-15 and the CNSA 2.0 FAQ, are read first-hand and quote-checked (note 22).
  • A supplier's statement is evidence of its own grade. What signs a firmware, which modules a controller carries and whether the installed version has a route forward come from the supplier; the workbench records such a statement as reported evidence on its own ledger, joins it to a scanned server by model and firmware version, and shows the two side by side with every disagreement visible; it never becomes a finding (note 23).
  • The plan is handed over as a register. One row per step, grouped into the buckets a later phase is scoped by from a versioned pack, with the system, interface, mission thread, owner, classification, vendor path and cost the owner supplied beside the priority, deadline and blockers the rules computed, and the entries each step moves by fingerprint; the cost column is the owner's numbers summed once per service, nothing estimated (note 24).
  • What no tool could see is a queue, not a percentage. Each gap a scan leaves is an event with a stable id, its asset class, the reason and what fills it; a person closes one by citing evidence; coverage per class is counted from reached against reached plus open gaps (note 25).
  • Measured against the phase most organisations start with. Ten asks of a discovery-and-planning phase, nine answered from the ledger on the mini-agency's scan of 2026-11-09 (313 components, 183 not compatible, 10 gaps, 25 steps in three buckets) and one, the proof in a commercial consumer, named and waiting (note 26).

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
What this note's numbers cover: the four-service slice for the change path (one changed listener) and the eight-service estate for coverage — TLS, TLS behind PostgreSQL's upgrade, and SSH; wire and image evidence — on an x86_64 lab server, with the slice also run as arm64 under emulation. The code layer is not yet scanned on either. A separate set of targets measured what each scanner can see beyond the slice — databases and brokers over TLS, a client-certificate listener, an ML-DSA certificate (note 15).

Which model each of the pipeline's six roles needs is measured, on every model the lab holds (note 13): tracing a wire finding to its configuration line needs a 120B model; drafting a change plan, reading a call site and classifying an algorithm run on a 31B model on four L4s, the call-site read with reasoning on; naming a tool's spelling and resolving a conflict between layers go back to rules. A successor to the 120B, measured in the same slot, did not displace it; the same model's reasoning setting moved its result more than the change of model did.

Since 2026-10-20 the inventory is Structured: every listener on the eight-service estate has a complete dependency chain — listener, certificate, service, mission function, data lifetime — with each discovered link resting on named ledger events and each supplied link labelled (note 06); 188 of its 220 entries are recorded as having no verifier; its three file-versus-wire conflicts are settled by rule; and the investigator traced one finding per listener to its configuration line, eight of nine agreeing with the key and the ninth correcting it.

Since the same evening it is Managed: OMB M-26-15 is carried as data, each rule in the memo's own words, and the assessor places each service's key establishment and signatures in the memo's queues with their dates — 14 items open, 2 met, 7 blocked on a supplier whose software cannot offer post-quantum cryptography, none yet in a validated module — and shows a decision record per item (note 07). Watch mode records what changed between scans and re-examines only that. Since 2026-10-21 the CBOM itself is on its own page: the document's makeup, any entry field by field with the standard's fields and the project's told apart and each traced to its ledger event, what a model was given from the entry and what it answered, the CBOM against the previous scan's, and a second projection of the same ledger rebuilt in milliseconds with no scan (note 01). And a model now drafts the change for software the harness has no renderer for, from the CBOM's entries and the trace; the draft is rehearsed on a copy of the service before anyone can approve it, and a verifier with a fourth, TLS 1.2 probe decides whether it holds (note 16). The first, for the records database, was rehearsed enforced and waits for approval. The one model job tried for the rung, a plain-words explanation of each item's queue, fell below its floor and is not used.

What is not yet built or measured: the code layer (no source scanner runs yet, so the key's code-layer decoy is untested); client-side posture; the full twelve-service estate; the bundle loaded on a second host with the network cut.

Where trust stops today: approvals are written by the harness process on the strength of a sign-on at the front door, not signed by the approver. The ledger's timestamps are the harness's clock, bracketed within two seconds by the signing service's; a verdict is re-derived from the runner's own log and raw output before it is shown as verified. What neither covers is how long a person's decision waited before the harness recorded it. The limits are stated on the page.

The mini-agency is the only estate the workbench changes; a network of one's own can be scanned and planned, never changed (the guide). This is a personal research project, not a Dell product, reference architecture or supported offering.

docs.title: What is a CBOM, and what is in one?
The answer
docs.text: A Cryptography Bill of Materials is an inventory of the cryptographic assets in a system — the algorithms, certificates, keys and protocols — written as a CycloneDX bill of materials, the same format used for software bills of materials, with cryptographic assets as a component type of their own and dependencies between them. CycloneDX is ratified by Ecma International as ECMA-424, and CBOM support has been part of it since version 1.6. That much is standard. What an agency must put in one is not yet fixed: OMB M-26-15 requires a central CBOM fed from three kinds of evidence, and Executive Order 14412 has told CISA and NIST to publish the minimum elements of a CBOM by March 2027. Until then each agency decides what its CBOM contains, and every vendor fills the gap with its own fields. This project's position is that a CBOM is worth having only when every entry carries its evidence, when it is a projection of a record rather than a document someone edits, and when it is the thing a change is made from and verified against.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
A bill of materials for cryptography answers the question a spreadsheet cannot: what cryptography is actually in use, where, and what depends on it. The OWASP guide puts the purpose plainly: discovering, managing and reporting on cryptographic assets is "the first step on the migration journey to quantum-safe systems and applications", and the trouble is that cryptography is "typically buried deep within components". So a CBOM reuses the machinery built for software supply chains — CycloneDX's components, evidence and dependencies — and adds the vocabulary cryptography needs.

Three ideas carry it:

  • A cryptographic asset is a component. CycloneDX 1.6 adds cryptographic-asset beside application, library, container, file and the rest. An algorithm, a certificate, a key, a protocol is a thing in the inventory with a name, a reference and properties.
  • Properties say which variant. The guide's example is the one that matters for this project: the presence of SHA-1 versus HMAC-SHA-1 "makes a difference", so a CBOM captures the parameter set, the curve, the mode, the key size, and the quantum security level, not just a family name.
  • Dependencies say what uses what. The guide distinguishes a library that provides an algorithm from an application that uses it, and a protocol that uses an algorithm (its example: "TLS 1.3 uses ECDH/secp256r1"). That is the chain from a listener to the key exchange it negotiates to the certificate it serves to the key file behind it.

docs.title: The mechanism
docs.text:
CycloneDX 1.6's schema defines a CBOM precisely. The asset types and the fields that matter most, from the schema this project validates against:

assetType Carries Fields the schema defines algorithm A cryptographic function primitive (one of fifteen: kem, key-agree, signature, pke, hash, mac, block-cipher, stream-cipher, ae, kdf, drbg, xof, combiner, other, unknown), parameterSetIdentifier, curve, mode, padding, cryptoFunctions, classicalSecurityLevel, nistQuantumSecurityLevel, executionEnvironment, implementationPlatform, certificationLevel certificate An X.509 or other certificate subjectName, issuerName, notValidBefore, notValidAfter, signatureAlgorithmRef, subjectPublicKeyRef, certificateFormat, certificateExtension protocol TLS, SSH, IPsec, IKE, SSTP, WPA type, version, cipherSuites, ikev2TransformTypes, cryptoRefArray related-crypto-material Keys and other material type (private-key, public-key, secret-key, key, ciphertext, signature, digest, nonce, seed, salt, shared-secret, token, password, credential, …), with size, format, state, and an algorithmRef

Every cryptographic asset may carry an oid, the object identifier that names it unambiguously (ecdsa-with-SHA256 is 1.2.840.10045.4.3.2, whatever a tool calls it). Relationships go in the document's dependencies list: each entry names a component by its bom-ref and lists what it dependsOn and what it provides. Evidence — where the asset was seen — goes under evidence.occurrences, with a location.

What the schema does not define is as important. There is no field for who owns an asset, when it must be migrated, which policy puts it in which queue, whether a file found in an image is actually in use, or what observation the entry rests on. CycloneDX's answer is properties: name-value pairs under a namespace the producer chooses. That is where a vendor's schema, or this project's, lives.

docs.title: What the policy requires
docs.text: OMB M-26-15, Appendix A, section 6, names the three sources an agency's automated inventory draws on — software composition analysis, static and dynamic testing "to find cryptographic functions in code", and network scanners "to detect protocols and cipher suites" — and says they populate "a central Cryptographic Bill of Materials". It does not say what fields that CBOM holds. Executive Order 14412 directs CISA and NIST to publish the minimum elements of a CBOM within 270 days of 2026-06-22, which is 2027-03-19. Until that is published, "a CBOM" means "a CycloneDX document with cryptographic assets in it", and two agencies' CBOMs need not agree on anything else.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
The workbench's CBOM for the eight-service mini-agency (scan run 01M5DG85J78FF3FVG3GDH26SWZ, 2026-10-21) is a CycloneDX 1.6 document of 254 components: 47 cryptographic assets seen on the wire, 182 in images, 9 listeners, 8 services and 8 images. By the standard's four asset types, 139 are related cryptographic material (keys, keystores), 62 algorithms, 19 certificates and 9 protocols. Its dependencies list carries the chain from each service to its listeners and images, from a listener to what it negotiates and serves, and from a served certificate to the file holding its key.

One entry: the certificate the records database serves after PostgreSQL's TLS upgrade, as the document carries it (two long values shortened):

{
  "type": "cryptographic-asset",
  "bom-ref": "fp:03f50533afef3d47…",
  "name": "RSA",
  "cryptoProperties": {
    "assetType": "certificate",
    "certificateProperties": {
      "certificateFormat": "X.509",
      "subjectName": "CN=records-db.agency.test,O=Mini Agency",
      "issuerName": "CN=Mini Agency Internal CA,O=Mini Agency",
      "notValidBefore": "2026-10-19T18:44:39Z",
      "notValidAfter": "2029-01-21T18:44:39Z"
    }
  },
  "evidence": {"occurrences": [{"location": "172.16.106.30:5432"}]},
  "properties": [
    {"name": "pqch:layer", "value": "wire"},
    {"name": "pqch:subject", "value": "{\"host\":\"172.16.106.30\",\"kind\":\"endpoint\",\"port\":5432,\"protocol\":\"postgres\"}"},
    {"name": "pqch:asset-type", "value": "certificate"},
    {"name": "pqch:role", "value": "signature"},
    {"name": "pqch:name", "value": "RSA"},
    {"name": "pqch:parameters", "value": "{\"key_bits\":2048,\"signature\":\"ecdsa-with-SHA384\",\"spki_sha256\":\"74092eaa…\", …}"},
    {"name": "pqch:fingerprint", "value": "03f50533afef3d47…"},
    {"name": "pqch:evidence", "value": "01M5DGB4PY85H2ANQA75X4H3PK"},
    {"name": "pqch:tools", "value": "testssl.sh"},
    {"name": "pqch:in-use", "value": "true"},
    {"name": "pqch:verifiable-by", "value": "cert-parse"},
    {"name": "pqch:family", "value": "rsa-sig"},
    {"name": "pqch:quantum-vulnerable", "value": "true"}
  ]
}

Read it field by field, as the workbench's CBOM page does:

Field Defined by Says From type, cryptoProperties.assetType CycloneDX a cryptographic asset, a certificate the scanner's observation certificateProperties.* CycloneDX whom it names, who signed it, when it is valid testssl.sh's parse of the served certificate evidence.occurrences CycloneDX where it was seen: the listener the same observation bom-ref, pqch:fingerprint CycloneDX / project the identity of the observation; the same certificate in the next scan has the same reference a hash of layer, subject, type, role, name and key pqch:evidence project the ledger event holding the tool's output, its path and SHA-256 the scan pqch:role, pqch:family, pqch:quantum-vulnerable project a signature, RSA, quantum-vulnerable the rule quantum/vulnerable/1 reading OMB M-26-15's table pqch:verifiable-by project a change to it is confirmed by parsing the served certificate the rule verifier/class/1

One entry, field by field: the standard's ten say what and where, the project's thirteen say what it rests on.

The standard says what the asset is and where; the extension says what the entry rests on and what follows from it. The chain is in the standard's own terms: the listener listener:172.16.106.30:5432 depends on this certificate, and the certificate depends on the file /etc/pg-tls/server.crt in the records-db image, joined by a rule that found the same public key in both. Above the listener, the records-db application component carries what no scan can discover — mission function "benefits records", a data lifetime of 75 years, high-value asset, owner "Records office" — each labelled supplied, with the person and the event that recorded it, and what the policy rules made of it: prioritized by all three of the memo's criteria, its key establishment in the queue due 2030-12-31.

Three things can be done with this document that a spreadsheet cannot do:

  • Project it again. A flat inventory of 62 rows, one per asset in use for key establishment or signatures, with the system, owner, queue and evidence, is rebuilt from the same 535 ledger events in 19 ms; no scanner runs. Its field list is a data file. When the minimum elements are published, meeting them is another such file.
  • Compare it. Two CBOMs of the same estate are compared component by component, because an observation's reference is its fingerprint: two consecutive scans of the unchanged estate compare as 254 unchanged.
  • Hand it to a model. The investigator is given one entry's observation, the service its chain leads to, and that service's build files, and asked which line causes it; for the jump host's X25519 entry it named line 4 of sshd_config in two steps and 23 s on Nemotron 3.5 Super VL. The answer is recorded as the model's claim beside the entry, never in it.

Two baselines are written from the same ledger in the same format, so the workbench's CBOM can be scored against an answer key beside CBOMkit alone and all the scanners alone.

docs.title: What follows
docs.text:
• Ask for the format, not the brand. A CBOM that is not CycloneDX 1.6 or later is a vendor's private inventory. The format is the one thing already settled, and it is what the tooling — CBOMkit, the viewers, the scanners — reads and writes.
  • Ask what each entry rests on. The schema allows a CBOM with no evidence at all. An entry without a tool, an observation and a hash is an assertion.
  • Expect the minimum elements, and plan for more. When CISA and NIST publish them, a CBOM built on evidence will meet them by projection; one built as a document will need re-collecting.
  • Ask to see one entry, field by field. Which fields are the standard's, which are the producer's, and what each rests on. A CBOM whose producer cannot answer that for every field is not auditable.
  • Treat the CBOM as a projection. Here it is rebuilt from the ledger on demand and never edited; a change to the estate is an event, and the CBOM follows. That is what makes it the thing a change is made from and verified against (note 08) and what an auditor can check (note 12).

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
Covered: the CycloneDX 1.6 CBOM model as the schema defines it, what M-26-15 and EO 14412 require of a federal CBOM today, and how this project's CBOM uses the standard parts and the extension namespace, on the eight-service mini-agency; the anatomy, the second projection and the comparison as the workbench's CBOM page shows them.

Not covered: the minimum elements CISA and NIST will publish, which do not exist yet; CBOMs for firmware and hardware; the CycloneDX 1.7 changes; how commercial platforms map their inventories to the format. The EO 14412 figures are carried from the project's facts table, which records that they were read through a summarizing tool and are to be checked against the source before publication.

docs.title: What does federal policy require, and by when?
The answer
docs.text: Two documents set the clock for United States federal civilian agencies. Executive Order 14412 (2026-06-22) requires post-quantum key establishment on high-value assets and high-impact systems by the end of 2030 and post-quantum digital signatures on them by the end of 2031, and directs CISA and NIST to publish the minimum elements of a cryptography bill of materials (CBOM) within 270 days, which is 2027-03-19. OMB memorandum M-26-15 (2026-06-24) turns the order into a programme: a migration plan from each agency within 120 days (2026-10-22), a discovery phase through 2027 in which the inventory is built, and a central CBOM fed from three kinds of evidence. The inventory is therefore required before anyone has said what it must contain. That gap — five months between the discovery phase starting and the minimum elements appearing, and the risk that an inventory built to one shape is measured against another — is the reason this project keeps every finding with its evidence on a ledger and treats the CBOM as a projection of that record. National security systems are on a separate clock, CNSA 2.0, with new acquisitions compliant from 2027-01-01, what cannot support the suite phased out by 2030-12-31 and the suite mandated by 2031-12-31.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) replaces the public-key algorithms a large quantum computer could break — RSA, Diffie-Hellman and elliptic-curve schemes — with algorithms NIST standardized in 2024: ML-KEM (FIPS 203) for key establishment and ML-DSA (FIPS 204) for signatures. Key establishment comes first because traffic recorded today can be decrypted later once the key exchange is broken ("harvest now, decrypt later"); a signature forged later does not retroactively undo anything signed today.

A CBOM is the inventory of an organization's cryptography: every algorithm, key, certificate and protocol in use, where it was found and what depends on it, in the CycloneDX format (note 01). A high-value asset (HVA) is a federal system designated as such for the information it holds or the function it serves; a high-impact system is one whose loss would have severe effect under FIPS 199. M-26-15 adds systems with highly sensitive data and any the agency judges particularly exposed. These are the systems the dates apply to; everything else is Phase 5.

docs.title: The dates
docs.text:
Date What Source What it asks of an inventory 2026-06-22 EO 14412 signed EO 14412 — 2026-10-22 Each agency's PQC Migration Plan due to OMB and ONCD (passed) M-26-15 §1 The plan names an inventory approach before the inventory exists 2026–2027 Phase 1: strategy, planning and discovery — inventory, assessment, governance, accountable officials M-26-15 §3.D The inventory is built in this window 2027-01-01 New national security system acquisitions CNSA 2.0 compliant NSA CNSA 2.0 FAQ Ver. 2.2, Timeframe, read first-hand 2026-11-09 A separate clock for a separate community: the suite is mandated for national security systems by 2031-12-31 2027-03-19 CISA and NIST publish the minimum elements of a CBOM EO 14412 (270 days) Until then, "a CBOM" means CycloneDX 1.6 plus whatever an agency or vendor adds; after it, an inventory is measured against a published list 2027–2028 Phase 2: pilots and early migration of prioritized systems M-26-15 §3.D The inventory must say what first: owners, deadlines, blockers 2028–2030 Phase 3: prioritized migration of key establishment M-26-15 §3.D The first queue 2030-01-02 TLS 1.3 supported M-26-15 §4 Hybrid key establishment in TLS is a TLS 1.3 mechanism; a listener on 1.2 alone cannot offer ML-KEM 2030-12-31 Key establishment post-quantum on HVAs and high-impact systems EO 14412; M-26-15 Phase 3 The first queue closes 2031 / 2031-12-31 Phase 4: signatures post-quantum on the same systems M-26-15; EO 14412 The second queue; it waits on validated modules and certificate chains After 2030 / after 2035 Every quantum-vulnerable signature and key-establishment scheme deprecated / disallowed under NIST standards, at any key size NIST IR 8547 (final, 2026-10-27), Tables 2 and 4 For a system the dates above do not prioritize, RSA-3072 or P-384 is deprecated after 2030, not acceptable to 2035; the plan has to say which source set each date 2035 Phase 5: full migration of remaining systems M-26-15 §3.D — The dates on one line: the inventory is built in Phase 1, and what it must contain is published part way through it.

NIST IR 8547, Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards, sets the clock for everything the two documents do not prioritize. In its final form (2026-10-27) every quantum-vulnerable public-key family at or above 112 bits of classical strength is deprecated after 2030 and disallowed after 2035: ECDSA and RSA signatures, EdDSA (at or above 128 bits), finite-field and elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman and MQV, and RSA key establishment (Tables 2 and 4). The 2024 draft deprecated only the 112-bit parameter sets after 2030, so RSA-3072 and P-256 read as acceptable until 2035; the final removes that reading. Deprecated means the algorithm may still be used with the risk accepted; disallowed means it is no longer approved. For prioritized federal systems the report itself points to the earlier dates of M-26-15 and EO 14412.

The workbench carries both documents as policy packs, each quote checked against the text it was read from (policy/packs/m-26-15.yaml, policy/packs/ir-8547.yaml). Each open migration item's deadline is the earlier of the memo's queue date and the report's disallowance, and the item names which source set it. The deprecation date travels beside it:

Item Deadline Set by Deprecated after Prioritized key establishment 2030-12-31 M-26-15 §3.A, Phase 3 2030-12-31 (IR 8547 Table 4) Prioritized signature 2031-12-31 M-26-15 Phase 4 2030-12-31 (IR 8547 Table 2) Remaining system, either function 2035-12-31 M-26-15 Phase 5 and IR 8547 (the same date) 2030-12-31

The report gives years ("after 2030", "after 2035"); the pack carries the last day of each year and marks the dates computed. For a prioritized signature the report's deprecation comes a year before the memo's deadline: use in 2031 is still within the memo's schedule, with the risk accepted. The tables' parameter condition (at or above 112 bits of classical strength, 128 for EdDSA) is checked where the finding carries a key size, read through SP 800-57 Part 1's strength table: a key below it is already disallowed under SP 800-131A Rev. 2 and gets no 2035 date; a name with no key size is marked unchecked. DSA and OpenSSH's sntrup761x25519 are in no row of either table, and an item that also holds a covered name says so instead of dating them.

Two further requirements shape what the inventory has to hold. M-26-15 Appendix A §6 says the central CBOM is populated from software composition analysis, static and dynamic testing of code, and network scanning — the three evidence layers this project calls code, host and wire. And on enforcement it says devices must be configurable to use only acceptable algorithms: an inventory that records what a listener offers, but not whether it still accepts the old algorithm, cannot show that requirement met (note 08).

docs.title: What the gap means for how an inventory is built
docs.text:
The minimum elements are a list that does not exist yet. Three ways to build an inventory in the meantime:

Approach When the minimum elements arrive A spreadsheet or a document edited to today's best guess Re-collected by hand against the new list; nothing in it can show where its rows came from A CBOM document written directly by scanners Re-scanned, and anything the scanners did not keep — the raw output, the rule that linked two findings — is gone A ledger of findings with their evidence, the CBOM projected from it Re-projected: the same record, a new shape, no re-scan. Fields the list does not ask for are dropped from the projection and kept in the record

The third is this project's design (ADR-0001 in the repository, the ledger is the system of record): the ledger is the system of record, the CBOM is rebuilt from it, and the CBOM carries more than any minimum is likely to ask — dependencies, data lifetime, the evidence hash for every entry, the listener's posture, the verifier verdict for every change. The bet is that the published minimum will be a subset of these, and the way to find out which is to hold them all and project.

The same gap is why the project starts now rather than waiting for the list. The discovery phase is this year and next; an agency that waits for the minimum elements before building an inventory arrives at the pilots phase with nothing to pilot.

docs.text:
Covered: the dates and requirements in EO 14412 and OMB M-26-15 as they bear on a cryptographic inventory, and CNSA 2.0's three dates. M-26-15 was read first-hand (again on 2026-10-20, from the PDF with sha256 515af704…), and so was the CNSA 2.0 FAQ (Ver. 2.2, on 2026-11-09, sha256 bc430341…) after NSA's site had refused it to the harness three times. Not covered: what the minimum elements will turn out to be; agency-specific plans; how the dates apply to systems outside the prioritized categories beyond Phase 5; national security systems in any detail (planned as note 11).

docs.title: What can be seen on the wire, on a host and in code — and what cannot?
The answer
docs.text: Three kinds of evidence feed a cryptographic inventory, and each answers a question the others cannot. A targeted wire scan asks one listener what it accepts — every group, every suite, every version, its certificate — and gets a complete answer for that listener and nothing about its clients. Passive capture of a network's traffic shows what every client offers and what every server chooses in real handshakes, across the whole estate at once, including clients and servers nobody listed; it cannot see what a server would accept but was never asked for, and in TLS 1.3 it cannot see the server's certificate at all. Host and code evidence — files in images, call sites in source — shows what is installed and written, which is where a wire finding gets traced to a line that must change, but not whether any of it runs or is reachable. The inventory OMB M-26-15 asks for names all three (Appendix A §6). A scan of the listeners alone misses the clients that can never do post-quantum key exchange, and a capture alone misses every certificate behind a TLS 1.3 listener.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
A TLS handshake begins with the client listing what it supports — key-exchange groups in order of preference, signature algorithms, protocol versions — and the server choosing one of each. A hybrid post-quantum group such as X25519MLKEM768 combines a classical exchange with ML-KEM, so the session is protected if either holds. Whether a session is post-quantum is therefore decided twice: the client has to offer a hybrid group, and the server has to choose it. An inventory that sees only one side cannot say which side is the obstacle.

The two sides of a handshake, and which side each way of looking can see.

Passive capture is the only way to see the client side without touching the client: a switch mirror copies every frame crossing a trunk to a port where a sensor (Zeek here) parses the handshakes and records what each side said. Nothing is sent. The sensor's port has no address.

docs.title: The mechanism: what each layer yields
docs.text:
Evidence Sees Does not see Targeted wire scan of a listener (testssl.sh, ssh-audit, paired probes) Everything the listener accepts: every group, suite and version, the certificate chain and its key, whether the old algorithm is still accepted after a change Any client; which of the accepted options are ever used; listeners not in the scope Passive capture at a mirror (Zeek) For every real handshake: the client's offered groups, versions and signature algorithms, the server's chosen group and version, the server name; SSH key exchange and host-key algorithms as negotiated; every client and server that spoke, listed or not What a server would accept but was not offered; TLS 1.3 certificates; anything that did not cross the mirrored trunk; frames the mirror dropped Host evidence (cbomkit-theia on images and hosts) Keys, certificates and libraries present in files, with their parameters Whether a file is served or loaded; what a running process negotiates Code evidence (CBOMkit source scanners, rule packs) Call sites: which algorithm a program asks a library for, and where Runtime configuration that overrides the code; what the deployed binary does

What a code rule finds, and what it cannot decide. A rule pack matches lines that name a cryptographic library: OpenSSL::PKey::RSA, Digest::SHA256, JWT.decode. A match is a candidate, not a use. In 18F/identity-idp at its pinned commit, a Ruby pack of twelve patterns matched 85 lines under app/, lib/ and config/. A model reading each line in its context (the call-site-read role: Gemma 4 31B with reasoning on, three calls each) judged 79 to be live cryptographic uses and 6 not: a documentation comment, and five exception handlers (rescue OpenSSL::Cipher::CipherError) that name a library class and call nothing. Its three calls agreed on 75 of the 85 and split two to one on the other 10. On the two candidates that are among spike S3's labelled call sites, its judgement matched the label. The judgement is the CBOM's pqch:in-use for each code entry, labelled as the model's.

What a rule pack matched and what a reading made of it: 79 uses, 6 candidates that were not.

Two details of the capture layer matter in practice:

  • The VLAN tag on a connection is the originator's. A mirror of a trunk carries each frame with the tag of the segment it was on when it reached the trunk, and the sensor records the tag of the first packet, which the client sent. A listener's own VLAN is not in the capture; it is inferred from the tags the clients on its subnet carried, and labelled as inferred.
  • Capture loss must be measured, and offload turned off. A trunk is usually faster than the mirror port; the sensor counts gaps in TCP streams as loss. With generic receive offload on, the network card merges segments before the sensor sees them, and those merges are counted as loss too, so the figure can read many times what the host actually dropped. Every count from a capture is reported beside its loss figure.

docs.title: One inventory from two layers
docs.text: The capture and the targeted scan are not two reports to read side by side. Each observation becomes a CBOM entry named by its fingerprint — what the asset is and where it is, not which tool saw it — so the same key exchange on the same listener is one entry whether Zeek saw it chosen or testssl.sh found it accepted. Merged, that entry carries both tools and both ledger events, and a listener's entries together give the readings a planner needs without anyone lining up two reports: a hybrid group accepted and never chosen, a server that accepts none while its clients keep offering one.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
Covered: TLS and SSH handshakes as Zeek's ssl, ssh and x509 logs and a handshake-level script record them; the three evidence layers as this project uses them.

Code: one repository, one language, twelve patterns; the candidates are only as complete as the pack, and no CBOMkit source scanner has run yet. The model's judgements were not checked line by line beyond the six rejections and the two labelled sites.

Not covered: traffic that never crossed the trunk (two devices on one VLAN talking directly); QUIC and DTLS; encrypted client hello, which would hide the server name; what a mirror by VLAN rather than by trunk would add; client certificates; the signature algorithms clients offer, which the sensor records but this note does not analyze.

docs.title: How does a finding become a dependency chain?
The answer
docs.text: A finding is one observation: a tool saw this algorithm, certificate or key at this place. It becomes a dependency chain when the record can say what the observation rides on and what rides on it, link by link, and can show for each link how it knows. In this workbench a chain for a wire entry has five links above the observation: the listener it was seen on, the certificate or host key that listener serves, the service that serves the listener, the mission function that service carries, and how long the data it handles must stay secret. The first three are discovered: a rule asserts each from evidence already on the ledger and names the events it rests on. The last two, and whether the service is a high-value asset, are supplied: typed in by the system owner, because no scan can see a mission, and recorded with a human actor and the label supplied. A chain is complete when every link is present. A supplied link is never counted as coverage, and the CBOM carries the label on every one, so a reader can tell at a glance which parts of the chain the evidence found and which parts a person said.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
The five rungs of the maturity model ask five questions, and the Structured rung asks two: what depends on this, and how long must the data stay secret. The first is what makes an inventory usable for migration — a certificate is changed on a listener, a listener belongs to a service, and a service is what an agency can take down, schedule and own. The second is what sets the order: traffic recorded today can be decrypted once the key exchange that protected it is broken, so a service whose data must stay confidential for seventy-five years is in a different queue from one whose data is stale in a year, whatever the two listeners look like on the wire. OMB M-26-15's prioritization criteria — high-impact systems, high-value assets, highly sensitive data — are properties of systems and data, not of cipher suites.

Nothing on the wire or in an image says what a service is for or how long its data lives. Those facts come from the organization. The design question is how to carry them beside the evidence without letting them pass for evidence, and the answer here is the same one the ledger gives for everything else: every link is an event with an actor, and the actor's kind is what it is. A rule's link names the events it was computed from. A person's link names the file it was typed in, with the file's hash.

docs.title: The mechanism
docs.text:
The discovered links. Three rules, each recording link.asserted events with a rule actor and status: discovered:

Link Rule Evidence the link rests on served certificate → file in the image link/public-key/1 The SHA-256 of the public key (SubjectPublicKeyInfo, or the OpenSSH fingerprint for a host key) is the same in the wire finding and the file finding; both findings' events are the link's inputs listener → service link/service/1 The scope, generated from the estate's compose file, names the service for the listener; and the runner's record of the scan (binding/scope/1) says a container at that address ran the scope's image for the whole scan. The binding event is the link's input. A listener that was not bound gets no service link, and the chain says why image → service link/service/1 The same binding events: the container found serving the service's listener runs this image

The listener itself rests on the scan.completed event, which carries the tool, its version and image digest, and the raw output by path and hash (note 12).

The supplied links. The owner's facts live in one file, agency/context.yaml:

# agency/context.yaml
schema: pqch.context/1
supplied_by: the system owner
services:
  records-db:
    mission_function: benefits records
    data_lifetime_years: 75
    high_value_asset: true

For each service the scope names, each fact becomes a link.asserted event with a human actor (the operator who ran the scan), status: supplied, the file's path and SHA-256 as source, and the same file in the event's evidence list. A service in the file that the scope does not name gets no event; a service the scope names with no entry in the file gets a chain whose last links are marked missing.

The projection. The CBOM, rebuilt from these events, carries the chain as components and dependencies in CycloneDX's own terms: an application component per service, which depends on its listeners and on a container component per image; the container depends on the files found in it; a listener depends on the assets it negotiates and serves; a served certificate depends on the file holding its key. The supplied facts are properties of the service component — pqch:mission-function, pqch:data-lifetime-years, pqch:high-value-asset — and a pqch:supplied property lists each one with the event that carries it and who supplied it. The scorer reads that list: a supplied item in the answer key counts as carried only when the service component holds the fact and labels it; a fact carried without the label is reported as a defect, and no supplied item is ever coverage.

Two more rules that make a chain honest. verifier/class/1 records, for each class of finding present (layer, asset type, role), which verifier could confirm a change to it — the paired probes for key establishment on the wire, the certificate parse for a served certificate, none for anything read from a file — and the CBOM carries the kind on each entry as pqch:verifiable-by. conflict/resolve/1 settles each disagreement between what a file says and what the wire shows, in the vocabulary spike S3 labelled: not-served when no listener of the image serves the file and every precondition for saying so holds (every listener scanned, bound to the scope's image, every served certificate found in the image); tool-limit when one tool parsed a certificate from a file and another reported nothing for it; cannot-tell otherwise, with what is missing named. A model may explain a conflict beside the rule's answer; it never settles one (note 13).

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
The portal's X25519 key-exchange entry, from the eight-service estate scanned on 2026-10-20 (run 01M5CTXE9PH6Y2BKPHZPZ9KFK6):

Link Status What it rests on listener TLS 172.16.106.10:443 discovered scan.completed: testssl.sh 3.2.4, raw output by hash certificate RSA (2048) discovered the wire finding; link/public-key/1 to /etc/nginx/tls/portal.crt in pqch-agency/portal by SubjectPublicKeyInfo hash service portal discovered link/service/1: the scope names portal for the listener; binding/scope/1 found container pqch-agency-portal-1 running the scope's image for the whole scan mission function: benefits enrollment supplied link.asserted by the operator; agency/context.yaml sha256 recorded data lifetime: 10 years supplied the same high-value asset: no supplied the same

The portal's chain: three links the rules found from ledger events, three the owner typed in and the record labels.

The same image holds a second certificate, /etc/ssl/legacy/portal-2019.crt, that no listener serves. Its chain stops at the image: the file is linked to the service through the image, marked not in use by in-use/not-served/1, and the conflict between the file and the wire is settled by conflict/resolve/1 as wire, not-served, with the in-use event and the served certificate's finding as inputs. The records database's chain carries a 75-year data lifetime and high-value status; its listener is mixed (hybrid key exchange offered, classical still accepted, RSA key transport too), and that pair of facts is what the Managed rung will turn into a place in the first queue.

On the page, each listener shows its chain as a list, one link per line with its status and the event behind it, and each entry shows which verifier could confirm a change to it. The receipts panel counts the chains complete, the service links discovered, the facts supplied and labelled, the entries with no verifier, and the conflicts by outcome.

docs.title: What follows
docs.text:
• Discovered and supplied are different colours of the same record. An inventory that mixes what it found with what it was told cannot be audited; one that refuses to carry what it was told cannot be used for prioritization. Carry both, label every supplied link, and never let a supplied fact raise a coverage score.
  • The service link is where a wire scan meets the organization's map. It rests on something the runner observed — the container at the address and the image it ran — not on a name in a spreadsheet. On an estate the harness did not build, the equivalent evidence is whatever the operator's own deployment record can show; without it, the link is supplied and labelled so.
  • Most of an inventory has no verifier. On this estate 188 of 220 entries are files in images or SSH host-key algorithms, for which no change can yet be shown to have landed by a probe. Saying so per entry is what keeps the Agile rung's claim — time-to-change, verified — honest about what it covers.
  • Conflicts are rules' work. Every conflict on this ledger was settled by a rule from evidence the ledger already held; the one measured role a model was given for this never reached its floor (note 13). The reasons that need a configuration layer — a default applying, a line overridden, a stale file — are not decided yet, because no configuration scan runs yet.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: Covered: the eight-service mini-agency, nine listeners (TLS, TLS behind PostgreSQL's upgrade, SSH), eight images, on an x86_64 lab server; the chain from a wire or image entry up to the owner's facts. Links are discovered from wire and image evidence only; no source or configuration scan contributes a link yet, so a chain stops at the file holding a key and does not reach the line of code or configuration that selects it (the investigator's trace is a model's claim recorded beside the chain, not a link in it). The owner's facts are the mini-agency's planted ones. The Managed rung — owners, deadlines, queues computed from the lifetime and the posture — is not built.

docs.title: How is a migration priority computed?
The answer
docs.text: A migration priority answers two questions for each system: does it come first, and by when must each kind of cryptography it uses be post-quantum. Both answers are in OMB M-26-15, the memorandum that governs federal civilian agencies' migration, and both can be computed. The memo names the systems to prioritize — a high-impact system, a High Value Asset, a system whose data is expected to remain mission-sensitive in 2030 — and the queues: key establishment for prioritized systems by the end of 2030, signatures in 2031, everything else by 2035, and TLS 1.3 support by January 2, 2030. A rule reads those criteria against facts the system owner supplies, reads the memo's table of quantum-vulnerable algorithms against what was found, and places each system's key establishment and its signatures in a queue with a date. Two further rules say what stands in the way: whether the system's software can offer a post-quantum algorithm at all, and whether a validated cryptographic module that does so exists. Each is a rule over a dated measurement, and each cites the words it rests on.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
Three ideas carry the computation.

Prioritization is the memo's, not the tool's. An inventory tool that ranks by its own score invents a policy. M-26-15 §3.C.2 already says which systems come first, so the rule is a reading of that list: a system is prioritized when any criterion holds, and the record says which.

Two clocks, because two attacks. Key establishment protects confidentiality now: traffic recorded today can be decrypted once the key exchange that protected it is broken ("harvest now, decrypt later"). A signature protects authenticity at the moment it is checked, and a forgery needs a working quantum computer at that moment. So the memo moves key establishment first and signatures a year later, and a system appears in two queues, one per function.

A blocker is a state with evidence, not a note. "We can't, the vendor doesn't support it" is the most common reason a migration stalls, and the least often checked. Asking the software's own runtime what it can do turns the claim into a measurement; asking NIST's list of validated modules what they cover turns the second common claim — "we must use a validated module and none supports it" — into one too.

docs.title: The mechanism
docs.text:
The pack. The memo is carried as data, policy/packs/m-26-15.yaml: the criteria, the table's rows, the queues with their sections and dates, the replacement and enforcement clauses. Each entry carries the memo's own words. The loader refuses the pack if any quote does not occur, in order, in the text extracted from the memo's PDF, whose SHA-256 the pack records; a paraphrase does not load. A date the memo states is stated; a date it gives only as a year (Phase 4, "2031") is carried as the year's end and marked computed.

The rules.

Rule Decides From quantum/vulnerable/1 Per algorithm name: its family and whether the memo's table makes it quantum-vulnerable. A name the table does not list is vulnerable when asymmetric, by the table's footnote 13 policy/algorithm-families.yaml, the pack's table pack/scope/1 Which policy governs a service: M-26-15 unless the owner marks it a national security system (§3.B) the owner's fact priority/m-26-15/1 Which of §3.C.2's criteria hold the owner's facts: FIPS 199 impact, high-value status, data lifetime queue/m-26-15/1 Per service and function, the vulnerable algorithms it still offers or holds in use, the queue and the deadline; met when none the findings joined to the service by the dependency chain deadline/tls13/1 Per TLS listener, whether TLS 1.3 was offered the TLS versions of the cipher suites the listener accepted blocker/supplier/1 Whether the software can offer a post-quantum algorithm in that function at all; when not, the item is marked for replacement (§3.C.3) the capability snapshot blocker/validated-module/1 Whether a validated module is in use, available, or does not exist for the library and algorithm the CMVP snapshot

The data-lifetime criterion is computed: data handled on the assessment date stays sensitive until that date plus its lifetime, and the criterion holds when that reaches 2030.

The two snapshots. The capability snapshot runs each image with no network and its entry point replaced, and asks the runtime for its own list: openssl list -kem-algorithms, ssh -Q kex, Erlang's ssl:groups(), the classes in the Java runtime. Where an image ships no tool that can list its library's algorithms — the nginx images ship no openssl command — the probe records the library package and checks it is the same build as an image whose capability was observed on the wire. The CMVP snapshot reads NIST's search for active certificates and each certificate page's list of approved algorithms, and keeps every page's hash. Both are files in the repository with a date in their name; a rule never reaches the network.

The record. Every result is an assessment.made event naming its inputs — the supplied facts, the findings, the item — and its source: the pack, the PDF's hash, the section. The CBOM carries the result on each service component (pqch:owner, pqch:queue, pqch:deadline, pqch:state, pqch:migration with the blockers) and on each asset (pqch:family, pqch:quantum-vulnerable). The page shows a decision record per open item: owner, queue and date, why it is there, its blockers, and the approval state of any change that answers it.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
The mini-agency on 2026-10-20 (scan run 01M5DFXYNNG08S8ADTDF48WYFE):

Service Prioritized by Key establishment Signatures Blockers records-db high impact, HVA, lifetime kex-2030: DH-2048, RSA key transport and X25519 beside the hybrid group sig-2031 none from the supplier; a validated module with ML-KEM exists and is not in use sftp-legacy high impact, HVA, lifetime kex-2030: DH-1024 and six more sig-2031: DSA, ECDSA, Ed25519, RSA supplier: OpenSSH 6.6 has no post-quantum algorithm; replace pq-gateway high impact, HVA, lifetime met: X25519MLKEM768 only met: ML-DSA-65 only — queue lifetime (7 years) kex-2030; TLS 1.2 only, so also tls13-2030 sig-2031 supplier: Erlang/OTP 27's TLS lists no ML-KEM group, though it links OpenSSL 3.5.9 legacy-app lifetime kex-2030; TLS 1.2 only sig-2031 supplier: Java 8 has neither ML-KEM nor ML-DSA portal, api lifetime kex-2030 sig-2031 none from the supplier bastion none (data sensitive for one year) remaining-2035 remaining-2035 supplier, signatures only: OpenSSH 10 has ML-KEM key exchange and no post-quantum host key

The two queues as the rules placed the estate in them, and the half of the open items no setting can move.

Two rows show what the blocker rules are for. The queue's broker runs on an Erlang/OTP whose cryptographic library has ML-KEM, and a reader of its package list would call it ready; its TLS stack does not offer the group, so the item is blocked on the supplier. The records database is not blocked on its supplier — PostgreSQL 18 on OpenSSL 3.5 lists ML-KEM and ML-DSA — and is configured to offer the hybrid group, but it still accepts X25519, finite-field Diffie-Hellman and RSA key transport, so its item stays open: enabled is not enforced (Appendix A §5).

A model does not decide any of this, and on this pack does not yet explain it either. The plan gave one job to a model: retrieve the pack's passages for an item and explain, in plain words, why the item sits in its queue, with the queue it names checked against the rule that placed it there. The floor was written before the first call: every open item passes by the majority of three calls, one excepted, and no call names another queue. The job reached 3 of 14 items, with three harmful calls, at 3.2 s a call on Gemma 4 31B on four L4s. Retrieval, not the model, failed: the item's description named algorithms, so the three nearest passages were rows of the memo's table, and the queue's own passage was among them for only 3 items; on those three the model passed all nine calls. On the broker's key-establishment item retrieval returned the TLS 1.3 queue's passage, and the model named that queue. The role is unbound; the page shows the rule's basis alone (lesson 34).

docs.title: What follows
docs.text:
• Carry the policy as quotes a loader checks. A rule that says "the memo requires X" is only as good as the reading behind it; a pack whose every rule is the memo's own words, refused when a word is wrong, can be audited by anyone holding the PDF.
  • Ask the runtime, not the package list. A library that supports an algorithm is not a protocol stack that offers it; measure what the software will negotiate before calling a blocker a supplier's (lesson 32).
  • A validated module is a property of the certificate, not of the library's version. The OpenSSL project's own validated provider covers neither ML-KEM nor ML-DSA, while one vendor's validated rebuild of it covers both; a module shipped and not activated is not in use (lesson 33).
  • Most of the work is blocked or waiting. On this estate half the open items are blocked on a supplier, and no item is in a validated module today. A migration plan that lists systems without these two states lists work that cannot start.

docs.title: When no configuration change is possible: the package
docs.text:
A blocked item has nothing to render, draft or rehearse, but it still needs a record an owner can act on. The workbench issues a change package per blocked item, written by a rule (package/supplier/1) from the ledger and the snapshot, never by a model:

Field What it holds Why no configuration change The blocker's basis and the runtime's own list of what it supports, by path and SHA-256 What would unblock it Any service in the same snapshot running the same product that does list an algorithm for the function — an upgrade path the estate already holds — or none What the memo says §3.C.3, quoted: such systems "must be identified and given priority for replacement or decommissioning" The CBOM entries it covers Each entry on the service's listeners for the function, by fingerprint, with the files it is served from The test that will count The verifier check that applies once the software is replaced Rollback, rehearsal None, and not rehearsed: nothing is applied

On the mini-agency the seven packages cover 19 CBOM entries on four services. Six have no upgrade path in the estate. The seventh does: the SFTP drop's OpenSSH 6.6 lists no post-quantum key exchange, while the jump host's OpenSSH 10.0 lists mlkem768x25519-sha256 — an upgrade, then a one-line configuration change of the kind the jump host's own change already rehearsed. In NIST's crypto-agility plan (CSWP 39-upd1, Fig. 3) this is the mitigation output beside migration.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: Covered: the eight-service mini-agency, its planted owner's facts, M-26-15 read first-hand, the capability of each image's runtime measured on 2026-10-20, and NIST's CMVP active certificates matching OpenSSL, Java, Erlang and OpenSSH on the same day. Not covered: CNSA 2.0's dates as a queue; its pack is read first-hand (the FAQ Ver. 2.2, 2026-11-09) but governs no service here, and the queue rule is the memo's. Not examined: the validated software version on each certificate (in each Security Policy, not read), modules in process, products in CISA's product-category list (§3.C.4), client-side support, and whether a supplier's next release adds what is missing. Deadlines are the memo's; an agency's own plan may set earlier ones.
