docs.title: How is a question to the CBOM answered, and how is the answer checked without asking a model?
The answer
docs.text: A question in plain words is embedded; the eight components whose passages lie nearest to it, and the chain each sits in (an asset's listener, a listener's service), are handed to a model as numbered passages, each with the ledger event ids that are its evidence. The model returns a typed reply: the answer, the components it rests on, the event ids it cites. A rule then checks each citation: the event must exist in the ledger, and it must belong to a passage the model was shown; a component must be one it was shown. The page prints the answer, each citation with its verdict, and the passages. The model never decides whether it cited well. Retrieval and the answer are measured separately against floors written before the first run.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text: A CBOM (cryptography bill of materials: the inventory of an estate's algorithms, keys, certificates and protocols, with where each was found) is a document, and a document can be asked questions. The risk in letting a model answer is that it answers from what it knows rather than from the document, and names things the document does not hold. Two things close that gap: the model sees only passages built from the CBOM, and every claim it makes about provenance is checked by code against the ledger the CBOM was built from. The ledger (an append-only, hash-chained record of every finding, assessment and decision, from which the CBOM is rebuilt) is what makes the check possible: every fact in the CBOM has an event behind it, so a citation is a thing that can be looked up.

docs.title: The mechanism
docs.text:
1. Passages. One per component, built from the same anatomy the CBOM page shows: kind, label, bom-ref, every field and value, what it depends on and what depends on it, and the sorted set of ledger event ids behind those fields. Embedded once per CBOM (the embed tier) and cached beside the run.
  2. Retrieval. The question is embedded as a query; the eight nearest passages by cosine are taken. Then a rule adds, for each hit, its parents two hops up the CBOM's dependency graph. A question about a service is usually answered by the assets that make it what it is, and the assets are what the embedding finds; the chain brings the service along so the model can name it.
  3. The answer. Role ask-cbom, one call through the inference seam with a JSON schema on the reply: answer, components (bom-refs), citations (event ids), not_in_passages. The system prompt says what an event id looks like and that a component's hash is not one.
  4. The check. For each citation: in the ledger, and among the shown passages' events. For each component: among the shown. A hash of a shown component cited as an event is read as a component naming; a ref written bom-ref: X, /bom-ref X or [n] is normalized. Anything else that fails is shown as failing, and the page says the answer is unsupported.

The ledger is not written: a question is not an event of the estate.

From question to checked answer: the model answers from passages, and code checks every citation against the ledger.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text: Question: Which SSH listener still offers the 1024-bit Diffie-Hellman group? The nearest passages are the DH-1024, DH-2048 and DH-GEX wire assets on 172.16.106.20:22 and the listener itself; the chain adds the bastion service. The reply names listener:172.16.106.20:22, cites the finding events behind the DH-1024 asset, and passes. Asked the same on the first version of the page, the Nano NIM cited the DH-2048 asset's hash as an event: the rule marked it failing, which is the page working as intended.

docs.title: What the measurement says
docs.text:
Part Floor (of 12) Nano 9B NIM Super VL 120B, medium effort, without the chain rule Super VL, with it Retrieval, recall@8 11 11 (with the rule) 9 10 Answer contains the expected phrase, all three repeats 10 7 10 11 Every citation passes, all three repeats 12 10 10 9 Median latency a question — 22 s 57 s 34 s

Neither arm clears all three floors on 2026-11-04. The larger model answers correctly; the citation floor is total by design and three questions missed it: invented event ids near real ones (caught), bom-refs given as citations (now read as component namings), and one question whose three replies were cut short of valid JSON by a 4,000-token budget shared with the model's thinking (the budget is now 8,000). Retrieval reached its floor on one run and missed by one on the next: the embedding of a question is not bit-stable across runs on this engine, and the eighth nearest passage can change. The role is bound to the deliberate tier as the best measured arm, below floor, and the page shows every verdict (kit/inference.yaml).

On a second GB10 with Lightning alone (2026-11-04). The six example questions, one call each, through the page on a Dell Pro Max GB10 whose only engine is Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B NVFP4 with thinking on, with the Llama Nemotron embed NIM for retrieval: at a reply budget of 8,000 tokens three of six replies were cut short; at 16,000 two; at 20,000 none, with 2,790 to 9,065 completion tokens a reply and 22 to 73 s a question. Five of six then passed every citation and named the expected component; the sixth (what signs the message queue's certificate) declined, correctly noting the issuer the passages show but no stated signing relation. The same question used 2,790 tokens on one run and over 16,000 on another, so the budget is set for the role's worst call, not its typical one (lesson 55).

With thinking off, the binding on that GB10 (2026-11-05). The full evaluation set, twelve questions with three repeats each, on the same engine with thinking off: every citation passed on 12 of 12 items, the expected phrase on 10 of 12 (the floor), at a median of 2.8 s a call and 6.1 s at the slowest of 36. Retrieval put the expected component in the passages on 10 of 12, one under its floor, and no engine changes that: the shortfall is in the index. Thinking on took 22 to 73 s a question for no better citations, so the role is bound to the fast tier without thinking, and the answer arrives while the presenter is still speaking. The reply's shape is written into the prompt and validated by the seam with one retry, because the engine's structured-output grammar with thinking off ran one call in five to its cap (lesson 58).

Through the lab gateway, on the published run (2026-11-05). The same twelve questions, three repeats each, against the mini-agency scan the public demo shows. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL at medium-effort thinking, served on the lab GB10 and reached through the gateway, named the expected phrase on 12 of 12 and passed every citation on 12 of 12, at a median of 55 s a call. It is the first arm to reach both answer floors. Gemma 4 31B on the lab's four L4s with thinking off reached 2 and 3: 26 of its 36 replies ran past the 1,200-token cap the page gives a non-thinking call and were cut short of valid JSON. Retrieval put the expected components in the passages on 10 of 12 for both, under its floor of 11, as on every engine measured. The lab's role is bound to Super VL. The public demo, which has no model, shows the six example questions answered once by that binding, labelled as recorded, with every citation checked again when the site is built (lesson 63).

docs.title: What follows
docs.text: An agency can let a model answer questions about its inventory on its own machine, if the answer is grounded in passages from the inventory and every citation is checked by code against the record the inventory came from. The check is cheap and exact; the model's quality shows up as answers the check marks unsupported, not as answers that mislead. A floor written first says when the page is usable.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: Twelve questions on one estate, written from the answer key, three repeats, two engines on one GB10. Not a benchmark of retrieval methods; not a measure of the page on a real estate's CBOM; the question set is small and will grow. Lesson 34 holds: retrieval is scored on its own before the model is blamed.

docs.title: How is one server inventoried as an estate, below its operating system as well as on the wire, and planned from its CBOM?
The answer
docs.text: A server holds cryptography in four places, each with its own owner and its own clock: the listeners it exposes (changed by its software), its own files (changed by its administrators), its firmware's trust databases (changed by firmware updates) and its management controller (changed by the controller's firmware and its settings). A scan of the listeners alone sees the first. The workbench reads all four as one estate, through its runner, into one signed ledger; projects a CBOM in which the server is a CycloneDX device with its firmware as components; and plans from it, separating what the owner can set today from what waits for an update, a requirement or the vendor. A run can be exported as a recording, its identifiers replaced, and replayed elsewhere into a new ledger, so a real server can be shown and planned where it cannot be reached.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
A CBOM (cryptography bill of materials) is an inventory of the algorithms, keys, certificates and protocols an estate uses, with where each was found and what depends on it. For a network, the listeners and the images behind them are most of it. For one server, much of the cryptography that decides its future is below the operating system:

  • The firmware's trust databases. UEFI Secure Boot (the firmware feature that checks a signature on every bootloader and driver before running it) keeps four databases: the platform key (PK), which signs updates to the key-exchange keys (KEK), which sign updates to the allowed signers (db) and the revoked (dbx). Every one of them is a certificate with a key and an expiry, checked for the life of the hardware.
  • The TPM (trusted platform module), whose measurement banks name a hash algorithm.
  • The management controller (a baseboard management controller, BMC: Dell's iDRAC, HPE's iLO), a second computer on the board with its own TLS and SSH, its own certificates, its own firmware and its own settings. It is reached over the network and configured separately from the operating system.

None of these is visible to a scan of the operating system's listeners, and none changes when the operating system is patched.

The four places, who changes each, and what the runner reads there; a listener scan sees only the first.

docs.title: The mechanism
docs.text:
1. The scope. The server is an external estate, with the operator's authorization in its scope. The scope lists the server's listeners as endpoints (and the controller's), and adds the server under systems (the paths that may be read, its addresses, whether its firmware is read) and the controller under controllers (read through DMTF Redfish, GET requests only).

2. The runner reads; nothing is installed. Ten jobs, each recorded as scan.completed with its raw output and hash:

Job Reads Produces postgres-tls-offer one PostgreSQL SSLRequest per database listener whether TLS is offered at all; TLS is scanned only where it is (lesson 51) ssh-targeted, tls-targeted each listener's offers, on the wire key exchange, host keys, certificates, protocol versions system-theia, system-files an archive of exactly the scoped paths, packed read-only by the runner as its own user certificates, public and private keys, keystores; what could not be read, listed (lesson 52) system-firmware the Secure Boot variables, DMI and the TPM from sysfs, in the same archive every certificate in PK, KEK, db and dbx with its key and dates; the BIOS version; the TPM's banks; whether Secure Boot is on controller-redfish the controller's Redfish API, GET only its configured SSH and TLS, SNMP, FIPS mode, identity certificates, firmware inventory

The runner's user decides what the files say. The archive is packed by the runner as whatever user it runs as, so that choice is part of the result and is recorded with it ("read as uid 1001" or "read as uid 0"). Read as an ordinary user, a server shows the public half of each key pair and lists the private halves as unreadable (lesson 52). Read as root, the same paths show the private keys too, and the unreadable list is empty. Root is needed only for the read: the runner mounts the scoped paths read-only under /host, so even a root runner can open them but cannot change them. The kit runs this as a second runner beside the mini-agency's (kit/compose.system.yaml), with its own signer and its own key, so a server's ledger is signed apart from the test estate's.

3. The ledger and the CBOM. Findings go on the wire, host or the new platform layer; what is not a cryptographic asset (the device, its firmware versions, its security settings) is a platform.observed event. The CBOM, rebuilt from the ledger, carries the server as a device that depends on its firmware, its listeners and its files; the BIOS depends on the keys its databases hold and the TPM's banks; the controller's firmware depends on its own configuration, certificates and listeners. Every entry names the ledger events it came from.

4. The plan. Rules over the run, in four waves and four lanes (the server's services, its operating system, its controller, its firmware):

Wave What it holds Now settings: a database listener with no TLS, SNMP v1 and v2c, FIPS mode, a privileged read of what the unprivileged read could not open Next updates: software that offers ML-KEM key exchange, certificates issued by the organization's CA in place of self-signed ones, the 2023 UEFI CAs before Secure Boot is turned on Then requiring the hybrid key exchange once clients can follow; reissuing the host's own keys as their software allows The vendor controller firmware with ML-KEM; a post-quantum firmware-signing root and a way to rotate PK, KEK and db; an attestation of the algorithms behind the controller's identity certificates

Dates come from the policy pack: with no owner's facts, a single server is not prioritized, so its key establishment and signatures fall in OMB M-26-15's remaining queue (by 2035), and the plan states the earlier dates (2030 and 2031) that would apply if the owner named it high-value.

5. Recording and replay. pqch system export writes the run's scope and raw outputs with the operator's identifiers replaced (each also in upper and lower case and as hexadecimal bytes, since a controller's SNMP engine ID carries the service tag that way), every MAC address and UUID replaced by a consistent stand-in, and a leak check that writes nothing if any pattern survives. pqch system replay on another host checks each raw output against the recording's hash and records a new run whose every job says where it was replayed from and when the server was read.

docs.title: What follows
docs.text: An agency inventorying servers should read each one four ways, not one, and keep the four in one record: the parts that move with an operating-system update, the parts that move with a firmware update, and the parts that move only when the vendor ships something are different work on different clocks, and the plan has to say which is which. A management controller is a server of its own on the same board; it belongs in the inventory with its own listeners and certificates. And an inventory read without privileges should say what it could not read, rather than present a partial picture as whole.

docs.title: Reading a server the runner is not on
docs.text: The runner packs a server's scoped paths under its own root, which is how the first server was read: its paths mounted read-only into the runner. A server elsewhere carries a route in the scope, via: {kind: ssh, host, user, known_hosts}, and the runner sends the packer's own source to that host's python3 over SSH and reads the same archive back. Nothing is installed on the remote and nothing is written to it; the manifest's read_as_uid is the SSH user's, so an unprivileged read says so as it does locally. Host-key checking is strict against the scope's known_hosts file, which the operator supplies: a host not in it is refused, never accepted on first use. One scope may list many systems, each with its own route, and pqch scan-system reads them in turn; each controller in the scope is read through the runner as before. A supplier's statement about the model joins each server's read by model and firmware version (note 23), and the modules it names are looked up in the dated CMVP snapshot for their status and whether ML-KEM and ML-DSA are among their approved algorithms.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: One server read on the host the runner runs on; the SSH route is tested against a stand-in ssh that runs the packer locally, not yet against a second real server. The controller reader's resource paths are Dell iDRAC 9's; other controllers serve Redfish under other paths. The Secure Boot reader parses X.509 and SHA-256 entries; other signature types are listed by GUID. The plan's rules are written for this kind of server and will grow with the next.

docs.text:

  • UEFI Specification 2.10, section 32 (Secure Boot and the signature databases): the PK, KEK, db and dbx and the EFI_SIGNATURE_LIST format the firmware reader parses.
  • DMTF Redfish (DSP0266): the API the controller reader uses, GET only.
  • OMB M-26-15, section 3.D and Appendix A: the queues and deadlines the plan's dates come from.
  • Lessons 51 and 52: a refusal probed rather than timed out; a read that lists what it could not open.

docs.title: What does a federal authorization ask of a CBOM tool itself, and where does the workbench stand?
The answer
docs.text:
An agency authorizes a cryptographic inventory tool the way it authorizes any system on its network. It holds the tool to the controls of NIST SP 800-53 under its Risk Management Framework, and adds the policies that bear on software, cryptography, artificial intelligence and accessibility. The tool's purpose earns no exemption. A tool that judges an estate's cryptography is judged on its own first.

Read against those controls, the workbench's foundation is what an assessor looks for:

  • a signed, hash-chained record
  • the CBOM rebuilt from it
  • scanning bounded by a scope the runner enforces
  • images by digest
  • models used only where measured
  • changes verified by probe

The three findings that would stop an authorization today are all in the shell around that foundation:

  • one owner with no roles, so a person can propose and approve their own change
  • the workbench's own cryptography running in no validated module
  • plain HTTP to the page, and to the models unless a deployment turns on the seam's TLS requirement

None of them requires the foundation to be rebuilt.

The review of 2026-11-06: nothing underneath fails; the three blockers are in the shell.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
A cryptography bill of materials (CBOM) is the inventory of an organization's cryptography: every algorithm, key, certificate and protocol in use, where it was found and what depends on it, in the CycloneDX format.

An authorization to operate (ATO) is an agency official's decision to accept the risk of running a system, after an assessment against a baseline of controls chosen for the system's impact level. A cryptographic inventory tool is usually assessed at moderate impact: what it holds is a map of the estate's weakest cryptography, and it can change production configuration.

Five bodies of requirement apply, beside the security baseline:

Requirement What it asks of the tool FIPS 140-3 (through SP 800-53 SC-13) Cryptography that protects federal information runs in a module the Cryptographic Module Validation Program (CMVP) has validated, for the algorithm used, with that module active OMB M-26-05 and CISA's 2026 SBOM minimum elements An agency may require a current SBOM of the software; what one must hold OMB M-25-21 Each AI use inventoried; whether any is high-impact decided; minimum practices for those that are Section 508 The interface meets WCAG AA; an Accessibility Conformance Report for procurement Supply-chain exclusion orders (FASCSA) No excluded product, including AI models: DHS's order 2026-01 excludes DeepSeek and products built on it from civilian systems

docs.title: The mechanism: what an assessor reads
docs.text:
An assessor reads a tool the way a reviewer reads a design. Who can act, and how is it recorded? What protects the data in transit, at rest and in the record? What runs with privilege? What can the vendor show about the software itself? Where does a model decide something?

The workbench answers each of those from its record (ADR-0001: the ledger is the system of record). That makes its gaps unusually easy to see: each is a place where the record is right but the thing around it is not.

Question What holds What would stop an authorization Who may act? Every approval is an event naming the person and how they were authenticated, covered by a signed checkpoint before the runner applies anything; the scope names the system, the person and role who authorized it, and a window the runner enforces No roles: any signed-on person may propose, approve and apply, and the page approves and applies in one request (P0) What protects the record? SHA-256 chain; ML-DSA checkpoints (ML-DSA-65, or ML-DSA-87 by setting) from a signer with no network that keeps its own record, with each caller's uid from the kernel; every ledger names the cryptographic libraries and FIPS state it was written under The signing and hashing run in OpenSSL builds with no validated FIPS provider active (P0) What protects the traffic? Internal-only bridges with explicit subnets; the inference seam can require TLS with a named CA and record how each call travelled; management-controller sessions can be held to a CA, a pin, or the certificate the same read observed (not yet to one an earlier read saw) The page itself is plain HTTP, and the TLS requirements are settings a deployment has to turn on (P0 until it does) What runs with privilege? The runner refuses anything outside its fixed, digest-pinned profiles and the scope; the capture service is fully confined; the harness services hold no capability and cannot gain one, and wire-probe jobs run with none (set in the compose files and the runner; not yet exercised in a running stack) The runner's Docker socket is root on the host, and the jobs that read archives keep Docker's default capabilities (P1) What can be shown about the software? Images by digest, an offline bundle checked blob by blob and its sums signed with ML-DSA, an SBOM of the harness image on demand, a licence table, CI actions pinned by commit with a dependency audit No CBOM of the workbench by its own pipeline yet; the SBOM carries no component hash (P1) Where does a model decide? Only in roles measured against a floor written first, each with a card; every call recorded with model, engine, hardware and prompt hash; a model-set fact in the CBOM says which model set it; the seam can refuse a model of an origin not on the allowlist; no model verifies a change The allowlist works only once each model's origin is declared in the config (P1) Is the content current? Policy packs as data, every passage cited; NIST IR 8547 beside M-26-15, each deadline naming the source that set it CNSA 2.0 still read second-hand (P1)

The checkpoint algorithm adds one point. For the ledger's integrity to count under SC-13, ML-DSA has to be on the module's certificate. The OpenSSL FIPS Provider's certificate 4985 lists no post-quantum algorithm. In the CMVP snapshot of 2026-10-20, one OpenSSL provider does: Chainguard's, certificate 5523, validated 2026-09-15. A post-quantum audit trail and a validated one are, for now, a choice of base image.

docs.title: Worked example: the approval of one change
docs.text:
A change to the portal's key exchange on the four-service slice follows this path: it is proposed, a person approves it, the runner applies it, and paired probes verify it (a model-drafted change is also rehearsed on a twin first). Today it fails an assessor on one point.

  • What passes. The ledger shows the proposal, the rehearsal, the approval with the approver's name and how they were authenticated, a checkpoint signed either side of the approval, the apply, and two verdicts.
  • What fails. Nothing on that record, and nothing in the runner, stops the person who asked for the proposal from approving it, in the same request that applies it.

The change that passes keeps the whole path:

  • the approval event records the role and the authentication context from the identity provider
  • the runner refuses an approval by the requester
  • the apply becomes a separate act

The ledger gains three fields and the runner three refusals. Separation of duties is a property the record can then prove, not one the operator promises.

docs.title: What follows
docs.text:
• Review the tool before building on it. The cheapest moment to find that a foundation cannot pass is before a customer depends on it. Here it can, and the work is in the shell, ordered as milestone M8 of the plan.
  • Hold the tool to its own standard. A CBOM tool should produce its own SBOM and CBOM, sign its releases with the algorithm it recommends, and run that algorithm in a module validated for it. Each is a demonstration as well as a control. An SBOM tool's output is not yet a minimum-elements SBOM: Syft over the workbench's image names every package but hashes none of them, and finds a producer for only 56% and a licence for 58%.
  • Make each requirement a setting before making it a default. A check that refuses plain HTTP, an expired controller certificate or an unpinned image changes a running deployment the day it ships. Shipped as a setting, recorded when used, it can be turned on deployment by deployment.
  • Label every fact a model produced. The record already says which facts a model made. The CBOM a consumer reads has to say so too, or an agency cannot complete its AI inventory from it.
  • Check origin in the seam, not in a comment. A model of excluded origin is one configuration change away on any shared inference host. The seam that binds tiers to models is the place to refuse it.
  • Ask the customer four things first:
  • whether the system is a national security system, which brings CNSA 2.0 and NSA approval of the workbench's own cryptography (CNSSP 15)
  • the impact level
  • the identity provider and the claims it sends
  • the inventory template they file

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
Covered: the findings, the workbench at commit f3f2621; the table's "what holds" column, branch m8-now after milestone M8's first part (2026-11-06) and its review (2026-11-08), not yet merged or deployed; its configurations for the lab and for one box, read against SP 800-53 Rev. 5 controls at a moderate baseline, FIPS 140-3 through the repository's own CMVP snapshot, NIST IR 8547 (read first-hand), and OMB M-26-05, M-25-21, the FASCSA order and CISA's 2026 SBOM minimum elements through summaries that agree with one another.

Not covered:

  • no control was tested and no running service was probed
  • no penetration test, and no assessment under SP 800-53A
  • FedRAMP, which applies only to a hosted offering
  • Department of Defense impact levels and STIGs, which a defense customer makes mandatory

The findings with their evidence are kept privately with the plan; this note states what holds generally.

docs.text:

  • FIPS 140-3 and the CMVP validated modules list — what counts as validated cryptography; certificates 4985 and 5523 as recorded in the repository's snapshot.
  • NIST IR 8547 (final, 2026-10-27) — the 2030 deprecation and 2035 disallowance of every quantum-vulnerable family.
  • OMB M-26-05 (2026-01-23) — attestation rescinded; SBOM on request.
  • CISA, 2026 Minimum Elements for a Software Bill of Materials (2026-07-29) — what an SBOM must hold.
  • OMB M-25-21 — AI use-case inventory and minimum practices for high-impact AI.
  • DHS FASCSA exclusion and removal order 2026-01 — DeepSeek and products built on it.
  • Section 508 (36 CFR 1194) and WCAG — accessibility.
  • Related notes: what federal policy requires, and by when; what an auditable record contains; where models belong.

docs.title: What does "compatible" mean for one CBOM entry, and what cannot be told from the evidence?
The answer
docs.text:
A discovery phase ends with every entry in the inventory tagged against the policy that governs the system it belongs to: compatible, not compatible, or unknown, with the vendor's supportability noted where it is known. The workbench makes that tag a rule's judgement on the ledger, one per entry, and adds a fourth state the three leave out: outside the pack, for an entry the policy says nothing about. The four together cover every entry, so a count of compatible entries is never inflated by the ones nobody judged, and a count of unknowns is a measured gap rather than a silent pass.

The rule is compatibility/entry/1. It runs once per entry (one per finding fingerprint, so an asset two tools both saw is judged once), under the pack that governs the entry's service: OMB M-26-15 for an agency's information system, CNSA 2.0 for a service the owner marks a national security system. The judgement names the pack, the section, the algorithm's family, the basis in the pack's own words, and whether it is provisional. The CBOM carries it as the pqch:compatibility property, the inventory projection as three columns, and the CBOM page and the plan as four counts.

Four statuses, and the slice's 47 entries sorted into them under M-26-15; unknown is a count, not a pass.

docs.title: The mechanism
docs.text:
What the entry is judged on. The CBOM names every asset by a normalized algorithm name (X25519, RSA, ML-DSA-65, SHA-256) and a role: key establishment, signature, encryption, hash. A certificate is judged by the algorithm of the key it certifies, which is what signs with it. A key file is judged by its algorithm, looked up first in the signature table and then in key establishment. RSA seen in an encryption role is RSA key transport, judged as key establishment. A protocol version (TLS 1.2, TLS 1.3) is not an algorithm and is outside the pack; the TLS 1.3 obligation is a rule of its own (deadline/tls13/1, note 03).

How M-26-15 decides. The memo's pack carries two lists from its Appendix A: the quantum-resistant algorithms (§1: FIPS 203, 204, 205, and a hybrid whose classical and post-quantum parts must both be broken) and the quantum-vulnerable table (§2) with footnote 13, which asks that any asymmetric algorithm not definitively known to be quantum-resistant be treated as vulnerable. So an asymmetric entry is compatible when its family is on the resistant list and not compatible otherwise, footnote 13 included: Ed25519 and OpenSSH's sntrup761x25519 are not compatible under this pack because the memo does not name them resistant, not because anyone has broken them. The memo says nothing of AES or SHA-2, so a hash or a symmetric algorithm is outside the pack.

How CNSA 2.0 decides. The suite names one algorithm per function at one parameter set. Its pack lists them by function, and the rule compares names: ML-KEM-1024 is compatible for key establishment and ML-KEM-768 is not, so the hybrid X25519MLKEM768 that M-26-15 accepts is not compatible under CNSA 2.0, and ML-DSA-65 is not where ML-DSA-87 is required. SHA-256 is not compatible where the suite names SHA-384 and SHA-512. A hybrid whose post-quantum part is the suite's own (SecP384r1MLKEM1024) is unknown, a count and not a verdict: the FAQ says a hybrid is compliant only where NSA identified one, names one for IKEv2 and none for TLS, so the pack lists it as unsettled. LMS and XMSS are in the suite for signing firmware and software only, and SHA3-384 and SHA3-512 for a hardware's internal integrity checks only. The rule reads where the entry is: on the platform layer (a system's firmware, its Secure Boot databases, its management controller) those names are compatible; a SHA-3 hash on the wire or in a file is not compatible; and an LMS or XMSS key in a file is unknown, because the evidence does not say what the key signs. The pack was read first-hand from the FAQ (Ver. 2.2, October 2026) on 2026-11-09, after NSA's site had refused the download to the harness three times; every quote in it is checked against the FAQ's text by the loader, and no status is provisional. A pack that is not read first-hand says verified: false, and the rule copies that into each judgement's basis and into the page's heading until it is; when such a pack is corrected the next assessment of the same ledger gives the final statuses, and the ledger's events are not rewritten.

Why unknown is a state and not a default. The slice has one entry the rule cannot judge: a private key file the reader could not open, whose algorithm is therefore not identified. A rule that folded it into "compatible" would be reporting a pass with no evidence; one that folded it into "not compatible" would be scheduling work nobody can scope. Either way the number would be wrong. Kept apart, the unknowns are the manual gap-fill queue a discovery phase plans for: each is an entry to open by hand, a vendor to ask, or a reader to improve.

Why outside-the-pack is a state too. A pack is a document's words as data, and the rule may say only what the document says. M-26-15 governs asymmetric cryptography; it does not bless SHA-256 or AES-128, and a tag of "compatible" on them under that pack would be a claim the memo never makes. The fourth state says so. Under CNSA 2.0, which does name a hash and a symmetric algorithm, the same SHA-256 entry is not compatible, and the two packs' counts differ for that reason alone.

Vendor supportability. The tag a discovery phase wants beside each not-compatible entry is whether the vendor has a path: an update, a replacement, or no statement. That fact does not come from the wire or the host; it is a supplier's attestation, imported as graded evidence and joined to the entry by model and version. It is the next item in the plan (M10, supplier attestations), and until it lands the status stands alone.

docs.title: Worked example: the four-service slice
docs.text:
Status All entries In use What they are compatible 2 2 the hybrid X25519MLKEM768 on two listeners not compatible 39 34 RSA, ECDSA and DSA keys and certificates; X25519, the NIST curves and finite-field DH groups; Ed25519 and sntrup761x25519 by footnote 13 unknown 1 1 one private key file the reader could not open outside the pack 5 4 SHA-1 and SHA-256, which the memo's table does not name; the two SSH listeners' protocol entries

The five entries that are not in use and not compatible are the retired certificate and the keys behind it, which no listener serves (note 06 on in-use). They are in the inventory, tagged, and excluded from the migration's count by the in-use judgement, not by the compatibility one; a reader who wants them back in the count has both numbers.

Measured 2026-11-09 on x86_64 from the slice's recorded scanner output, at the commit that introduced the rule; tests/test_managed.py reproduces the counts.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
• The rule judges algorithm names and key algorithms. It does not judge key sizes against a pack's parameter conditions beyond what the name carries; the IR 8547 key-size check lives in the queue rule (note 07), and a 1024-bit RSA key is not compatible for the same reason a 4096-bit one is.
  • Under CNSA 2.0 an entry's application is read from its layer and nothing finer: a firmware entry counts as firmware signing or a hardware integrity check, and an LMS or XMSS key outside firmware is unknown until someone says what it signs. No LMS, XMSS or SHA-3 entry exists in the mini-agency, so the rule is tested on constructed entries, not measured on a scan.
  • A pack read first-hand (M-26-15, IR 8547) is checked quote by quote against its source text when it loads; the compatibility block adds no quote of its own and rests on the resistant and vulnerable lists the pack already carries.
  • The counts above are the slice's. The full mini-agency's counts appear on its CBOM page after the next scan; a run recorded before the rule existed shows no counts, since its ledger holds no such judgements and the projection invents none.

docs.title: What can a supplier's attestation stand in for in a CBOM, and what can it not?
The answer
docs.text:
A server's cryptography is not all reachable by a reader. A scan sees its listeners; its own files can be read; its firmware's Secure Boot databases and TPM banks can be read; its management controller answers Redfish with its firmware inventory, settings and certificates (note 20). What no reader reaches is what the supplier built in: the algorithm each firmware image is signed with, the cryptographic modules inside a controller's firmware and whether any is validated, and the route from the installed version to one that carries post-quantum algorithms, if there is one. Those are the facts a discovery phase is told to fill by hand, and they are the facts the risk register needs most: an update path or a replacement is the difference between a firmware release and a hardware refresh.

The workbench takes them from the supplier, as a statement, and keeps the statement in its place. A pqch.attestation/1 document names the supplier, the date, and for each product (vendor and model as the firmware reports them) each firmware by name and version with what signs it, what its listeners offer, its post-quantum roadmap and one of four supportability words: update, replace, end-of-life, no-statement. pqch attest records it on a run of its own as attestation.recorded events graded reported, keyed by the document's hash, so the same document twice is a no-op and a revised one a new claim with the old one still on the record. Nothing in it becomes a finding.

Then it is joined, not merged. For every closed system scan whose device is the product, the run records attestation/match/1: firmware by firmware, the version the server reported beside the version the statement is about, and whether they agree. The hosts page shows the supportability words per server, the server's CBOM page shows the statement beside the scan in one table, and the server's plan writes the supplier's answer onto the steps that wait for the supplier. The server's CBOM itself is unchanged: it is a projection of what the server showed, and the statement is another document about the same hardware.

Observed on the left, reported on the right, joined by model and version; the example's four outcomes counted; the right column never becomes a finding.

docs.title: The mechanism
docs.text:
What the statement can stand in for. Three things the readers cannot reach, and nothing else:

  1. What signs a firmware image. The platform verifies a signature before it runs the image; the algorithm and key size behind that signature are the supplier's, invisible from inside the running system. The statement names them per firmware and version.
  2. The modules inside a firmware. A controller's HTTPS and SSH are served by a library in its firmware; whether that library is a validated module (and under which CMVP certificate) is a supplier's fact. The statement lists the modules and their certificate numbers, or null where none.
  3. The route forward. Whether the installed firmware will receive a post-quantum signing root, an ML-KEM hybrid in its listeners, or nothing; in which version and by when. The statement carries the algorithms, the version, a date or null, and the supportability word.

What it cannot stand in for. Anything the server itself shows. The installed firmware version is the server's to report, and the statement is matched to it, never substituted for it: a statement about version 2.4.0 joined to a server at 2.3.1 is shown as a disagreement, with both numbers, and the plan's supplier step says so in words ("version 2.4.0, not the installed 2.3.1"). What a listener accepts on the wire is measured by the targeted scan; the statement's list of what the controller offers is shown beside it and settles nothing when they differ. Which certificates the Secure Boot databases hold is read from the firmware's variables; the statement's chain is a claim about what ships, not about what is on this board after years of updates. A statement marked illustrative: true stands in for nothing at all: every page that shows it says it is a worked example and not the supplier's own.

Why reported is a grade and not a source. The ledger already distinguishes who observed a finding (the tool, its version, the raw output's hash). A statement differs in kind: the workbench did not watch it being made and cannot reproduce it. It is therefore graded reported and kept on a run of its own, where a reader can verify the chain, read the document, and see the hash that ties each event to it. When the estate projection over many runs lands (M9), the grade is what decides precedence: observed on the wire, observed on the host, parsed from a file, reported in a document, in that order, and never by vendor or tool. Until then the join is at the pages, and the server's CBOM stays a pure function of the server's run.

Why the join is by model and version and nothing finer. A supplier states facts per model and firmware version, because that is the unit it ships and signs. A service tag or serial would join to one server, but the statement is not about one server, and the recording export replaces such identifiers in any case. Model and vendor are compared case-insensitively with whitespace collapsed, because a firmware's product_name and a controller's Model do not always agree on either; firmware names likewise. A version of any covers every version of that firmware on that model, for a statement that is about the product line rather than a release.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
The repository's example statement (agency/attestations/example-supplier.yaml, an invented supplier and product, marked illustrative) names three firmware on one model: a BIOS at 2.4.0 signed with RSA-3072 and SHA-256, with an LMS and ML-DSA-87 signing root planned for 3.0.0 in 2028 and supportability update; a management controller at any version offering X25519 and the NIST curves, with an ML-KEM hybrid on the roadmap and no date; and a network adapter signed with RSA-2048 and no-statement. Joined to a server reporting a BIOS at 2.3.1, the controller at 7.1.0 and an NVMe drive:

Firmware The server reports The statement is about Outcome BIOS 2.3.1 2.4.0 another version: shown, not resolved the controller 7.1.0 any the same: the statement applies the network adapter not reported any named but not reported the NVMe drive 1.2 not named reported but not named: a gap for the supplier

The plan's supplier step for the controller then reads, after its own reason, "The supplier's statement (…, illustrative; reported, not observed) says of the installed version: supportability update; X25519MLKEM768 in version 8.0.0, no date given". The step is still the plan's; the supplier's words are attached to it, labelled, and the step's due date does not move for them.

Measured 2026-11-09 in tests/test_attest.py; the example is not a real vendor's statement and the lab's own server has none recorded.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
• The format is this project's; a supplier's real statement will arrive as a PDF or a spreadsheet and be transcribed into it, and the transcription is the operator's act, recorded as the human actor on the event.
  • Supportability is the supplier's word, not a judgement: update means the supplier says an update exists or is planned, not that it has shipped or that the operator can install it.
  • The join reads the latest matching statement. Two suppliers' statements about one model (an OEM's and a component maker's) are not yet combined; M9's conflict rules are where that belongs.
  • The statement does not yet reach the CBOM entry's compatibility status (note 22); it will when the estate projection can carry a reported claim beside an observed one.

docs.title: What does a later phase need from a discovery phase, field by field, and where does each field come from?
The answer
docs.text:
A discovery phase does not deploy anything. It ends by handing the phases that do a plan they can be scoped and costed from. The workbench writes that hand-off as a register: one row per plan step, grouped into the buckets the later phases are organised by, with the facts a planner needs beside each step and the CBOM entries the step moves named by fingerprint, so every row can be traced back to the record. Each column comes from one of three places, and the register says which: the owner (typed in, labelled supplied, never computed), the rules (computed from the CBOM and the policy packs, with the event behind each), or the plan itself (the step, its bucket, its order).

The register is available three ways: on the plan page as the "handed to the next phase" section, as a live download from the run (register.csv, register.json), and written beside the run's CBOMs by pqch plan export, so it travels with the record.

Every column of the register comes from the owner, the rules or the plan, and the register says which; the cost is the owner's number with its basis.

docs.title: The mechanism
docs.text:
The owner's facts. No scan can discover which system of record a service belongs to, which interface it serves, which mission thread stops when it does, what classification its enclave carries, what the vendor has said, or what a fix would cost. These are typed in by the system owner in the context file, recorded on the ledger as supplied links with a human actor and the file's hash as evidence, and carried on the service's component with every other supplied fact under pqch:supplied (note 06 on supplied links; the scorer never counts one as coverage). The six facts added for an engagement are system, interface, mission_thread, classification (one of unclassified, cui, confidential, secret, top-secret), vendor_path and cost_to_fix. A cost is a mapping of amount, currency and basis, and the context file refuses a bare number: a figure with no basis is a figure nobody can check.

The rules' columns. Priority and its criteria come from the memo's rule over the owner's impact, high-value and lifetime facts (note 07); the deadline and the document that set it from the queue rule; whether the step is blocked on its supplier from the capability snapshot; the year the data stays sensitive through from the lifetime and the assessment date. Each is an event on the ledger, and the plan page shows the event.

The plan's columns. The step, its title and why, its wave and due date, its state (ready, waiting, done) and what it waits for, the CBOM entries it moves by fingerprint, and its bucket.

The buckets. Later phases are scoped by kind of work rather than by service: identity, PKI and signing (certificate authorities and what they issue, keys, firmware-signing roots and the boot chain); infrastructure and data protection (key exchange on the wire, the controller's settings, what the supplier ships for them); applications and mission systems (software that cannot take post-quantum cryptography and must be replaced or upgraded). A fourth bucket, inventory, holds the reads the discovery itself still owes (a path an unprivileged scan could not open). The mapping from a step to a bucket is a pack, policy/buckets.yaml, versioned, by the step's id prefix first and its kind second; a step no row places is reported as unplaced and counted, never hidden. On the slice none is.

The cost. The register sums the owner's cost_to_fix per currency, once per service, and reports how many services carry no number. It is the owner's arithmetic, not an estimate: the sum's basis says so, and each addend's basis travels in its own column. Where a planner wants a model of cost, that model sits outside the register and cites it.

docs.title: Worked example: the four-service slice
docs.text:
Bucket Steps on the slice What they are Identity, PKI and signing the CA's new root and the reissues under it; retiring the unserved certificate the internal CA that issued the slice's certificates, and the leaves Infrastructure and data protection offering and then requiring the ML-KEM hybrid on each listener; TLS 1.3 where it is missing the key-exchange lane of each service Applications and mission systems replacing the SFTP appliance whose software lists no post-quantum algorithm the one step nothing configurable can move; its row carries the owner's vendor path and a planted cost of 40,000 USD with its basis

One service costed, three not; the register says so rather than filling the blanks. Measured 2026-11-09 in tests/test_register.py.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
• The columns are this project's reading of what a later phase needs. A customer's register will have its own; the mechanism is a projection, so a different column list is a different projection over the same ledger, as the inventory is (note 01).
  • The buckets' names follow the usual three-way split of post-quantum work; a programme with a different split edits the pack and the plan regroups.
  • The register is as current as the plan: computed from the scan and the change runs since when served live, and frozen at its write time when exported beside the run. Both say which.
  • The vendor's path on a service is the owner's note. A supplier's statement about hardware is a different thing, recorded as evidence of its own grade (note 23).

docs.title: How much of an estate's cryptography can a tool reach, by asset class, and how is the rest kept from disappearing into a coverage figure?
The answer
docs.text:
No tool reaches all of it, and every discovery phase knows this: a phase that scopes one plans for manual gap-fill of what the tools cannot see, by asset class. The question is what happens to those gaps between the scan and the person. In most tools they become a percentage, and a percentage is a place for a gap to hide. The workbench writes each gap down instead. At the end of a run's rules, gap/record/1 appends one gap.recorded event per gap, with the kind, the asset class, the exact subject, the reason in words, and what would fill it. The CBOM page lists them as a queue; pqch gap list prints them; a person closes one with pqch gap fill, which records a gap.filled event citing the evidence brought (a run on this deployment and an event on it, both checked to exist) and the basis in words. Coverage per asset class is then a count, reached against reached plus open gaps, and it moves only when a gap is recorded or filled.

Gaps as slips under each asset class, not as a percentage; one filled by evidence a person brought, and the fill holds on the next scan.

docs.title: The mechanism
docs.text:
The kinds. The rule knows nine kinds of gap, each with the class it falls in and what fills it:

Kind Class Why it is a gap What fills it key file not opened key files the reader found a key or keystore it could not open (permissions, encryption) a privileged read-only read, or the owner's statement of the key's algorithm and size algorithm unidentified entries an entry names no algorithm any table places the material opened by a reader that can name it, or the owner's statement listener not scanned listeners the scope names it and no job ran against it a scan that reaches it scan failed listeners every job on it ended other than ok the job run again once its cause is removed no owner's facts services the scope names the service and nobody supplied its facts the system owner's facts in the context file unreadable path key files a path the scan's user could not read on a server a privileged read-only read controller certificate key unknown controller the controller reports the certificate's issuer and dates and not its key the supplier's statement of the algorithms behind the controller's identities no supplier's statement firmware no attestation names the model the supplier's attestation (pqch attest, note 23) firmware not attested firmware the server reports a firmware the statement does not name the statement extended to it

Why an event and not a count. A gap recorded as an event has a subject a person can act on and an id that persists. Its id is the hash of its kind and subject, not of the run, so the same unread key on the next scan is the same gap; a fill recorded against it holds. Each recorded gap names the finding or scan event it rests on in its inputs, so the queue is traceable like every other projection. A run on which the rule found nothing still carries the rule's own assessment event with zero counts, so a page can tell "no gaps" from "nobody looked".

Why filling needs evidence. pqch gap fill refuses a gap nobody recorded, a run that is not on this deployment, and an event that is not on the run it names. What it records is a person's judgement that the cited evidence fills the gap, with their name and basis; it does not change the inventory, which is a projection of the evidence itself. If the evidence is a supplier's statement, the statement is already on the ledger as reported evidence; if it is a later scan that read the file, that scan's finding is in the CBOM. The fill is the record that someone looked and closed the loop.

Why coverage is counted from the queue. For each class the page shows reached against reached plus open gaps. Listeners: endpoints in the scope with a successful scan against those without. Entries: fingerprints judged against those whose algorithm is unidentified. Key files: files read against paths unreadable and keys not opened. Services: those with supplied facts against those without. Firmware: reported firmware the supplier has named against those it has not; with no statement at all, none is reached. Controller: certificates with a known key against those without. A class with nothing to count is not shown. The figure cannot be improved by a scan that sees less; it can only rise when a gap is recorded as filled or a later scan reaches what the earlier one did not.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
The four-service slice records one gap: a private key file whose algorithm no reader identified, an entry gap; its four listeners and four services are all reached. Filled by citing an attestation run (as the owner's statement of the key would be), the entries class reads 100 percent and the gap is listed as filled with the person's name, the run cited and the basis. A later scan of the same estate records the same id, so the fill stands.

A synthetic server read whole, with one unreadable path and no supplier's statement, records three: the path, the controller's listener no job reached, and the missing statement, which counts the three reported firmware as zero of three reached. With the example statement recorded, a fresh read of the same server records one gap in that class, the drive the statement does not name, and the class reads two of three.

Measured 2026-11-09 in tests/test_gaps.py. The full mini-agency's and the lab's numbers appear on their CBOM pages after their next scan; a run assessed before the rule existed says so rather than showing zero.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
• The nine kinds are what the workbench's own evidence can tell it is missing. A gap it cannot detect (a device not in the scope at all) is a scope question, not a queue entry; the scope's authorization and the capture's summary are where that is answered.
  • Coverage per class is this project's definition and is stated on the page. It is not a statement about the estate's cryptography as a whole, only about what the scope asked for and what was reached.
  • The fill is a person's record and carries their name; the workbench does not judge whether the evidence suffices, it records that someone did.

docs.title: What does a discovery-and-planning phase ask of a CBOM tool, and what does this one answer, measured?
The answer
docs.text:
The phase an organisation starts its post-quantum work with is not a migration. It is a discovery and a plan: find every piece of cryptography in scope, record it in a cryptography bill of materials, decide what is not compatible with the policy that governs the system, map each such item to its system, interface, mission thread and owner, build a risk register, and hand the phases that deploy a schedule and a cost. It deploys nothing. Its deliverables are the CBOM, the compatibility assessment, the dependency map, the register and the plan; its gaps are what no tool could see, filled by hand; its hardware half is the supplier's to attest.

Ten asks follow from that, and the table below says what the workbench answers for each, measured on the mini-agency on 2026-11-09, and where the answer stops. The workbench is a research project and an exploration, not a product (BRIEF); what it offers such a phase is the method, the record and the instruments, each one checkable.

What the phase asks What the workbench answers Measured on the mini-agency Where it stops Where the CBOM lives and who maintains it A signed, append-only ledger is the record; the CBOM is a projection rebuilt from it; approvals, resolutions and fills are events on it (note 12) 897 events, 313 components, same ledger same document one deployment, one owner's ledger; roles by setting (ADR-0008) Discovery across the asset classes Wire, host, code and platform readers; the SBOM beside them; any tool's CBOM imported and scored (note 15) 35 of 35 keyed wire items; 8 images' SBOMs, 43 crypto libraries, 13 in use HSMs and crypto modules by attestation only; the code layer one repository Every entry tagged against the governing policy compatibility/entry/1: compatible, not compatible, unknown, outside the pack, provisional under a pack not read first-hand (note 22) 8 / 183 / 11 / 19; in use 8 / 173 / 11 / 17 An entry's application is read from its layer only (firmware or not) Vendor supportability on the hardware A supplier's attestation as reported evidence, joined by model and firmware version, never a finding; modules looked up in the CMVP snapshot (note 23) an illustrative statement; the lab's server has none recorded no real supplier's statement yet The dependency map The plan's shared dependencies: the certificate authority, the library build, the shared key, the client trust anchor (note 17) 25 steps, 4 shared dependencies the lab's and a server's plans have their own rules System, interface, mission thread, owner, classification per item Owner-supplied facts, labelled supplied, on the service component and every register row (note 24) 8 services with all four; none invented typed in; the owner's inventory is the source A risk register with impact, exposure, vendor path and cost The register: priority and its criteria, deadline and what set it, blocked on the supplier, the vendor's path and the cost as the owner's words, summed once per service 25 rows; docs.title: The mechanism, in one pass through the pages
docs.text:
A reader shown the workbench follows the phase's own order:

  1. The test agency, so the answer key is on the table before the tool is: eight services, every weakness planted, decoys in every layer.
  2. Inside the CBOM: the document's counts, then every entry tagged under its pack with unknown counted apart; the claims kept where two tools described one entry; the gap queue with coverage per class; one entry opened field by field with the evidence behind each field, the referenced signature algorithm and public key among them; the same record projected as an inventory.
  3. The plan: the steps, the shared dependencies drawn, what comes first and why, and at the end the hand-off: the three buckets and the register to download.
  4. Hosts, for the hardware half: a server read whole, the supplier's statement beside what the server showed, the modules against the CMVP snapshot, and the firmware the statement does not name as gaps.
  5. Imports: a vendor's CBOM of the same estate scored against the key, and the scan and its imports projected as one document with every disagreement shown.
  6. The ledger, last: the events behind every number above, hash-chained and signed, with the record page listing each document and its hash.

The waits, the numbers and the engines are labelled as the stage labels them; nothing in the pass is a model's judgement of whether a thing worked.

docs.title: What this changed about the claim
docs.text: The BRIEF's claim is about taking the mini-agency from Opaque to Agile with a CBOM built from evidence and verified by re-scan, with the models' roles measured. A discovery-and-planning phase stops before Agile: it asks for the Structured and Managed rungs done thoroughly and handed over, and it asks three things the claim did not name: that every entry be judged under a policy with the unknowns kept apart, that what no tool could see be written down rather than averaged away, and that the supplier's part of the inventory be taken in as evidence of its own grade. All three are now rules on the ledger, and each is measured above. The claim's own clauses are untouched by them: the score, the baselines, the verifier and the roles table read the same.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
• The numbers are the mini-agency's, a planted estate with an answer key. The lab's own estate and its server are read the same way; their numbers are the owner's and stay off the public copy.
  • Four answers are complete in mechanism and waiting on an outside party for their proof: a real supplier's statement, a commercial engine to re-upload into, and a second real server for the SSH route. The CNSA 2.0 primary documents were read on 2026-11-09 and the pack rewritten from them.
  • The workbench is not the tool such a phase would accredit; it is the method and the record shown working, with every number traceable to an event. The gaps between that and an accreditation are the federal readiness rows in the plan, three of which became settings on 2026-11-09 (marking, retention, roles and separation of duties).
